cards.title: P versus PSPACE
cards.formal: Does every language decidable by a deterministic Turing machine using polynomial working space have a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm? Equivalently, do there exist a machine A and constants C,k such that A decides truth of every closed quantified Boolean formula of encoded length n in at most $C(n+1)^k$ steps?
cards.definitions: P consists of languages decided by one deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed polynomial worst-case time bound. PSPACE consists of languages decided by one deterministic Turing machine which halts on every input and visits at most C(n+1)^k work-tape cells, for some constants C,k, on inputs of length n. The input is read-only and is not charged as work space; a fixed finite tape alphabet is used. PSPACE imposes no polynomial time bound. A closed quantified Boolean formula has the form Q₁x₁⋯Qₘxₘ φ(x₁,…,xₘ), where each Qᵢ is ∃ or ∀, quantified variables are distinct, and φ is an explicitly encoded Boolean formula using AND, OR, and NOT, with no free variables. Every quantifier ranges over {0,1}. The number of quantifiers and their alternations may grow with n; the input is not restricted to a fixed number of blocks. Use any standard explicit binary encoding, reject malformed inputs, and count its full bit length n. Truth means the usual nested Boolean quantifier semantics. This language, TQBF, is PSPACE-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions. No oracle, advice, randomization, or promise is allowed. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove P=PSPACE or P≠PSPACE. The first outcome asserts a deterministic polynomial-time decision procedure for every polynomial-space language; the second asserts a polynomial-space language with no deterministic polynomial-time decision procedure.
cards.why: This asks whether reusing a feasible amount of memory can provide computational power beyond feasible running time. It is a central unresolved separation even when the allowed language class is enlarged from NP to all of PSPACE, and it organizes the complexity of quantified reasoning, games, and verification.

importance.reason: A defining question about the relationship between the two basic computational resources, time and working memory. It is a top-priority foundational class separation.

progress.text: Quantified Boolean formulas provide a PSPACE-complete target. Chandra, Kozen, and Stockmeyer characterize deterministic polynomial space as alternating polynomial time.
Shamir proves IP=PSPACE, giving an interactive-proof characterization without resolving deterministic polynomial-time computation.
Williams proves the O(sqrt(t log t)) space simulation of time-t multitape machines, improving the decades-old O(t/log t) bound. It yields fixed-exponent time lower bounds for linear-space languages.
Williams’ MFCS invited survey discusses this simulation and further space-complexity developments. It supplies no separation of the unions P and PSPACE.

context_blocks.text: Time measures the total number of computation steps; space measures how much information the machine retains at once. Space can be reused. For example, a machine can evaluate a quantified formula by recursively exploring possible choices and reusing its work area when it returns from a branch. The resulting computation may inspect exponentially many choices while keeping only a polynomial amount of information.

Alternating quantifiers express a finite game of choices: existential moves try to make the final formula true, and universal moves challenge them. For example, ∀x∃y (y=x) is true because y may depend on x, whereas ∃y∀x (y=x) is false. Both variables range over {0,1}. A winning strategy for a longer formula can have exponentially many branches even though each play has polynomial length. Polynomial-time alternation captures exactly PSPACE.

The inclusion P⊆PSPACE is immediate, but its strictness is unknown. P≠NP would imply P≠PSPACE because NP⊆PSPACE. A proof of P=NP, however, would collapse the polynomial hierarchy without automatically giving a polynomial-time algorithm for formulas with an unbounded number of quantifier alternations. This separates the present question from merely solving satisfiability.

The theorem IP=PSPACE characterizes the same space class through interaction: a polynomial-time randomized verifier can check claims from an unbounded prover using a bounded-error interactive protocol. The prover’s assistance is a resource. Removing the prover to obtain an ordinary deterministic polynomial-time algorithm is not a consequence of that characterization.

Williams’ time-to-space simulation gives a concrete advance in the comparison of these resources. For time bounds t(n)≥n, a time-t multitape computation can be simulated in O(√(t log t)) working space. A consequence is that some linear-space languages require time n^(2−ε) for every ε>0. The lower-bound exponent remains bounded: the result does not exhibit a polynomial-space language outside every polynomial time bound.

cards.title: L versus P
cards.formal: Is L=P? Equivalently, does the Circuit Value Problem have a deterministic algorithm that always halts and uses O(log(n+2)) bits of working memory on an input of binary encoding length n?
cards.definitions: L consists of total decision languages recognized by a fixed deterministic Turing machine with a read-only input tape and a fixed finite number of initially blank read/write work tapes over fixed finite alphabets. The input can be revisited freely; all visited work-tape cells count toward space, but the read-only input itself does not. For each language there must be a constant C such that every n-bit input uses at most C log₂(n+2) work bits and the machine halts. Acceptance is a final state, not a long output tape usable as memory. A halting machine in this model has only polynomially many possible configurations on a fixed input, so its time is automatically polynomial. P is the class of languages decided by uniform deterministic Turing machines in O((n+2)ᶜ) time for some fixed c. Circuit Value receives an explicit topologically ordered DAG of AND, OR, and NOT gates, Boolean input values, and one designated output gate, and asks whether its value is 1. The entire gate and input encoding counts toward n; malformed encodings are rejected. There are no random bits, oracle, advice, auxiliary catalytic tape, or restrictions on circuit depth. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove L=P or L≠P in the read-only-input model defined here. Equality means that every polynomial-time decision language admits a halting deterministic logarithmic-space machine; inequality means that at least one such language admits none.
cards.why: This is a fundamental question about how much memory efficient computation needs. It asks whether all of polynomial-time reasoning can be reorganized around logarithmic working storage, and connects circuit evaluation, graph reachability, recomputation, and the structure of space-bounded complexity.

importance.reason: A canonical unresolved boundary between time and memory, asking whether any polynomial-time decision problem intrinsically needs more than logarithmic workspace.

progress.text: Ladner’s logspace completeness theorem for Circuit Value supplies a universal P-complete problem for the question.
Reingold proves undirected connectivity is in L. This resolves a major special case of low-memory graph computation without handling all directed reachability or P-complete problems.
Williams obtains the O(√(t log t)) deterministic space simulation and square-root-type circuit-evaluation space bounds. These remain far above logarithmic space in the general case.
Blais’s logarithmic-space notes explicitly state that strictness between these basic classes remains unknown and fix the read-only-input convention needed to formulate the question.

cards.status_note: The Winter 2026 logarithmic-space notes explicitly leave the basic containments unresolved. A primary-source and later-result search on 11 September 2026 found no resolution of L versus P. The square-root-space simulation remains above logarithmic space for general polynomial-time computations.

context_blocks.text: A polynomial-time algorithm may keep a large table of intermediate results. A logarithmic-space algorithm has room for a fixed number of indices into its input: one position among n symbols needs about log₂ n bits. It can revisit the read-only input and recompute intermediate values, but it cannot retain an arbitrary n-bit table. The question asks whether this severe memory restriction still permits every polynomial-time decision task.

Circuit Value is a concrete complete problem for P under logarithmic-space reductions. Evaluating gates in topological order uses polynomial time and readily stores their values. An alternative may recompute gate values, but shared dependencies make naive recursive expansion expensive in both stack space and repeated work. Completeness says that a logarithmic-space solution to this one task would extend to all polynomial-time decision problems.

Logarithmic workspace already forces polynomial time for a halting deterministic machine: revisiting the same full configuration would produce an infinite loop. Consequently the question does not grant unlimited superpolynomial recomputation while retaining membership in L. The polynomial time exponent can nevertheless depend on the machine, so lower bounds for one fixed time budget are insufficient.

L⊆NL⊆P, where NL allows nondeterministic logarithmic-space computation. A proof that L≠NL would therefore separate L from P, but L=NL would not itself settle L=P. Reingold resolves undirected reachability in logarithmic space; directed reachability remains a separate NL-complete target, and Circuit Value represents the potentially larger class P.

Recent time-to-space simulation substantially improves general upper bounds without reaching logarithmic space. Williams simulates time t in O(√(t log t)) space and obtains an analogous square-root-type space bound for Boolean circuit evaluation. With polynomial t, the guarantee is still polynomial space. This advances the tradeoff while leaving the much smaller O(log n) target unresolved.

cards.title: Nonuniform TC⁰ versus NC¹
cards.formal: Is TC⁰⊊NC¹ for the nonuniform circuit classes defined below? Equivalently, does there exist a Boolean function family f=(f_n:{0,1}^n→{0,1}) in NC¹ such that for every fixed depth d≥1, exponent k≥1, and constant M≥1, there is an n for which every depth-at-most-d majority circuit computing f_n exactly has size greater than M(n+1)^k?
cards.definitions: A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with input nodes x_1,…,x_n, optional constants 0,1, and one output. Depth is the maximum number of gates on an input-to-output path. Size is the number of gates plus the number of wires; if an input is repeated at a gate, each occurrence counts as a wire. A majority circuit has AND and OR gates of arbitrary positive fan-in, NOT gates of fan-in one, and MAJ gates of arbitrary positive fan-in m, with output 1 exactly when strictly more than m/2 inputs equal 1. TC⁰ consists of all families with such circuits of size M(n+1)^k and depth at most d for every n, for some constants M,k,d depending on the family. NC¹ consists of families with circuits over AND, OR, NOT, with fan-in at most two (one for NOT), size M(n+1)^k, and depth at most b log_2(n+1), for fixed M,k,b. Circuits may share intermediate gates. Both classes are nonuniform: an arbitrary separate circuit may be chosen for each input length, without any requirement to compute its description. The output must be correct on every input; no randomness, approximation, promise, or distributional error is allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove TC⁰⊊NC¹ or TC⁰=NC¹ for the nonuniform families defined here. Strictness requires a single NC¹ family with no polynomial-size constant-depth majority-circuit family; equality requires that every NC¹ family admit such a family.
cards.why: One of the central small-circuit questions: whether a constant number of counting layers can perform every logarithmic-depth Boolean computation. A resolution would clarify the power of threshold circuits, finite-group computation, and the role of sequential dependence in parallel computation.

importance.reason: A flagship unresolved containment between basic circuit classes, with explicit complete problems and connections to arithmetic, algebraic automata theory, and lower-bound amplification.

progress.text: Hesse, Allender, and Barrington place division and iterated multiplication in DLOGTIME-uniform TC⁰, demonstrating the arithmetic power already available at constant depth.
Chen and Tell show how improvements in the depth dependence of superlinear wire lower bounds for certain NC¹-complete problems would yield superpolynomial TC⁰ lower bounds.
Dawar and Evans characterize uniform NC¹ with typed monoids and unary generalized quantifiers. The containment comparison remains open.
Chen, Tal, and Wang prove superquadratic gate lower bounds for depth-two weighted threshold circuits for an E^NP function; the result does not supply an NC¹ separation against every constant depth.

cards.status_note: The source and subsequent-work checks on 11 September 2026 found no equality or separation of these nonuniform classes. The 2026 depth-two result concerns a function in E^NP and polynomial circuit size; the typed-monoid result concerns uniform classes. These conclusions have different quantifiers and models from the target.

context_blocks.text: The two models trade different resources. A majority gate can aggregate arbitrarily many bits in one step, whereas a binary Boolean gate sees only two. NC¹ permits logarithmically many layers of binary computation. A majority of polynomially many bits can itself be computed by a polynomial-size logarithmic-depth Boolean circuit, so a constant number of majority layers gives TC⁰⊆NC¹. The open issue is whether counting in a fixed number of layers can also replace every logarithmic-depth computation.

Arithmetic tasks are an instructive warning against judging depth from familiar sequential algorithms. Hesse, Allender, and Barrington prove that integer division and iterated multiplication have even DLOGTIME-uniform TC⁰ circuits. A binary long-division procedure takes many dependent steps, but that procedure does not establish a lower bound on all circuits for division. These arithmetic problems therefore cannot serve as the missing separation.

There are concrete complete problems on the NC¹ side. Evaluating a Boolean formula, and evaluating a product of elements of the fixed permutation group S_5, capture NC¹ under very simple reductions. S_5 consists of the 120 permutations of five objects, with permutation composition as its operation. Chen and Tell study these complete problems in their lower-bound amplification results.

Chen and Tell prove a conditional amplification theorem connecting certain mildly superlinear wire lower bounds to a separation of the full classes. Its hypothesis imposes a specific quantitative dependence on circuit depth. Thus a lower bound proved only at one fixed depth, or with an insufficient exponent at growing constant depths, is a different statement from their theorem’s hypothesis and from the conjecture here.

Dawar and Evans give an algebraic characterization of uniform NC¹ using typed monoids in FSTTCS 2025, extending earlier work on uniform TC⁰. Typed monoids allow infinite algebraic structures while restricting recognition through finitely many types. This supplies another mathematical language in which to compare the classes. Their theorem is a characterization, not a separation, and its uniform scope must be kept distinct from this card’s formulation.

Chen, Tal, and Wang’s 2026 preprint proves n^(2.5−ε) gate lower bounds for depth-two linear-threshold circuits computing a function in E^NP. Here E^NP allows deterministic time 2^{O(n)} with an NP oracle. A linear-threshold gate tests a weighted sum, while this card fixes unweighted majority gates. More decisively, the result treats one depth, a polynomial size bound, and a hard function not shown to belong to NC¹. The target here concerns an NC¹ family against every fixed depth and every polynomial size bound.

cards.title: Berman–Hartmanis conjecture
cards.formal: For every pair of languages A,B⊆{0,1}* that are NP-complete under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, does there exist a bijection f:{0,1}*→{0,1}* such that f and f⁻¹ are computable in deterministic polynomial time and, for every string x, x∈A if and only if f(x)∈B?
cards.definitions: A language is a set of finite binary strings, including a specified membership decision for every string; malformed encodings are therefore part of the language convention. NP consists of languages L for which x∈L exactly when some witness of length polynomial in |x| is accepted by a deterministic polynomial-time verifier. A many-one reduction from L to A is a total deterministic polynomial-time function g with x∈L iff g(x)∈A. A is NP-complete if A∈NP and every L∈NP reduces to A in this sense. The desired f is a permutation of all finite binary strings, taking members to members and nonmembers to nonmembers. Its running time is polynomial in its input length, and its inverse has a polynomial bound in the inverse input length. The algorithms and polynomial bounds may depend on the fixed pair A,B, but not on the particular input string. No advice, oracle, randomness or length-preservation requirement is allowed. This is the unconditional conjecture; P≠NP is not an assumption.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that every pair of polynomial-time many-one NP-complete languages is polynomial-time isomorphic, or prove that some pair has no bijection with both directions computable in polynomial time. The statement is unconditional: P≠NP is not an added hypothesis.
cards.why: A fundamental test of what NP-completeness means beyond mutual reducibility: does it impose one efficiently reversible structure on all complete decision problems? It links padding, cryptographic inversion, uniformity and the limitations of relativizing methods.

importance.reason: A defining structural-complexity conjecture about the entire NP-complete degree, stronger than P≠NP and supported by substantial restricted-model theorems and oracle barriers.

progress.text: Berman–Hartmanis prove isomorphism for paddable complete languages and formulate the unrestricted conjecture.

context_blocks.text: NP-completeness normally identifies problems by their ability to simulate one another. A reduction may map many distinct instances to the same target instance, leave most target strings unused, and erase information that would be needed to reconstruct its input. The isomorphism conjecture asks for a much more rigid relationship: an efficiently reversible relabelling of the entire instance space. Its claim includes every artificially constructed NP-complete language, not only the familiar examples used in applications.

The distinction is visible in the quantifiers. Choosing one clever reduction from SAT to another problem and discovering that it is many-to-one says nothing decisive about whether some other reduction could be a bijection. Conversely, an abstract bijection between two infinite sets is not enough: it might take exponential time to compute or invert. The conjecture requires both computations to be efficient, while allowing a polynomial change in the lengths of instances.

Padding supplies the strongest classical evidence. A paddable language has an efficient injective way to append arbitrary recoverable auxiliary information without changing the answer. For satisfiability, fresh variables and a suitably delimited formula encoding can carry extra bits while preserving whether the original formula has a satisfying assignment. Berman and Hartmanis used padding to show that the standard NP-complete examples known at the time are polynomial-time isomorphic. The unresolved step is proving that arbitrary complete languages possess enough recoverable structure.

The conjecture implies P≠NP, but its negation does not automatically imply P≠NP. To see the first point, suppose P=NP. Then the nontrivial languages {0} and 0{0,1}* would both be NP-complete: decide the source problem and output a fixed yes string or no string. Yet a bijection preserving membership cannot map a one-element yes-set onto an infinite yes-set. This elementary obstruction also explains why the unconditional conjecture must be distinguished from its version conditional on P≠NP.

The connection with one-way functions depends on more than difficulty inverting a particular reduction. An NP-complete language can have many reductions from SAT, and invertibility of one map does not determine whether a different efficient isomorphism exists. The Hartmanis problem column distinguishes one-way functions, scrambling functions and easy-cylinder hypotheses; these additional structural conditions are not interchangeable.

Oracle results go in both directions. Kurtz, Mahaney and Royer construct random-oracle counterexamples using scrambling functions. Fenner, Fortnow and Kurtz construct a different oracle setting in which the conjecture holds. These are results about relativized computation, where the algorithms can query a supplied set. They do not settle the ordinary conjecture, but they show that an argument valid uniformly across all such oracle settings cannot choose its truth value.

Restricting the completeness reductions can produce affirmative theorems. Agrawal, Allender and Rudich prove an isomorphism theorem for sets complete under nonuniform AC⁰ reductions, with nonuniform depth-three AC⁰ circuits computing the isomorphisms and their inverses. Here AC⁰ means polynomial-size Boolean circuits of constant depth with unbounded-fan-in AND and OR gates and negations. Both the restricted completeness hypothesis and the availability of nonuniform circuits matter; dropping them would be a stronger statement.

Agrawal and Watanabe further relate structural assumptions about one-way functions to nonuniform isomorphisms. Under their stated hypotheses they obtain P/poly isomorphisms, permitting polynomial advice that depends on input length. This does not provide the uniform polynomial-time algorithms demanded here. The broad question remains whether NP-completeness itself forces reversible structure, or whether some complete languages have an intrinsically different organization of their yes and no instances.

Nareddy and Mishra’s 2025 preprint studies recovery of Boolean truth tables after random corruptions. It states the Berman–Hartmanis conjecture explicitly and derives, conditionally on it, recovery guarantees for every NP-complete language after partitioning instances by the length of their image under an isomorphism. This is an application of the conjecture as a hypothesis, not a proof of it.

cards.title: Strictness of the polynomial hierarchy
cards.formal: Is $\Sigma_k^{\mathrm P}\subsetneq\Sigma_{k+1}^{\mathrm P}$ for every integer k≥0? Here Σ₀^P=P, and Σₖ^P for k≥1 consists of languages definable by k alternating blocks of polynomially bounded Boolean quantifiers, beginning existentially, followed by a deterministic polynomial-time predicate.
cards.definitions: A language L is in Σₖ^P if there exist a polynomial p and a deterministic polynomial-time predicate R such that, for every binary input x, $x\in L\iff\exists y_1\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}\ \forall y_2\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}\cdots Q_k y_k\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}:R(x,y_1,\ldots,y_k)=1$, where Qₖ is existential for odd k and universal for even k. Each yᵢ is an entire string, so k counts quantifier blocks, not individual bits. The predicate is polynomial-time in the combined input length. k is fixed for a class membership claim and cannot grow with |x|; p and R may depend on k and L. Let Πₖ^P consist of complements of Σₖ^P languages, and let PH=⋃ₖ≥0Σₖ^P. In particular Σ₁^P=NP and Π₁^P=coNP. These are uniform, unrelativized classes of total decision languages. Strictness at level k means that some language in Σₖ₊₁^P is absent from Σₖ^P. The separating language may depend on k. All classes use ordinary Turing computation with no advice or external oracle.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove strict containment at every finite level, or prove equality Σₖ^P=Σₖ₊₁^P for some fixed k. Equality at any adjacent pair collapses all higher levels to that level, so a collapse at even one finite level answers no. Proving strictness for finitely many levels or relative to an oracle does not answer yes.
cards.why: This is the organizing conjecture behind the computational cost of alternating existential and universal reasoning. It strengthens the basic P-versus-NP distinction across all fixed quantifier depths and underlies many conditional lower bounds in complexity, verification, and graph problems with nested solution requirements.

importance.reason: A foundational conjecture asserting that every further alternation increases computational power. It governs a large family of complexity classifications and has major circuit-lower-bound consequences.

progress.text: Meyer and Stockmeyer introduce the hierarchy; Stockmeyer develops its structural properties and complete problems.
Oracle constructions show that all levels can be distinct in a relativized world. Karp–Lipton-type theorems connect small circuits for NP to a collapse of the unrelativized hierarchy.
Rossman, Servedio, and Tan establish infinitude relative to a random oracle with probability one. Their proof comes from an average-case lower bound separating consecutive constant circuit depths.

Hirsch and Volkovich study the Linear Ordering Principle, related small complexity classes, and Karp–Lipton-style conditional collapses. These are implications under hypotheses, not an unconditional collapse or separation of PH.

cards.status_note: Explicitly conjectured in the primary-source survey and Wigderson’s hierarchy discussion. Research through 10 September 2026 yielded no unrelativized proof of infinitude or finite collapse. Random-oracle infinitude and conditional Karp–Lipton collapses are not recorded as resolutions.

context_blocks.text: NP captures a single existential choice of a certificate. A second block permits a statement of the form “there is a candidate that survives every challenge”; a third permits a response to every challenge. Polynomially many bits may be chosen at each stage. The question is whether every additional fixed stage enables some decision problem that cannot be expressed with fewer stages and a polynomial-time final check.

The hierarchy is monotone because unused quantifier blocks can be inserted. Its collapse property is much stronger: if two neighboring levels coincide, all later alternations can be eliminated down to that level. Consequently the target is a single binary statement, not a request to classify an unspecified collection of logical formulas.

Strictness includes P≠NP at its first step, but P≠NP alone would leave the possibility of a later collapse. The conjecture also implies that PH is a proper subclass of PSPACE: if TQBF belonged to PH, it would belong to one fixed level, and PSPACE-completeness would force the whole hierarchy into that level. Allowing arbitrarily many quantifier alternations in the input is therefore a separate issue from allowing any fixed number.

The Karp–Lipton implication connects this conjecture to circuit complexity. Polynomial-size circuits for NP would collapse PH, so an infinite hierarchy would imply an NP language without polynomial-size circuits. Conditional collapse arguments are useful precisely because they can turn an assumption about nonuniform circuits into a conclusion about uniform classes; the conditional conclusion is not an established collapse.

Rossman, Servedio, and Tan prove that PH is infinite relative to a random oracle with probability one, through an average-case circuit-depth hierarchy theorem. Random membership bits supplied by an oracle are an extra computational resource. The result shows that strictness is compatible with, and typical in, that oracle model; it leaves the unrelativized hierarchy open.

cards.definitions: Languages are subsets of {0,1}*. PSPACE contains the languages decided by deterministic Turing machines that halt on every input of length n while using at most C(n+1)^a work-tape cells, for constants C,a depending on the machine. The read-only input tape is not charged, and there is no polynomial time limit. Set Σᵖ₀=P, the deterministic polynomial-time languages. For k≥1, a language L lies in Σᵖ_k if there are a deterministic polynomial-time predicate R and a polynomial p such that x∈L exactly when ∃y₁∀y₂∃y₃⋯Q_k y_k R(x,y₁,…,y_k)=1, where each y_i ranges over {0,1}^{p(|x|)} and Q_k is existential for odd k and universal for even k. Set PH=⋃_{k≥0}Σᵖ_k. The integer k is fixed for an entire language; it cannot grow with an input. Machines and predicates are uniform and have no advice or oracle. A fully quantified Boolean formula is an explicit Boolean formula using AND, OR and NOT, preceded by quantifiers binding every variable exactly once; variable names and the entire formula are binary encoded. Its truth uses the ordinary successive quantifier semantics over {0,1}. The language TQBF consists of its true well-formed encodings; malformed strings are rejected. The number of quantifier blocks in TQBF inputs is unrestricted.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves PSPACE⊆PH; the reverse inclusion is already known. Equivalently it places TQBF in one fixed Σᵖ_k, which would put every PSPACE language in that same level by polynomial-time reductions. A negative resolution proves that some PSPACE language, equivalently TQBF, is outside every fixed level. A separation at one fixed level or an oracle-relative result alone does not answer the question.

context_blocks.title: What is being compared?
context_blocks.text: Polynomial space lets a computation reuse a bounded amount of memory for a potentially very long time. The polynomial hierarchy instead organizes efficiently checked conditions by a fixed number of alternating existential and universal choices. For example, an existential block asks for a witness, a following universal block checks every challenge to it, and another existential block can give a response depending on that challenge. The question asks whether any polynomial-space computation can be expressed with a fixed number of such blocks.

context_blocks.title: Order of choices matters
context_blocks.text: The formula ∀x∃y (x=y) is true: after the value of x is fixed, y can take the same value. The formula ∃y∀x (x=y) is false because one bit cannot equal both possible values of x. Thus replacing a sequence of dependent choices by one initial guess changes the problem. A formula with arbitrarily many alternating choices describes a potentially long strategy, even though testing its final Boolean condition is straightforward.

context_blocks.title: Why polynomial space is enough
context_blocks.text: A quantified formula can be evaluated by recursively trying the two values of each variable and combining the answers according to its quantifier. The procedure reuses memory after finishing each branch; it need not store the exponentially large game tree. TQBF is PSPACE-complete. The standard alternation theorem also identifies polynomial-time alternating computation, with no fixed bound on its number of alternations, with PSPACE. Neither characterization shows that an arbitrary number of rounds compresses to a constant.

context_blocks.title: A union of levels has a subtle consequence
context_blocks.text: The definition of PH initially lets different languages use different fixed numbers of blocks. Nevertheless, equality with PSPACE would imply one common finite level containing all of PSPACE: TQBF would belong to some Σᵖ_k and every PSPACE language reduces to it. Therefore PH=PSPACE would collapse the hierarchy. Conversely, proving that the hierarchy has infinitely many distinct levels would separate it from PSPACE. A separation PH≠PSPACE alone does not establish that every hierarchy level is distinct; this is why the card differs from the non-collapse question.

context_blocks.title: What later results do and do not show
context_blocks.text: Grüne, Johannes, Orlin and Wulf’s February 2026 results make many multilevel optimization problems complete for individual hierarchy levels or for PSPACE. Completeness locates the problems within the classes; it does not prove the classes different. Egidy’s 2026 oracle construction illustrates another distinction: relative to that oracle, PH collapses while remaining strictly below PSPACE. This is a statement in a model with an additional oracle, rather than a resolution for ordinary machines. Historical preprints claim equality or non-collapse, but the sources checked here do not establish either as a settled theorem. The review did not independently audit those claimed proofs.

cards.title: NEXP versus nonuniform TC⁰
cards.formal: Is there a language L∈NEXP such that, for every fixed circuit depth d≥1, every fixed exponent k≥1, every constant C≥1 and every N≥1, some n≥N has no depth-at-most-d Boolean circuit of size at most C(n+1)^k with AND, OR, NOT and majority gates that computes L correctly on every n-bit input? Equivalently, is NEXP⊄TC⁰ for nonuniform TC⁰?
cards.why: Tests whether the algorithmic approach to circuit lower bounds can cross the threshold-gate barrier.

cards.definitions: NEXP=⋃_{a≥1}NTIME(2^{n^a}): a language is accepted by one nondeterministic Turing machine whose every computation branch halts within exponential time 2^{n^a}, up to a constant factor, for some fixed a. An input is in the language exactly when at least one branch accepts. A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with n Boolean inputs, constants 0 and 1 and one output. AND and OR may have any positive fan-in; NOT has one input. A majority gate on m inputs outputs 1 when at least ⌈m/2⌉ of them are 1, including a tie when m is even. Fan-out is unrestricted. Size is the number of operation gates plus wires. Repeated connections count individually, so their multiplicities cannot encode uncharged weights. Depth is the maximum number of operation gates on an input-to-output path. All circuits compute exactly on every input; no average-case correctness or randomness is allowed. TC⁰ consists of languages having one fixed depth bound and one polynomial size bound across all input lengths. The family may be nonuniform: no algorithm is required to construct its nth circuit. NEXP machines are uniform and have no oracle or advice. The formal quantifiers permit the lower bound to be witnessed at infinitely many input lengths, rather than requiring failure at every sufficiently large length.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves that one language in NEXP has no polynomial-size constant-depth majority-circuit family, with depth and polynomial exponent both unrestricted constants. A negative resolution proves NEXP⊆TC⁰. A bound ruling out only n^k gates for one fixed k, or only one fixed circuit depth, does not by itself establish the displayed separation.

context_blocks.title: Small depth still permits powerful gates
context_blocks.text: A constant-depth circuit applies only a bounded number of layers, but a majority gate can inspect many inputs at once. For three bits it returns 1 on 110 and 111, while returning 0 on 100. Thus majority is not a bounded-fan-in local operation. TC⁰ permits many such gates in parallel and lets their outputs feed later layers. The depth bound stays fixed as input length grows, while the number of gates and wires may be any fixed polynomial.

context_blocks.title: Why parity is not enough
context_blocks.text: Parity is difficult for constant-depth circuits using only AND, OR and NOT, but it is easy for majority circuits. A threshold test for whether an n-bit input has at least t ones is implementable with a majority gate and suitable constants. Two adjacent threshold tests identify an exact number of ones, and taking an OR over odd counts gives parity with a polynomial number of gates in constant depth. This example shows why a lower bound for the weaker gate set cannot simply be reused after majority is added.

context_blocks.title: What NEXP contributes
context_blocks.text: The hard language need only have a nondeterministic exponential-time algorithm; it need not be in P or NP. That is a generous uniform computation budget, making the lack of a known separation striking. Nevertheless, counting the truth tables that have no small circuits does not automatically identify one language within this budget. The assertion requires one language that defeats every fixed polynomial size and every fixed depth, rather than a different unrestricted truth table for each desired bound.

context_blocks.title: The established nearby separation
context_blocks.text: Williams proves that NEXP does not have polynomial-size ACC circuits. ACC allows constant-depth Boolean circuits with gates testing the number of 1 inputs modulo a fixed integer. TC⁰ can implement these modular tests by combining threshold comparisons. It is therefore a more permissive class, and excluding ACC does not exclude TC⁰. The original 2011 reference supports this nearby theorem, not the stronger conclusion asked here.

context_blocks.title: The 2026 results retain important restrictions
context_blocks.text: Chen, Tal and Wang prove super-quadratic gate lower bounds for depth-two linear-threshold circuits, with a hard function in E^NP, exponential time with an NP oracle. Their n^(2.5−ε) bound is still a fixed polynomial and addresses depth two. A September preprint claims near-cubic wire bounds in that setting; its source also carries a critical comment, and it is not independently verified here. Wire counts and gate counts are different quantitative parameters. Ren and Williams obtain near-maximum general circuit bounds with a promise-Merlin–Arthur oracle and one bit of advice. None of these statements supplies the required ordinary NEXP language outside all of nonuniform TC⁰.

cards.title: Sliding-scale PCP conjecture
cards.formal: Do constants a,b,c>0 and q≥1 exist such that 3-SAT has a verifier using at most a log₂(N+2) random bits and q queries to a proof of at most (N+2)^b symbols over an alphabet of size at most (N+2)^b, with perfect completeness and soundness at most (N+2)^(−c)?
cards.definitions: N is the bit length of an explicitly encoded 3-CNF formula. A uniform deterministic polynomial-time verifier receives the input, a uniform random bit string and oracle access to a fixed proof string. It reads at most q alphabet symbols, each encoded with O(log N) bits, and accepts or rejects. Queries may be adaptive. On a satisfiable formula some proof is always accepted; on an unsatisfiable formula every proof has acceptance probability at most (N+2)^(−c). Polynomial bounds and all constants are universal. No cryptographic soundness assumption or interaction is allowed.

context_blocks.text: The PCP theorem achieves constant error with a constant number of queries. Driving soundness down to an inverse polynomial while retaining a constant number of queries would give substantially stronger verification and constraint-satisfaction gaps.

Dinur, Harsha and Kindler obtain inverse-polynomial error with polyloglogarithmically many queries. Their paper explicitly names the constant-query polynomial-alphabet endpoint as the sliding-scale conjecture in this regime. This is different from asking that a constant-error PCP have linear proof length.

cards.why: A central quantitative PCP barrier controlling the strength of gap amplification and inapproximability.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.

cards.title: CLS versus FP
cards.formal: Does every total search problem in CLS admit a deterministic polynomial-time solution algorithm, equivalently CLS⊆FP?
cards.definitions: CLS is the class of total search problems reducible in polynomial time to ContinuousLocalOpt, with the source’s polynomial-time representations and explicit Lipschitz and accuracy parameters. Solutions may be an approximate local optimum or a valid violation certificate for the supplied promises. FP here means a polynomial-time algorithm that returns a valid output on every instance, not equality between decision languages.

context_blocks.text: Continuous local search formalizes a broad class of optimization tasks for which a local progress argument guarantees a solution. The equality CLS=PPAD∩PLS places that class simultaneously in two major total-search frameworks.

That classification does not provide a polynomial-time algorithm. The open target asks whether the common part is tractable, rather than whether the two classes intersect. Gradient-descent complexity supplies a concrete motivation for this algorithmic frontier.

cards.title: Hartmanis–Stearns conjecture
cards.formal: For every integer b≥2 and every real x∈[0,1), if a deterministic multitape Turing machine generates the base-b digits of x in order with a constant bound on the time between successive digits, must x be rational or transcendental?
cards.why: A proof would impose a strong arithmetic restriction on numbers generated at the fastest possible asymptotic output rate. The checked 2024 source also records that the conjecture would rule out linear-time integer multiplication on multitape Turing machines.

progress.text: Linear-time and real-time sequence generation are shown to coincide for multitape machines.
The published revisiting paper proves transcendence restrictions for pushdown and exponential-growth morphic models.
ICALP work proves additional word-based transcendence results while explicitly retaining the full conjecture.
Automata compute digits from specially represented inputs; a June thesis abstract still describes the general conjecture as open.

cards.definitions: Write x=∑_{n≥1}d_n b^(−n), where d_n∈{0,…,b−1}, using the unique expansion that is not eventually all b−1; a terminating expansion continues with zeros. Rational means x=p/q for integers p,q with q≠0. Algebraic means P(x)=0 for a nonzero polynomial P with integer coefficients; transcendental means not algebraic. A machine has a finite control, a fixed finite tape alphabet, and a fixed finite number of two-way infinite work tapes, each with one head and initially blank. Each transition reads the symbols under the heads, writes at those cells, changes state and moves each head at most one cell. It may also append one digit to a separate write-only output stream; written digits are irrevocable. It starts with no input and no advice or oracle and runs indefinitely. There must be a constant C≥1 such that its first digit appears by step C and, writing t_n for the step at which d_n appears, 1≤t_(n+1)−t_n≤C for every n≥1. The finite machine and C may depend on the fixed x and b, but not on n. This is the constant-delay, or real-time, convention used by this card. Restricting to [0,1) only removes an integer part, which does not change rationality or transcendence.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the implication for all bases, numbers and machines just defined, or refute it by exhibiting an algebraic irrational x, a base b and a machine with proofs of correct infinite digit generation and a uniform constant delay. A computation of any finite prefix, a slower digit algorithm or a theorem restricted to finite automata does not settle the statement.

context_blocks.title: A steady stream of digits
context_blocks.text: For example, 1/7=0.142857142857… in base 10. A finite machine can cycle through the six-digit block forever with bounded delay. Every rational has an eventually periodic expansion, so rational numbers fit the model. In contrast, √2−1 is algebraic and irrational: it satisfies x²+2x−1=0. The conjecture excludes such numbers from all constant-delay generators, even though their digits are computable.

context_blocks.title: The finite description is not the resource bound
context_blocks.text: The same program must produce the entire infinite expansion; it cannot receive a longer precomputed digit table for each requested precision. Work tapes may grow without bound. The restriction is how many elementary steps separate outputs, not a fixed bound on memory. No claim is made that every transcendental number has such a generator.

context_blocks.title: Why sources also say linear time
context_blocks.text: Fischer, Meyer and Rosenberg establish that linear-time and real-time sequence generation coincide for multitape Turing machines. This concerns the existence of a suitable generator; a particular implementation with linear total time need not itself have bounded gaps. The constant-delay wording therefore agrees with the linear-prefix formulation used in the cited Hartmanis–Stearns literature.

context_blocks.title: What the partial results establish
context_blocks.text: Adamczewski, Cassaigne and Le Gonidec exclude algebraic irrationals from several restricted generation models, including a deterministic pushdown transducer supplied with a digit index. Their one-stack theorem is not a theorem about arbitrary multitape generators. The 2024 ICALP paper likewise obtains transcendence for particular word classes and explicitly retains the full conjecture.

context_blocks.title: The input representation matters
context_blocks.text: The 2026 automata result obtains a digit of a quadratic irrational from b^n supplied in a special Ostrowski numeration system. This is additional structured input, whereas the machine in this card starts blank and produces digits indefinitely. The authors do not claim a fast general digit generator, so that result is not a counterexample.

A proof would connect the arithmetic nature of numbers to a stringent computation bound and rule out linear-time integer multiplication.

cards.title: Linear-size circuits for stable ternary compaction
cards.formal: Is there an absolute constant C≥1 such that, for every integer n≥1, the function S_n:{0,1,2}^n→{0,1,2}^n that removes all symbols 2 and appends the same number of 2s on the right, preserving the order of the other symbols, is computed by a Boolean circuit with at most Cn gates in the model below?
cards.definitions: Encode symbols 0,1,2 as 00,01,10 respectively. The circuit has 2n input bits and 2n output bits, with arbitrary fan-out, binary AND and OR gates, unary NOT gates, and optional Boolean constant gates. Size counts all non-input gates, including constants; wires and output designations cost nothing. Correctness is required only on concatenations of the three valid encodings; output on inputs containing 11 is unrestricted. If i_1<...<i_m are exactly the indices with a_i≠2, the required decoded output is a_(i_1)...a_(i_m) followed by n−m copies of 2. In particular, 0s and 1s retain their relative order. The circuit may depend on n; no uniform construction algorithm, depth bound, monotonicity restriction or indivisible-record model is imposed. The constant C is independent of n.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation with the stated model, hypotheses and quantifier order. The proof must settle the entire target. A result conditional on an additional assumption settles only that conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof checked by a proof assistant and matching this statement.
cards.why: Test linear circuit size for a concrete, sequentially simple function whose stability requirement preserves substantial information.

importance.reason: A specific circuit-size barrier beyond generic lower-bound statements; stable compaction connects elementary data movement with unrestricted Boolean computation.

progress.text: Regan poses linear Boolean-circuit size for stable ternary compaction.
Asharov, Lin and Shi obtain small circuits for unstable compaction and short-key sorting while distinguishing the stable task.

context_blocks.text: A sequential scan can retain the 0s and 1s and place the dummy symbols at the end. The circuit question asks whether this global rearrangement can also be implemented with only linearly many bounded-fan-in Boolean operations.

cards.title: Formula versus circuit noise thresholds
cards.formal: For p in [0,1/2), let Reliable(p) mean that there exists a constant delta>0 such that for every n>=1 and every Boolean function f:{0,1}^n->{0,1}, some finite circuit C of the kind below satisfies Pr[C(x)=f(x)]>=1/2+delta for every input x. Is Reliable(p) true exactly for p<(3-sqrt(7))/4? In particular, is it false at the boundary as well as above it?
cards.definitions: A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with input sources x_1,...,x_n, constant sources 0 and 1, gates of fan-in at most two, and one designated output wire. Any Boolean function of a gate's input bits is allowed. Each gate is evaluated once in topological order and independently flips its correct Boolean output with probability exactly p. All outgoing wires from that gate carry the same resulting bit; reuse does not generate fresh independent copies. Inputs, constants, and wires are noiseless. Every computational gate, including the output gate when present, obeys the noise rule; there is no extra noiseless decoder. Fan-out is unrestricted, and different incoming paths may share gates. C may depend on p,n,f but not on x. Its size and construction time are unrestricted. The probability is solely over independent gate failures. Delta may depend on p but is common to all n,f,x. A formula is the restricted case in which computational gates have fan-out at most one, with input variables still allowed to occur repeatedly.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove or refute the stated equivalence for the full interval 0<=p<1/2, including p=(3-sqrt(7))/4. A proof or refutation must use the specified independent gate-flip model and a uniform positive correctness advantage across all functions.
cards.why: The problem asks how much unreliable local computation can be tolerated when arbitrary redundancy and reuse are available. It would determine whether sharing intermediate noisy values changes the fundamental threshold already known for formulas.

importance.reason: A sharp reliability boundary for general classical computation, separating the effects of gate errors from circuit size and design effort.

context_blocks.text: The success advantage must be fixed before choosing a function or its number of inputs. Allowing it to shrink with the function would describe a much weaker task. The noisy output itself is read, so the target does not assume an unlimited perfect final computation.

Unger establishes the exact threshold for two-input formulas, extending the earlier NAND-gate result, and conjectures the same threshold for circuits. Shared subcomputations correlate wire values even though the underlying gate failures are independent.

Later work studies asymmetric noise on AND and XOR gates and relates reliability to amplification. Its different gate-specific error assumptions and formula bounds do not settle the common-noise, unrestricted-fan-out proposition here.

cards.title: Closure of d-DNNF under negation
cards.formal: Do a constant c>0 and an integer k>=1 exist such that, for every finite variable set X and every d-DNNF circuit C over X of size s, there is a d-DNNF circuit D over X of size at most c(s+1)^k computing the Boolean complement of C on every assignment X->{0,1}? No algorithm for finding D within that bound is required.
cards.definitions: An NNF circuit is a finite rooted directed acyclic graph whose leaves are constants 0,1 or literals x,not-x for x in X, and whose internal nodes are AND or OR gates. Edges run from a gate to its inputs. The variable set of a subcircuit comprises the variables occurring in its reachable literals. Decomposable means that the input subcircuits of every AND gate have pairwise disjoint variable sets. Deterministic means that no assignment to X makes two different inputs of any OR gate both true. A d-DNNF satisfies both properties. Size is the total number of vertices plus edges; fan-in is arbitrary and part of that size. Evaluation has the usual Boolean meaning. No negation gates above leaves, additional variables, or requirement of compatibility with a common variable decomposition tree is allowed. Constants c,k are independent of X and C. The output D may use any decompositions meeting these conditions.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the universal polynomial size bound, or prove that no constants c,k satisfy it. Algorithmic difficulty of producing a small complement alone does not refute this size-existence statement.
cards.why: Deterministic decomposable circuits represent Boolean solution sets while supporting exact counting. Closure under complement asks whether a compact representation of satisfying assignments necessarily gives a comparably compact representation of nonsatisfying assignments, independently of construction time.

importance.reason: A central representational-closure question in knowledge compilation that separates succinctness from the cost of performing a logical operation.

context_blocks.text: Decomposability prevents conjunctions from sharing variables and determinism prevents disjunctions from sharing satisfying assignments. Negating a circuit syntactically need not preserve both properties.

The STACS 2026 discussion retains complementation as an open question. The separate algorithmic question asks for a polynomial-time procedure producing the complement. Such a procedure implies the size bound on this card; the converse is not established. Both targets are retained because an existence theorem would settle a representation barrier without necessarily supplying the algorithmic transformation.
The stronger polynomial-time construction question is retained as TCS-0306. The existence of small complementary circuits does not by itself give an efficient algorithm for constructing them.

cards.title: Near-linear-time approximation of reachability diameter
cards.formal: For an unweighted directed graph $G=(V,E)$, define $D(G)=\max\{d_G(u,v):d_G(u,v)<\infty\}$. Is there an absolute constant $C\ge1$ and one randomized word-RAM algorithm that, on every input, returns an estimate $D(G)/C\le\widehat D\le D(G)$ with probability at least 2/3 in $\widetilde O(n+m)$ worst-case time? Here $n=|V|$, $m=|E|$, words have $\Theta(\log n)$ bits, and self-distances are included, giving D(G)=0 on an edgeless graph. The constant and the hidden logarithmic exponent are independent of G.
cards.why: This asks how quickly an algorithm can summarize the routes that actually exist in a directed network. I include it because it exposes a basic weakness of transferring undirected diameter intuition to directed graphs and provides a concrete benchmark for algorithms based on reachability, sampling, and shortcuts.
cards.definitions: Distances count edges on a shortest directed path. The maximum concerns finite distances only; it is neither the longest simple path nor the maximum of the smaller of the two directional distances. $\widetilde O$ suppresses polylogarithmic factors. This card focuses the broader approximation–time tradeoff on near-linear running time.

progress.text: Theorem 9 gives an $n^{1/2+o(1)}$-approximation in near-linear time. Theorem 7 gives additive error $k$ in $O(nm/k)$ time; these guarantees leave the constant-factor near-linear target unresolved.

Corollary 5 conditionally excludes better-than-two approximation below the Boolean-matrix-multiplication exponent; its combinatorial version excludes truly subcubic combinatorial algorithms under combinatorial BMM. These results do not exclude every constant approximation.

cards.status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. Open Problem 1 at ESA 2026; the near-linear constant-factor target is a focused part of that broader question.

context_blocks.text: A directed graph need not be strongly connected. Taking the maximum over all ordered pairs then produces infinity as soon as one pair is unreachable, concealing the lengths of the routes that do exist. Reachability diameter discards unreachable pairs. On a one-way path of five vertices it is four, even though most ordered pairs have no directed route.

A familiar undirected idea is to search from an arbitrary vertex and use a farthest vertex as a witness. Directionality breaks its guarantee. Consider a long one-way path and an extra sink reached by an edge from the first path vertex. Searching from that sink sees no other vertex; searching toward it sees only the first path vertex. Both searches reveal a distance of one while the reachability diameter can be arbitrarily large. This is an illustrative counterexample to that particular pivot choice, not a lower bound against every sampling algorithm.

There is also a distinction between additive and multiplicative error. An estimate within $k$ of the truth is useful when $D(G)$ is much larger than $k$, but gives little information when the diameter is small. The question requires a useful relative guarantee on every input, including graphs whose longest finite shortest path has only a few edges.
The 2026 paper makes this a fine-grained algorithmic question and leaves a substantial gap for unweighted graphs. Its strong hardness results for weighted graphs do not settle the unit-weight case.

cards.title: Černý conjecture
cards.formal: Does every synchronizing complete deterministic finite automaton with n≥1 states have a reset word of length at most (n−1)²?
cards.definitions: An automaton here is a finite transition system A=(Q,Σ,δ), with |Q|=n, a finite nonempty alphabet Σ, and a total function δ:Q×Σ→Q. Extend δ to words by δ(q,ε)=q and δ(q,wa)=δ(δ(q,w),a). A word w is a reset word when |{δ(q,w):q∈Q}|=1. The automaton is synchronizing if at least one such word exists; its reset threshold rt(A) is the minimum number of letters in a reset word. The quantification ranges over every n and every finite alphabet and total transition function satisfying this promise. The common final state need not be specified beforehand. Initial states and accepting states play no role. The empty word handles n=1. No strong-connectivity, binary-alphabet, permutation-letter, or other structural restriction is imposed. Partial automata, nondeterministic transitions, and synchronizing only a prescribed proper subset of Q are different models.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that rt(A)≤(n−1)² for every synchronizing complete deterministic n-state automaton, or exhibit such an automaton with rt(A)>(n−1)² and prove that strict inequality. Alphabets and state counts are unrestricted as specified above.
cards.why: A central extremal problem in automata theory, with a simple finite-state formulation and a sharp explicit candidate bound. It tests whether local compression and algebraic structure can force globally short control sequences in every synchronizing system.

importance.reason: The flagship quantitative question about synchronizing automata, connecting finite-state control, extremal combinatorics, and linear-algebraic methods.

progress.text: Černý constructs an n-state family with reset threshold exactly (n−1)², establishing the sharp lower-bound target.
The classical Pin–Frankl compression argument gives a general cubic upper bound; the survey records (n³−n)/6−1 for n≥4.
Szykuła combines compression with avoiding words to improve the long-standing leading cubic constant.
Shitov improves that argument to a leading constant approximately 0.1654; the exponent remains three.
Volkov’s updated list records established special classes and their reset-threshold bounds while keeping the general conjecture open.
Zhu reports a proof for the one-cluster subclass in a preprint. This card does not independently certify that proof or extend it to unrestricted automata.
Szykuła’s AFL 2026 survey explicitly states the general conjecture and identifies the cubic Shitov estimate as the best known unrestricted bound.

cards.status_note: Szykuła’s survey posted 25 August 2026 explicitly states the unrestricted conjecture as open and records the cubic upper bound. Sources and later work were checked on 11 September 2026. The July one-cluster preprint is a restricted-class claim whose proof was not independently verified.

context_blocks.text: Synchronization asks how to restore a finite system to a known state when its current state is unknown. A fixed input sequence must work simultaneously from every possible starting state; it cannot observe the intermediate state and adapt its next letter. The length bound therefore measures the cost of an open-loop reset, rather than ordinary shortest-path navigation from a known vertex.

The proposed constant is forced by a concrete family. On states 0,…,n−1, let a cyclically increment the state and let b send n−1 to 0 while fixing the other states. For n≥2, the word b(a^{n−1}b)^{n−2} has length (n−1)² and resets this automaton. Černý’s construction also proves that no shorter reset word works. A proof of the conjecture must match this obstruction exactly.

Knowing that a reset exists is much easier than establishing its sharp maximum length. Pairwise merging gives polynomial criteria for synchronizability, and successive compression of subsets gives general polynomial length bounds. The bottleneck is how much progress one can force as the current set of possible states shrinks. Adding separate worst-case bounds for these stages gives a cubic estimate and can lose information about how the stages interact.

The August 2026 open-problems survey records a general upper bound of approximately 0.1654n³+o(n³), due to Shitov’s refinement of Szykuła’s result. The gap is therefore in the exponent as well as the leading constant: the conjecture asks for the exact quadratic bound (n−1)². Results for restricted transition systems do not establish that bound for all synchronizing automata.

A July 2026 preprint reports the conjectured bound for one-cluster automata: systems having a letter whose functional graph has exactly one directed cycle. Its sharper positive-level estimate uses the cycle length and the distance of off-cycle states from that cycle. This is a claim for a restricted class, and the later general survey still states the unrestricted conjecture as open.

sentences: A reset word drives a finite automaton to one common state, regardless of where it started.
The project asks whether every synchronizing complete deterministic automaton with n states has such a word of length at most (n−1)².
Explicit automata attain this length, so the proposed bound cannot be reduced.
The difficulty is coordinating successive mergers of possible states without paying a cubic total cost.
A solution would identify the exact worst-case effort required to regain control of an unknown finite-state system.

cards.context:
Synchronization asks how to restore a finite system to a known state when its current state is unknown. A fixed input sequence must work simultaneously from every possible starting state; it cannot observe the intermediate state and adapt its next letter. The length bound therefore measures the cost of an open-loop reset, rather than ordinary shortest-path navigation from a known vertex.

The proposed constant is forced by a concrete family. On states 0,…,n−1, let a cyclically increment the state and let b send n−1 to 0 while fixing the other states. For n≥2, the word b(a^{n−1}b)^{n−2} has length (n−1)² and resets this automaton. Černý’s construction also proves that no shorter reset word works. A proof of the conjecture must match this obstruction exactly.

Knowing that a reset exists is much easier than establishing its sharp maximum length. Pairwise merging gives polynomial criteria for synchronizability, and successive compression of subsets gives general polynomial length bounds. The bottleneck is how much progress one can force as the current set of possible states shrinks. Adding separate worst-case bounds for these stages gives a cubic estimate and can lose information about how the stages interact.

The August 2026 open-problems survey records a general upper bound of approximately 0.1654n³+o(n³), due to Shitov’s refinement of Szykuła’s result. The gap is therefore in the exponent as well as the leading constant: the conjecture asks for the exact quadratic bound (n−1)². Results for restricted transition systems do not establish that bound for all synchronizing automata.

A July 2026 preprint reports the conjectured bound for one-cluster automata: systems having a letter whose functional graph has exactly one directed cycle. Its sharper positive-level estimate uses the cycle length and the distance of off-cycle states from that cycle. This is a claim for a restricted class, and the later general survey still states the unrestricted conjecture as open.

cards.title: Sakoda–Sipser problem
cards.formal: Do universal constants C,k≥1 exist such that, for every n≥1, every finite nonempty input alphabet Σ and every two-way nondeterministic finite automaton A over Σ with at most n states, there is a two-way deterministic finite automaton D over the same alphabet with at most C(n+1)^k states satisfying L(D)=L(A)? Equivalence must hold on all finite input words, without a length bound.
cards.definitions: The read-only input tape contains a left endmarker, a word w∈Σ*, and a right endmarker. Each automaton has one head, initially on the left endmarker, a finite set Q of states with a designated initial state and designated halting accepting states. In each nonhalting configuration it uses its current state and the scanned symbol to choose a new state and a head displacement in {−1,0,+1}; moves outside the endmarkers are forbidden. A missing transition rejects that branch. A word is accepted if some finite computation reaches an accepting state. Infinite nonaccepting branches do not count as acceptance. For a deterministic automaton there is at most one available transition in each state-symbol pair, and its unique infinite run, if any, rejects. There is no work tape, rewritable input, second head, stack, counter, randomness or advice. State count includes all control and halting states, but the bound is independent of word length and alphabet size. The target is existence of D for each A; computing D from A is not required to take polynomial time. Standard endmarker and stay-put conventions change these state bounds only by polynomial factors.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of universal constants C,k giving an equivalent 2DFA with at most C(n+1)^k states for every n-state 2NFA, or prove that no such constants exist. In the negative direction, every proposed polynomial bound must fail on some source automaton; all language comparisons concern words of every length.
cards.why: A principal unresolved measure of the succinctness provided by nondeterminism. It isolates the issue in finite-state machines, connects to nonuniform space complexity, and asks whether revisiting read-only data can replace a large internal record of possible computations.

importance.reason: The flagship state-complexity problem for two-way finite automata, open since 1978, with unusually direct connections between finite-state descriptions and logarithmic-space complexity.

progress.text: Sakoda and Sipser formulate the polynomial-state simulation questions and conjecture that nondeterminism cannot always be removed with polynomial cost.
The Geffert–Mereghetti–Pighizzini simulation gives n^{O(log n)} states for unary two-way NFAs. It leaves a polynomial-versus-superpolynomial gap.
Kapoutsis characterizes polynomial-state simulation on short inputs by NL⊆L/poly, carefully distinguishing input-length restrictions and advice.
Clerici Lorenzini and coauthors obtain a polynomial-size normal form for two-way NFAs accepting letter-bounded languages.
Guillon and coauthors give polynomial-size complementation using self-verifying 1-limited automata, with rewritable annotations; the unrestricted read-only determinization question remains open.

Adeogun and Kapoutsis’ revised preprint establishes a quadratic 2DFA state lower bound for one-way liveness and the resulting NFA-to-2DFA conversion. This does not exclude a polynomial determinization bound.

cards.status_note: Checked on 11 September 2026. The STACS 2026 paper explicitly retains ordinary two-way determinization as open. Adeogun and Kapoutsis’ July 2026 revision supplies a quadratic lower bound, still compatible with polynomial determinization. Writable-annotation complementation and bounded-input-length simulations are separate results.

context_blocks.text: All four basic finite-automaton models—one-way or two-way, deterministic or nondeterministic—recognize exactly the regular languages. Their descriptions can nevertheless have very different sizes. The familiar subset construction gives an exponential conversion from a one-way NFA to a one-way DFA. The open issue is whether the deterministic machine can avoid that cost by repeatedly revisiting the original input instead of remembering all possible nondeterministic states at once.

A simple example shows why a one-way lower bound is insufficient. Over {0,1}, consider words whose r-th symbol from the right is 1. A one-way deterministic automaton must distinguish all binary suffixes of length r and therefore needs at least 2^r states. A two-way deterministic automaton can scan to the right endmarker, walk left r positions while counting in its finite control, and inspect the symbol. It uses O(r) states. Rereading changes the representation cost even though the accepted language is unchanged.

Known unrestricted upper bounds still pass through a one-way representation and are exponential in a polynomial of the number of states. At the opposite end, exponential separations are known if the deterministic target has restricted head motion, such as reversing only at endmarkers. Those restrictions can themselves make deterministic automata exponentially larger. A lower bound using them therefore cannot be transferred to an unrestricted 2DFA without another argument.

The unary case remains meaningful: the input then consists of repetitions of one letter, and only its length can carry information. Unary two-way NFAs can be simulated by two-way DFAs with n^{O(log n)} states. This is far smaller than an exponential bound but still exceeds every fixed polynomial. It demonstrates that even removing almost all input syntax does not make the remaining determinization question routine.

Connections to logarithmic-space computation require careful quantifiers. Kapoutsis proves that polynomial-state deterministic simulation on inputs of length at most the source state count is equivalent to NL⊆L/poly. Here L/poly allows a deterministic logarithmic-space machine polynomially long advice depending only on input length. That theorem concerns bounded-length agreement, whereas this card requires agreement on every word. It should not be restated as an unconditional equivalence of the full Sakoda–Sipser question with L=NL.

Clerici Lorenzini, Pighizzini, and Prigioniero study letter-bounded languages in 2025: languages contained in a_1*⋯a_t* for fixed letters. They obtain a polynomial-cost normal form in which nondeterministic choices and head reversals occur at endmarkers. The source language restriction is crucial; the theorem does not put every two-way NFA into that normal form.

Guillon, Prigioniero, and Taheri’s STACS 2026 theorem complements arbitrary two-way NFAs with a polynomial-size self-verifying 1-limited automaton. Such a machine can annotate input cells on their first visit; the construction uses a shared guessed annotation that subsequent traversals can inspect. It remains a recognizer of regular languages, but its ability to retain those annotations is absent from a 2DFA. Their introduction explicitly leaves ordinary determinization and ordinary two-way-NFA complementation open.

Adeogun and Kapoutsis’ July 2026 revision proves a quadratic state lower bound for deterministic two-way automata solving one-way liveness. The problem encodes paths through successive layers of a graph; a small nondeterministic automaton can guess a path, whereas a deterministic one must use more control states. The lower bound also applies to conversion from one-way NFAs. Quadratic growth is compatible with the polynomial simulation asked here, so this strengthens the documented lower-bound picture without resolving the conjecture.

cards.title: Generalized star-height problem
cards.formal: Does there exist a finite nonempty alphabet Σ and a regular language L⊆Σ* such that every generalized regular expression denoting L has Kleene-star nesting depth at least two, when complement is allowed without increasing that depth?
cards.definitions: Σ* is the set of all finite words over Σ, including the empty word ε. A regular language is one accepted by a finite deterministic automaton. Generalized expressions are finite expressions built from ∅, ε, and the letters a∈Σ using binary union E∪F, concatenation EF, complement E^c, and Kleene star E*. Their meanings are respectively the empty language, {ε}, {a}, language union, all concatenations uv with u∈L(E) and v∈L(F), Σ*∖L(E), and the union of all finite concatenation powers of L(E), including power zero {ε}. Set h(∅)=h(ε)=h(a)=0, h(E∪F)=h(EF)=max{h(E),h(F)}, h(E^c)=h(E), and h(E*)=h(E)+1. Define h_g(L)=min{h(E):L(E)=L}, which exists because every regular language has an ordinary regular expression. The question is whether h_g(L)>1 for at least one such L. There is no bound on expression size, number of complements, union or concatenation depth, automaton size, or alphabet size. Intersection is permitted as the abbreviation (E^c∪F^c)^c and does not add star depth. Backreferences, infinite words, additional predicates and auxiliary alphabets in the final expression are not part of the syntax.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that some regular language has generalized star height at least two, including a lower bound over all generalized expressions for that language, or prove that every regular language over every finite nonempty alphabet has a generalized expression of star height at most one. Expression size is unrestricted in both alternatives.
cards.why: A basic unresolved expressive-depth question for regular languages: determine whether Boolean operations eliminate every need for nested iteration, or whether a genuine second level exists.

importance.reason: A longstanding foundational problem connecting regular expressions, finite automata, algebraic language theory and logical descriptions.
