cards.title: Deterministic LOCAL MIS in O(log n) rounds
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic LOCAL algorithm that outputs a maximal independent set on every $n$-vertex simple graph in $O(\log n)$ synchronous communication rounds? Each vertex has a distinct $O(\log n)$-bit identifier, and the guarantee must hold for every valid identifier assignment and every maximum degree. The output must be independent, and every vertex outside it must have a neighbor inside it. No random bits are available.
cards.why: This measures the quantitative cost of removing randomness from a basic distributed task. I include it separately from randomized sublogarithmic MIS because the algorithm must work against every identifier assignment with no failure probability. An O(log n) result would match the familiar randomized worst-case benchmark and propagate through reductions to other symmetry-breaking problems.
cards.definitions:
LOCAL allows unbounded messages along input edges and unrestricted local computation. A vertex’s r-round view contains only its radius-r neighborhood and the identifiers and input data revealed there. The complexity is elapsed communication rounds until all vertices output. The target is uniform over arbitrary graphs, not restricted to bounded degree, planar graphs, or trees.

Nodes may know n and the maximum degree; the time guarantee must still be O(log n) uniformly over degrees.

progress.text: Balliu and coauthors prove a deterministic lower bound $\Omega(\min\{\Delta,\log n/\log\log n\})$. In particular, the general worst-case complexity cannot be substantially below logarithmic up to a log-log factor.
Rozhoň and Ghaffari obtain polylogarithmic deterministic network decomposition and consequently polylogarithmic deterministic MIS.
Ghaffari and Grunau improve MIS to $\widetilde O(\log^{5/3}n)$ rounds, where the hidden factors are polylogarithmic in $\log n$.
Bourreau, Brandt, and Nolin use the same deterministic MIS benchmark to improve Δ-coloring; their result does not give an O(log n) MIS algorithm.

context_blocks.text: Identifiers make deterministic symmetry breaking possible, but they do not automatically make it fast. Consider the rule that selects every vertex whose identifier is smaller than those of all its remaining neighbors, then removes the selected vertices and their neighbors. On a path with identifiers increasing from one endpoint to the other, each phase selects just the smallest remaining endpoint. This rule takes linearly many phases, even though much faster algorithms exist for paths.

Randomized MIS algorithms avoid adversarial identifier patterns by making new random choices. A deterministic algorithm has to arrange useful progress from the graph and identifiers alone. The existence of a good assignment of random choices is insufficient: processors must find suitable choices while paying for the communication that coordinates them.

Network decomposition supplied a general way to organize that work into small-diameter clusters that can be processed in groups. It settled the old question of whether polylogarithmic deterministic MIS is possible. The present target concerns the finer exponent and cannot be recorded as the already-solved polylogarithmic-time question.

The 2024 improvement reaches approximately $\log^{5/3}n$ rounds and avoids the log-squared cost of the standard decomposition-based route. Closing the remaining gap requires more than optimizing the constants of that route. The 2026 coloring reduction still uses this improved MIS bound as its benchmark.

cards.title: Two-dimensional sandpile prediction in NC
cards.formal: Is the following decision problem in logspace-uniform NC? An input gives positive integers W,H, an explicit W-by-H array c with entries in {0,1,2,3}, and two cells p,q in that rectangle. Extend c by zero to the whole integer square lattice and add one grain at p. Answer YES exactly when q eventually topples under the four-neighbor parallel sandpile dynamics defined below. The input length N includes every array entry, not a compressed representation.
cards.definitions: The four neighbor displacements are E={(1,0),(-1,0),(0,1),(0,-1)}. Set c_0(v)=c(v)+1 if v=p, and c_0(v)=c(v) otherwise. At each integer time t>=0 every vertex v with c_t(v)>=4 topples once, losing four grains and sending one to each neighbor. Equivalently, c_{t+1}(v)=c_t(v)-4 I[c_t(v)>=4]+sum_{e in E} I[c_t(v-e)>=4], where I is the indicator. The question is whether c_t(q)>=4 for some t>=0. The array is row-major with binary dimensions and cell coordinates; invalid encodings are rejected. The zero extension is an infinite lattice, not a periodic boundary or a boundary that absorbs grains. A supplied rectangle may contain extra zero rows or columns to include p and q. Finite initial mass eventually stabilizes. NC here means that for some fixed integers a,k the decision has Boolean circuits of size O(N^a) and depth O((log N)^k), with fan-in at most two, whose description is generated from 1^N in O(log N) work space. There is no requested time t in the input and the answer is exact, without random error.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove or refute membership of the specified language in logspace-uniform NC. Any complexity assumption used in a negative result must be stated explicitly.
cards.why: A local deterministic physical process can have a long cascade after a single perturbation. This problem asks whether its outcome permits an efficient parallel computation, addressing the boundary between prediction and sequential evolution.

importance.reason: A canonical unresolved parallel-complexity question for a simple two-dimensional dynamical system, connecting computational prediction with statistical physics.

context_blocks.text: The initial configuration is stable, so all activity comes from the extra grain. The requested output is a single eventual-toppling bit; computing the entire final configuration or a toppling at a specified time are related but different tasks.
The classical dimension-dependent results provide efficient parallel prediction in one dimension and P-completeness in dimensions at least three. They leave the planar case as a distinct question.

Recent work still separates the standard four-neighbor lattice from weighted or nonuniform grids. NC membership and P-completeness are not an unconditional exclusive dichotomy: a P-completeness result rules out NC only under NC != P.

cards.title: Triangle detection in CONGEST
cards.formal: For arbitrary simple undirected n-vertex networks, determine the optimal worst-case randomized round complexity of triangle detection in CONGEST, up to constant factors. Each vertex initially knows its distinct O(log n)-bit identifier and its neighbors, and may send a separate O(log n)-bit message in each direction of every incident edge per synchronous round. On a triangle-free graph all vertices must output NO; otherwise at least one must output YES. The joint answer must be correct with probability at least 2/3 on every input and identifier assignment. The algorithm is uniform, has private random bits, and may know n. The currently established bounds are $\Omega(\log\log n)$ and $\widetilde O(n^{1/3})$.
cards.why: I include this because it isolates the cost of learning one local pattern under network bandwidth constraints. A sharp answer would distinguish the communication needed for deciding existence from the communication needed for distributing all witnesses, and would test how far current lower-bound methods reach.
cards.definitions: $\widetilde O$ suppresses polylogarithmic factors. Local computation is unrestricted, vertex identifiers have $O(\log n)$ bits, and the communication graph is exactly $G$, not an all-to-all overlay. Nodes may know $n$. The output convention avoids charging the graph diameter merely to inform every vertex of a remote triangle. The triangle is a subgraph on three distinct mutually adjacent vertices.

progress.text: Chang, Pettie, Saranurak, and Zhang give $\widetilde O(n^{1/3})$-round algorithms for triangle enumeration, counting, and detection. The matching enumeration lower bound does not establish the same detection lower bound.
Assadi and Sundaresan prove an $\Omega(\log\log n)$ lower bound for deterministic and randomized detection, providing the first lower bound beyond a single round.
Censor-Hillel’s ADGA survey explicitly retains the round complexity of CONGEST triangle detection as an open problem after incorporating that lower bound.

cards.status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. The 2025 multi-round lower bound is included; the detection/listing distinction is essential.

context_blocks.text: Every vertex knows two of the three edges of a triangle containing it. The missing information is whether two of its neighbors are adjacent. If messages had unlimited length, neighbors could exchange their complete adjacency lists in one round. The difficulty comes from fitting the relevant information through bounded-capacity edges.

For example, a vertex with many neighbors cannot simply send its entire neighborhood to every neighbor in one short message. On the other hand, most pairs of its neighbors may be irrelevant, so transmitting every adjacency list can be wasteful. An algorithm must exploit the topology to decide which information needs to move and where it can be combined.

Detection asks for one bit of global evidence, whereas listing requires the network collectively to output every triangle. A graph can contain a cubic number of triangles. cards.title: Constant-round MIS in the congested clique
cards.formal: Is there a randomized algorithm that, on every n-vertex simple input graph, finds a maximal independent set in O(1) rounds in the Congested Clique model, with success probability at least $1-n^{-c}$ for every requested fixed $c>0$? Processor v initially knows its identifier and incident input edges. Every ordered pair of processors may exchange an O(log n)-bit message per synchronous round, whether or not the input edge exists. Each processor outputs whether it belongs to an independent set that dominates every vertex outside it. The algorithm must be uniform across inputs; it cannot be chosen after seeing the graph.
cards.why: I include this beside the LOCAL MIS problem because it tests a different limitation of distributed computation: restricted bandwidth despite universal communication. A constant-round algorithm would show that exact local domination needs only a bounded number of global exchanges. A lower bound would have to explain why distributed processing cannot avoid the bottleneck.
cards.definitions: Here $\Delta$ is the maximum degree of the input graph, not of the communication network. Messages to different recipients may differ. Local computation is unrestricted. $O(1)$ means independent of both $n$ and $\Delta$, with constants allowed to depend on the requested failure exponent. This is the unicast Congested Clique, rather than the weaker broadcast variant.

context_blocks.text: This changes the communication network while leaving the graph problem unchanged. A vertex can contact a distant processor immediately, so graph distance no longer limits the spread of information. Bandwidth still matters: one processor can receive only $O(n\log n)$ bits per round, whereas a general graph can contain $\Theta(n^2)$ independently specified edges. Sending the entire input to one leader is therefore not a constant-round solution.

That bottleneck is not itself a lower bound for MIS. A complete graph has many edges but is easy: a designated vertex can join the independent set and all others can stay out. The sought algorithm only needs enough information to coordinate a valid answer; it need not reconstruct every edge in one place.

Known algorithms exploit this by solving suitably sparse sampled subgraphs and reducing the remaining degrees. The general upper bound is $O(\log\log\Delta)$ rounds. The central question is whether a bounded number of communication phases can remove the need for repeated sparsification.

A closely related relaxation is already possible in constant rounds: a 2-ruling set remains independent but only has to put every vertex within distance two of a selected vertex. MIS requires distance one. This supplies a precise nearby success case against which to assess the unresolved target.

cards.title: Exact semidefinite feasibility in polynomial time
cards.formal: Is the following language in P in the ordinary Turing model: all lists of symmetric rational matrices A_0,A_1,…,A_m∈Q^{n×n} for which there exists a real vector x∈R^m satisfying A_0+sum_{i=1}^m x_i A_i⪰0? Both m and n are unbounded parts of the input, and the algorithm must decide exact nonemptiness in time polynomial in the total binary encoding length.
cards.definitions: Every matrix entry is an explicitly supplied rational number, with signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator; all matrices have the same size n≥1. A symmetric matrix M is positive semidefinite, written M⪰0, when zᵀMz≥0 for every real vector z, equivalently when all eigenvalues are nonnegative. The unknown x ranges over all real vectors, not just rational vectors. Singular feasible matrices count as YES. There is no strict-feasibility, boundedness, conditioning, rank, or distance-to-infeasibility promise, and no radius or accuracy parameter is supplied. The output is one bit specifying whether any feasible x exists; an explicit feasible point is not required. An affine subspace given by rational linear equations can be parametrized by rational Gaussian elimination, so this is also the rational-affine-subspace intersection formulation. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A basic boundary between numerical convex optimization and exact efficient computation. cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The primary literature retains general exact SDP feasibility as an open polynomial-time problem. Ramana’s dual does not establish NP∩coNP membership in the Turing model, and recent convex-polynomial optimization results address a different constraint family. This card permits real witnesses, singular feasible points, weak infeasibility and unbounded feasible regions.

context_blocks.text: Semidefinite constraints replace scalar nonnegativity by nonnegativity of a quadratic form in every direction. They include linear inequalities as the diagonal-matrix special case and support powerful relaxations in combinatorial optimization. Approximation algorithms are well developed, but their guarantees require attention to input geometry and numerical precision. De Klerk and Vallentin establish polynomial bit complexity for a short-step interior-point method under appropriate assumptions; their theorem is about controlled approximation, not arbitrary exact feasibility.

The unrestricted problem is decidable. Introduce a real n×n matrix Y and impose A_0+sum_i x_i A_i=YYᵀ. These are finitely many polynomial equations of degree at most two, and a real symmetric matrix is positive semidefinite exactly when such a factor exists. General real-algebraic decision procedures therefore apply. Henrion, Naldi and Safey El Din develop more specialized symbolic algorithms, including treatment of degenerate feasible sets. None of this supplies polynomial time when both input dimensions vary.

Exact feasibility can differ even from arbitrarily close approximation. The matrix M(t) with rows (0,1) and (1,t) has determinant −1, so it is never positive semidefinite. Yet as t tends to positive infinity, its negative eigenvalue (t−√(t²+4))/2 tends to zero. Thus these infeasible matrices approach the positive semidefinite cone arbitrarily closely. A numerical tolerance alone cannot distinguish this situation from a singular feasible matrix.

Rational input also need not admit a rational witness. Consider a block diagonal matrix with blocks [[x,2],[2,2x]] and [[2,x],[x,1]]. The first block is positive semidefinite exactly when x≥√2, and the second when |x|≤√2. The whole matrix is therefore feasible exactly at x=√2. All coefficient matrices are rational, but searching only rational substitutions would miss the solution. This example explains why the domain of the unknowns is part of the formal question.

Even rational feasible points can be enormous. Conditions x_1≥2 and [[x_{i+1},x_i],[x_i,1]]⪰0 force x_{i+1}≥x_i², hence x_k≥2^{2^{k−1}}. A block diagonal LMI encodes the chain compactly, while writing its final coordinate in ordinary binary needs exponentially many digits in k. Pataki and Touzov analyze how such growth arises beyond isolated examples, including connections to singularity degree. Large explicit witnesses obstruct a naive search algorithm; they do not prove that deciding existence is hard.

Ramana’s exact dual provides an alternative feasibility system of polynomial description size without regularity assumptions. In the Turing model, it implies that semidefinite feasibility belongs to NP if and only if it belongs to coNP. It does not establish either membership individually. The corresponding NP∩coNP theorem over exact real-number machines belongs to a different computational model. This distinction prevents a common overstatement of what SDP duality proves about bit complexity.
Pataki’s October 2025 work gives a new derivation and a fuller description of the feasible set of Ramana’s dual using facial reduction.

A separate STOC 2026 result by Slot, Steurer and Wiedmer obtains small approximate solutions for minimizing convex polynomials over polyhedra. That result concerns polynomial objectives with linear constraints; the authors explicitly contrast it with the large-solution obstacle for semidefinite programs. It does not settle general exact semidefinite feasibility.

cards.title: Conforti–Cornuéjols conjecture
cards.formal: Does every finite clutter with the packing property have the max-flow min-cut property? Equivalently, if every deletion/contraction minor satisfies unweighted integral packing–covering equality, must weighted integral packing–covering equality hold for every nonnegative integer weight vector?
cards.definitions: A clutter C on a finite ground set E is a family of subsets of E, no one properly containing another. In the original instance all members are nonempty; the empty family is allowed. A cover T⊆E meets every member, and τ(C) is the smallest cover size. A packing is a family of pairwise disjoint members, with maximum size ν(C). Deleting e removes e from the ground set and discards all members containing e. Contracting e removes it from the ground set and from every member, and retains only inclusion-minimal resulting members. A minor results from any sequence of these operations. The packing property means τ(C′)=ν(C′) for every minor C′. For the empty family both values are zero; for a minor containing the empty set both are defined as +∞, with the empty member permitted arbitrarily many times in a packing. For w∈ℤ_{≥0}^E, let τ_w(C)=min{Σ_{e∈T}w_e:T covers C}. Let ν_w(C) be the maximum of Σ_{F∈C}y_F over nonnegative integers y_F satisfying Σ_{F∋e}y_F≤w_e for every e∈E. Thus a weighted packing may use a member repeatedly, subject to capacities w. The max-flow min-cut property is τ_w(C)=ν_w(C) for every such w. The original nonempty-member assumption makes these weighted optima finite.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that the packing property implies τ_w=ν_w for every finite clutter and every nonnegative integer weight vector, or give a finite clutter and weight vector with the packing property and τ_w>ν_w. A counterexample must verify equality for all minors, not merely for the original unweighted clutter. Finite searches, proofs for a proper subclass, or fractional optimality alone do not resolve the universal statement.

context_blocks.text: Packing and covering often give two descriptions of the same combinatorial optimum. In a clutter, the unweighted equality can fail. Requiring equality after every deletion and contraction removes many such obstructions. The Conforti–Cornuéjols conjecture asks whether this local robustness already guarantees equality for every integer capacity vector.

For a concrete example, take E as the vertices of a bipartite graph and the clutter members as its edges. Covers are vertex covers and packings are matchings. This illustrates the familiar kind of min–max equality that the general conjecture seeks to characterize, without restricting its input to graph edge families.

If A is the member-by-element incidence matrix, the associated linear programs are min wᵀx subject to Ax≥1 and x≥0, and max 1ᵀy subject to Aᵀy≤w and y≥0. Equality of the two integer optima forces their values to agree with the fractional optimum by weak and strong duality. This is the standard MFMC integrality requirement.

Schrijver’s Survey Question 68 calls the target the assertion that every packing hypergraph is Mengerian. The terminology differs, but its packing property includes all minors and its conclusion includes arbitrary nonnegative integer weights. Checking only the all-ones weight on the original instance would yield a much weaker, insufficient hypothesis.

Abdi and Schwarcz’s July 2026 manuscript calls the statement the replication conjecture and explicitly retains it as open. It reports verification for clutters on at most ten elements and for a specified bounded-degree family of cuboids. These are finite or restricted confirmations, not a proof for arbitrary ground-set size.

The same work gives a finite set of weight vectors sufficient to test the MFMC property of a fixed clutter, with an improved bound on their entries. This makes checking individual instances more effective. The number and size of possible clutters still grow without bound, so instance-wise testability does not prove the universal implication.

cards.why: Identify whether all obstructions to weighted integral packing–covering duality are already visible as unweighted failures in minors, a central issue in integer programming and combinatorial optimization.

importance.reason: A central conjecture connecting minor obstructions, integral linear programming and packing–covering duality. Schrijver treats it as a major survey question, and a July 2026 primary paper develops both theoretical and computational methods around it.

cards.definitions: S²={x∈ℝ³: x₁²+x₂²+x₃²=1}. The energy is E_N(x₁,…,x_N)=Σ_{i≠j}−ln‖x_i−x_j‖₂, counting ordered pairs; collisions have energy +∞. E_N* is the infimum over all N-tuples on S². ln is the natural logarithm and ‖·‖₂ is Euclidean distance. The algorithm is one finite real-arithmetic program with a fixed finite list of real constants, independent of N. It has exact real registers and a finite-control tape machine with register copying, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero register, and branching on the sign of a register. Tape movements and each scalar arithmetic, comparison or copy operation have unit cost. Input is the integer N as an exact real value; output is a list of 3N real coordinates. Any finite tape/register storage used by the program is charged through its operations. There is no primitive logarithm, square root, floor, random sample or minimization oracle. Polynomial time is in N, not in log N. The inequality is a mathematical condition on the output; the algorithm need not evaluate the energy. This specifies the real-number computation convention in Smale’s problem; coordinates need not be rational and no bit-cost bound is asserted.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer supplies one permitted real-arithmetic program and constants C,K,k, fixed independently of N, with the stated running time and total-energy guarantee for every integer N≥2. A negative answer proves that no such program and constants exist. Failure of one construction, a lower bound for a restricted method, or energy estimates for finitely many cardinalities do not establish the negation.

context_blocks.text: Imagine placing mutually repelling particles on a sphere. For this problem, a pair contributes minus the logarithm of its straight-line distance through three-dimensional space. Bringing two points together sends their contribution to positive infinity. Spreading points lowers the energy, but the question asks for a guarantee against the best configuration of the entire collection, rather than against a locally stable arrangement. Exact minimizers are called elliptic Fekete configurations.

For two points the answer is concrete: opposite poles have distance 2, the largest possible distance on the unit sphere, and ordered-pair energy −2 ln 2. For general N an optimum still exists: the sphere is compact, collisions have infinite energy, and some distinct configuration has finite energy. Existence therefore is not the open part. The unresolved requirement is one fixed algorithm with a polynomial operation bound for every N.

The tolerance C ln N is an additive error in the total energy. It is small compared with its known expansion E_N*=(1/2−ln 2)N²−(N/2)ln N+aN+o(N), where a is a universal constant. Matching only the leading N² term, or even allowing a linear error, leaves far more uncertainty than the target permits. Uniform-looking points and good numerical values for finitely many N do not establish this error bound.

Smale’s original statement counts each unordered pair once. This card counts each pair twice, as in much subsequent literature. Both the optimum and excess energy are doubled, so the existence of a universal logarithmic-error constant is unchanged. The real-arithmetic model also comes from Smale’s formulation: a step manipulates an exact real value. A polynomial number of such steps does not assert polynomial bit complexity, and the output inequality does not give the program a free logarithm or minimization instruction.

The generalized Diamond ensemble supplies configurations for every N with a precisely analyzed expected energy: the two leading terms above plus a specified linear term and an O(√N ln N) remainder. These constructions quantify how well a structured distribution spreads points. That estimate is not a deterministic C ln N excess guarantee relative to the unknown optimum.

Beltrán and Hardy obtain the required logarithmic excess for a low-temperature Coulomb-gas distribution: at inverse temperature N, the mean excess is at most 9 ln N, and excess at most 10 ln N holds with probability at least 1−exp(−N ln N). The theorem analyzes the distribution, while polynomial-time sampling from it remains an additional computational issue. A probabilistic existence statement also differs from the deterministic algorithm asked for here.

Michelen and Yakir prove a central limit theorem for the energy of zeros of a rotationally invariant random polynomial, with fluctuations on the √N scale. This measures variation around that ensemble’s mean, not error from the global minimum.

Recent exact algebraic work by Armentano and coauthors classifies critical configurations with at most six points, and treats seven points under an antipodal-pair restriction. Such finite classifications do not supply a uniform algorithm for arbitrary N.

The original motivation connects low-energy spherical points, through stereographic projection, to well-conditioned polynomials and the complexity of finding polynomial roots. The energy question has its own stronger output guarantee; progress on polynomial conditioning or on a different Smale problem does not automatically resolve it. It also asks a basic algorithmic question in discrete potential theory: how cheaply can globally near-equilibrium configurations be constructed?

cards.title: Polynomial-time simplex pivot rule
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform deterministic primal-simplex pivot algorithm and a polynomial p such that, for every rational linear program max{cᵀx: Ax=b, x≥0} with A of full row rank, a finite optimum, and any supplied feasible basis B_0, the algorithm reaches a basis whose reduced costs are all nonpositive using at most p(L) bit operations in total? Here L is the binary input length of A,b,c and B_0, and every basis change must be a legal improving simplex pivot as defined below.
cards.definitions: A has m rows and n columns with 1≤m≤n; all rational numerators and positive denominators are explicit binary integers. A basis B is a set of m columns with invertible A_B. Its basic solution is x_B=A_B^{-1}b and x_j=0 for j∉B, and feasibility means x_B≥0. An entering column j∉B must have reduced cost r_j=c_j−c_BᵀA_B^{-1}A_j>0. Put a=A_B^{-1}A_j. Choose a leaving basic index i attaining θ=min_{k∈B:a_k>0}x_k/a_k, and replace i by j in the basis. The finite-optimum promise ensures that this minimum exists for an improving column. Ties may be resolved by the rule; θ=0 is an allowed degenerate pivot and counts toward the bound. The rule may inspect the whole input and maintain history, with all preprocessing, pivot selection, exact arithmetic, helper computations and memory operations charged to p(L). It must follow these basis exchanges on the supplied LP from B_0: it may not jump to another feasible basis or replace the feasible region by an extended formulation. The required terminal condition r_j≤0 for all j∉B certifies optimality. This is the supplied-feasible-basis optimization version; phase-I feasibility construction is not part of this card.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct such a rule and prove its total polynomial bit complexity for every promised input and initial feasible basis, or prove that no such rule exists. Merely bounding the number of pivots while leaving their selection computationally unbounded is insufficient. A lower bound for a prescribed family of rules, or for nonlinear objectives, does not establish the negative answer for all rules here.
cards.why: A fundamental question about whether local, improving basis exchanges can support efficient global optimization. It would explain a central practical algorithm and sharpen the relationship between polyhedral geometry, degeneracy and algorithmic access to an optimum.

importance.reason: A longstanding foundational problem about one of the most important optimization algorithms; the existence and efficient discovery of short improving basis paths remain unresolved even though LP itself is polynomial-time solvable.

progress.text: Spielman and Teng establish polynomial smoothed complexity for a simplex algorithm; this is a distributional guarantee rather than worst-case polynomial bit complexity.

Bach, Disser, Huiberts and Mosis strengthen the all-rules active-set lower bound to convex quadratic maximization. The latest preprint version is dated 22 October 2025.
Disser, Loho, Maat and Mosis publish superpolynomial lower bounds for specified ranking-based classes, with explicit information and memory restrictions.

Kukharenko and Sanità publish an antistalling rule bounding consecutive degenerate pivots at a nonoptimal vertex by n−m−1, given an improving feasible direction. It leaves the global pivot count open.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The STACS 2026 and March 2026 primary publications retain the general polynomial simplex question as open. This card fixes deterministic total bit complexity for legal improving primal-simplex pivots from any supplied feasible basis on a finite-optimum rational LP. Strongly polynomial algorithms, nonlinear active-set bounds and distributional performance are distinct formulations.

context_blocks.text: Linear programming already has algorithms with polynomial bit complexity, including ellipsoid and interior-point methods. The unresolved question is whether the same guarantee can be achieved while moving through bases by the simplex method. A pivot rule determines which improving direction to expose next and how to break ties. The STACS 2026 paper on ranking-based rules states that the general question remains open.

There are two obstacles to a polynomial guarantee. First, a short route to an optimal basis must exist under the permitted improving moves. Second, the rule must discover such a route efficiently. Knowing the optimum from another computation does not authorize skipping the route: every intervening basis exchange is still required. Likewise, a short path in the undirected graph of a polyhedron need not be a short path along improving edges.

The bit-complexity requirement is deliberately weaker than strongly polynomial simplex. It permits the running time to depend polynomially on the number of bits in coefficients. A strongly polynomial rule would instead bound its arithmetic work polynomially in m and n, together with appropriate bounds on the sizes of numbers used. Therefore this card does not assert that a positive answer alone settles Smale’s strongly polynomial LP problem or a diameter bound depending only on dimension and number of facets.

Degeneracy means several bases can describe the same vertex. A legal pivot with θ=0 changes the basis without improving the objective value, so an algorithm can stall even if the geometric route is short. Kukharenko and Sanità’s March 2026 paper bounds a block of consecutive degenerate pivots at a nonoptimal vertex by n−m−1, given an improving feasible direction. Such a direction can be obtained using an LP solver. This controls local stalling, but does not bound how many different nonoptimal vertices the method must visit.

Positive average-case results are also substantial. Spielman and Teng show polynomial smoothed complexity for a simplex algorithm under random perturbations of the input. Smoothed analysis studies the expected behavior around an arbitrary instance as a function of perturbation size. It helps explain good practical performance, but does not give a deterministic worst-case guarantee on every exact rational instance.

The 2026 ranking-based lower bounds exclude broader families than a single greedy rule. One result covers index-ranking rules with a specified limit on their memory states; another covers memoryless rules using rankings by index, reduced cost and objective improvement. Full access to numerical data and unrestricted polynomially bounded history are allowed in this card, so those lower bounds do not cover every candidate.

A striking neighboring result does exclude every pivot rule for the active-set method with a nonlinear objective. Disser and Mosis first use higher-degree polynomial objectives on the hypercube. Bach and coauthors then obtain the phenomenon for maximizing a convex quadratic function, published at SODA 2026. The direction of optimization matters: this is convex maximization. Their construction does not have a linear objective, and the authors explicitly distinguish it from a general simplex lower bound.

cards.title: Komlós conjecture
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal real constant C>0 such that, for all integers m,n≥1 and every real matrix A∈ℝ^{m×n} with ∑_{i=1}^m A_{ij}²≤1 for each column j, there is a vector x∈{−1,1}^n satisfying max_{1≤i≤m}|∑_{j=1}^n A_{ij}x_j|≤C?
cards.definitions: All matrices are finite. Columns may have arbitrary real entries, including negative entries. The sign vector may depend on the entire matrix; C may not depend on the dimensions or entries. This is an existence question, with no algorithmic or input-encoding requirement.

context_blocks.text: Discrepancy measures how accurately a fractional choice can be replaced by signs while controlling many linear constraints simultaneously. Komlós asks whether normalizing every column in Euclidean norm suffices to bound every coordinate of the signed sum by an absolute constant.

The 2025 improvement gives a polylogarithmic bound smaller than the classical square-root-logarithmic bound, but does not reach a constant. Komlós implies the Beck–Fiala conjecture after scaling an incidence matrix; the converse is not known. Both are retained as established landmarks with different hypotheses, rather than as unrelated questions.

cards.title: P-matrix linear complementarity in polynomial time
cards.formal: Is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given n≥1, a rational P-matrix M∈Q^(n×n) and q∈Q^n, outputs rational vectors z,w≥0 satisfying w=Mz+q and zᵀw=0?
cards.definitions: A principal submatrix M[S,S] uses the same nonempty index set S⊆{1,…,n} for rows and columns. M is a P-matrix when det M[S,S]>0 for every such S. All matrix and vector entries are explicitly listed as binary signed numerators and positive denominators; N denotes their total bit length including dimensions and separators. The algorithm is a deterministic multitape Turing machine whose running time, including output, is at most one polynomial p(N) independent of n and the entries. It must terminate within that bound on all syntactically valid rational inputs, but its output is required to satisfy the equations only when M is a P-matrix. No P-matrix recognition or certificate is supplied or required. Inequalities are coordinatewise, and zᵀw=Σ_i z_i w_i. There is no symmetry, positive-definiteness, sparsity, nondegeneracy or coefficient-size promise beyond rational encoding and the P-matrix condition. A numerical approximation alone is not an output solution.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.

context_blocks.text: Complementarity combines linear constraints with a discrete choice: in each coordinate, at least one of z_i and w_i must vanish. For example, when M is the identity, a negative entry of q is compensated by a positive z entry, while a positive q entry remains in w. For a general matrix the coordinates interact, so the zero pattern cannot be chosen independently.

The P-matrix condition guarantees exactly one solution for every right-hand side q. This removes failure of existence and ambiguity of the answer, yet does not supply a polynomial-time method to find that answer. The distinction is a central example of total search: a mathematical existence theorem can be much easier to state than a fast algorithmic realization.

Exact rational output is meaningful in the bit model. Once a complementary zero pattern is fixed, the remaining coordinates satisfy a nonsingular rational linear system on a principal submatrix. Determinant bounds give polynomial bit length for the solution. Thus the question does not hide an unavoidable exponentially long output.

Several matrix subclasses admit polynomial algorithms. Results for tridiagonal and Hessenberg P-matrices demonstrate how additional structure can make the problem tractable. Such restrictions are absent from this card. Likewise, a polynomial iteration count involving a condition-dependent parameter does not give a polynomial bound in the full input length without a bound on that parameter.

ETH’s 2025 research report identifies general P-matrix LCP as a major unresolved optimization question and relates it to unique-sink orientations. The current target concerns solving rational LCP instances, not recognizing the P-matrix promise and not solving every abstract orientation problem. It complements the existing cards for linear programming and exact semidefinite feasibility.

cards.title: Beck–Fiala conjecture
cards.formal: Is there a universal C>0 such that, for all integers m,n,t≥1 and every A∈{0,1}^{m×n} having at most t ones in each column, some x∈{−1,1}^n satisfies max_i |∑_j A_{ij}x_j|≤C√t?
cards.definitions: The matrix is the incidence matrix of a finite set system: its columns are elements and its rows are sets. Thus each element belongs to at most t sets. Empty sets and unused elements are allowed. The bound is independent of the number of elements and sets. The question asks for existence of a signing, without an algorithmic time requirement.

context_blocks.text: Bounded element frequency is a basic sparsity assumption in rounding problems. The conjecture asks whether its discrepancy cost is proportional to the square root of the frequency even when the system is arbitrarily large.

Recent results prove this scale for substantial ranges of t relative to the size of the system. The full statement includes all frequencies and remains stronger than those range-restricted results. The separate Komlós conjecture implies this statement by rescaling each incidence column.

cards.why: A central discrepancy conjecture governing how local incidence restrictions control global rounding error.

cards.title: Woodall’s conjecture
cards.formal: For every finite weakly connected loopless directed multigraph D that is not strongly connected, let τ(D) be the minimum size of a directed cut. Must D contain τ(D) pairwise arc-disjoint dijoins?
cards.definitions: A directed multigraph has a finite vertex set V and a finite set A of individually distinguished arcs; parallel arcs are allowed and loops are excluded. Weak connectivity means connectivity after forgetting arc directions. Strong connectivity means that every ordered pair of vertices is joined by a directed path. For ∅≠U⊊V, let δ⁺(U) be the arcs with tail in U and head outside U, and δ⁻(U) the arcs entering U. A directed cut, or dicut, is δ⁺(U) with δ⁻(U)=∅. Under the stated graph assumptions the family of dicuts is nonempty and each dicut has positive size, so τ(D)=min{|δ⁺(U)|:∅≠U⊊V, δ⁻(U)=∅} is a finite positive integer. A dijoin is a subset J⊆A meeting every dicut. Pairwise arc-disjoint means Jᵢ∩Jⱼ=∅ for i≠j. Every arc has unit capacity; no zero-capacity arcs or other weights are included.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of τ(D) pairwise disjoint dijoins for every stated D, or give a finite D satisfying the assumptions and prove that its maximum packing is smaller than τ(D). Since each dijoin must meet a smallest dicut, τ(D) is always an upper bound. An approximation by a constant fraction of τ, a fractional packing, or a theorem confined to a proper graph subclass is partial progress.

context_blocks.text: A dijoin selects arcs that collectively intercept every one-way boundary of a digraph. Packing dijoins asks how many separate selections can provide this complete coverage without sharing an arc. The smallest one-way boundary is an immediate bottleneck. Woodall’s conjecture says that this visible bottleneck is the only obstruction.

Schrijver lists this exact min–max equality as Survey Question 34. The adjacent Question 33 asks for a polynomial-time algorithm finding a maximum packing. The equality is the structural target here; no efficient construction is demanded as part of a positive answer.

The absence of weights matters. The stronger Edmonds–Giles statement permits arcs of capacity zero as well as one and is false. Deleting a zero-capacity arc can change which sets are dicuts, so it cannot generally turn a weighted counterexample into an unweighted one. The current formulation avoids that false strengthening.

Cornuéjols, Liu and Ravi prove that at least ⌊τ/6⌋ disjoint dijoins can be constructed in polynomial time. Their argument connects dijoin packing to nowhere-zero flows in the underlying undirected graph. This supplies a constant-factor guarantee while retaining the exact Woodall equality as open.

Weakly disconnected graphs have a zero-size cut and give a trivial zero-packing case. Strongly connected graphs have no dicuts, making the empty set a vacuous dijoin. Restricting the statement to the nontrivial case fixes the meaning of the minimum and maximum without changing the substantive conjecture.

This belongs to combinatorial optimization through the relation between packing and covering, integrality and constructive approximation. It is distinct from a minimum-cost dijoin problem or from maximum directed cut: those optimize different objects, even though some of the vocabulary overlaps.

cards.why: Determine whether the minimum directed-cut capacity exactly characterizes the number of independently usable directed-cut covers, extending the reach of integral packing–covering duality.

cards.title: Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant C<∞ such that, for every dimension n≥1, every isotropic log-concave probability measure μ on ℝⁿ, and every locally Lipschitz f:ℝⁿ→ℝ with finite second moment and finite gradient energy, $\operatorname{Var}_\mu(f)\le C\int\|\nabla f(x)\|_2^2\,d\mu(x)$? This is the Poincaré formulation of the Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture.
cards.definitions: The measure has a Lebesgue density ρ=e^{−V}, where V:ℝⁿ→ℝ∪{+∞} is convex and ∫ρ=1; allowing V=+∞ includes uniform distributions on full-dimensional convex bodies. Isotropy means ∫x dμ(x)=0 and ∫xxᵀ dμ(x)=Iₙ. Variance is Varμ(f)=∫(f−∫f dμ)²dμ, and ∇f is the almost-everywhere Euclidean gradient. Let C_P(μ) be the infimum of constants that make the displayed inequality hold for all the stated f. The requested bound is supₙ supμ C_P(μ)<∞, with μ ranging over isotropic log-concave measures in ℝⁿ. There is no symmetry, product structure, smoothness, or positive lower curvature bound on V. The universal constant may depend on none of n, μ, or f. In the isoperimetric convention used by the recent papers, ψμ is the reciprocal Cheeger expansion constant; ψμ² is comparable to C_P(μ) up to universal factors. Thus a bound on ψμ must be squared when expressed as a bound on the Poincaré constant used here.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: KLS links the geometry of high-dimensional convex sets to spectral gaps, concentration, and the efficiency of sampling. It asks whether covariance normalization alone removes every dimension-dependent bottleneck for log-concave measures, making it a central structural question behind continuous randomized algorithms.

importance.reason: A foundational high-dimensional geometry conjecture with substantial consequences for sampling, integration, optimization, and concentration inequalities.

progress.text: Kannan, Lovász, and Simonovits formulate the isoperimetric conjecture in connection with localization and random-walk sampling in convex bodies.
Klartag and Lehec obtain the first polylogarithmic bounds for the KLS isoperimetric constant using stochastic-localization techniques.
Klartag proves ψμ=O(√log n), equivalently C_P(μ)=O(log n), through an improved log-concave Lichnerowicz inequality.
Klartag and Lehec settle the thin-shell conjecture. The 23 February 2026 revision controls E(‖X‖₂−√n)² uniformly, a particular radial concentration target rather than the full Poincaré inequality.

Letwin’s preprint reports Var(XᵀMX)≤2E‖∇(XᵀMX)‖₂² for every symmetric M and isotropic log-concave X, and derives ψₙ=O((log n)^{1/4}). In this card’s normalization the resulting general-function bound is C_P=O(√log n), not O((log n)^{1/4}).

cards.status_note: The full KLS conjecture is explicitly open in the primary sources, including Letwin’s July 2026 preprint. Research through 10 September 2026 found no dimension-free general-function resolution. The recent quadratic-form and thin-shell results are not treated as proofs of the full conjecture; the July bound is labeled as a preprint result.

context_blocks.text: The inequality asks whether a function can vary substantially across a log-concave distribution while changing only slowly in the regions where that distribution places mass. Isotropy fixes the scale: each unit-direction linear function already has variance one and gradient energy one. The conjecture says that nonlinear functions cannot create an arbitrarily larger ratio as dimension grows.

The geometric version rules out a hidden bottleneck separating two substantial portions of the measure. For a log-concave density, the conjecture says that the best arbitrary separating set has boundary expansion comparable to an appropriate halfspace cut. Uniform distributions on convex bodies are included, so the question is not confined to smooth, strongly convex potentials where curvature can directly control a spectral gap.

The original algorithmic motivation was sampling by random walks. Poor expansion can trap a local walk in one part of a body for a long time; good expansion bounds its mixing. Sampling then supports volume estimation, integration, and convex optimization. A KLS theorem would improve the geometric ingredient in these analyses, though total algorithmic complexity would still account for access to the body, initialization, and the chosen walk.

Thin-shell concentration concerns the special observable ‖X‖₂. Klartag and Lehec’s 2025 result, revised in February 2026, bounds E(‖X‖₂−√n)² by a universal constant. This settles thin-shell concentration and also supports the resolved slicing question, but does not by itself control every test function in the Poincaré inequality. These neighboring geometric conjectures must therefore be tracked separately.

The remaining dimension dependence is small but substantive. Klartag’s 2023 theorem gives C_P(μ)=O(log n). Letwin’s July 2026 preprint reports a dimension-free inequality for quadratic forms and derives ψμ=O((log n)^{1/4}), hence C_P(μ)=O(√log n). The latter is a reported preprint improvement, and even that estimate still leaves a growing factor rather than the universal constant required here.

cards.title: Polynomial Hirsch conjecture
cards.formal: Do universal constants C>0 and k≥1 exist such that every nonempty pointed d-dimensional convex polyhedron with n facets has vertex-edge graph diameter at most C(n+d)^k?
cards.definitions: A polyhedron is an intersection of finitely many closed affine halfspaces over the real numbers. Work in its affine hull, identified with R^d, where d≥1, and require it to be pointed, meaning that it contains no affine line; this ensures that its vertices are present. Both bounded polyhedra, called polytopes, and unbounded pointed polyhedra are included. The number n counts distinct facets in an irredundant description, rather than repeated input inequalities. The graph G(P) has one vertex per geometric vertex of P and an undirected edge between u and v precisely when their segment is a bounded one-dimensional face of P. An unbounded ray is not an extra graph vertex or an edge to infinity. Graph distance counts edges, each at unit cost; diameter is the maximum distance between vertices and is zero for a one-vertex polyhedron. The constants C,k must be independent of dimension, facet count, coordinates, coefficient bit length and the choice of polyhedron. Real coordinates are allowed, and no simplicity or nondegeneracy assumption is made. Paths need not improve any objective function, and no algorithm for finding them is required.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: Determine whether all polyhedral feasible regions have uniformly short edge routes, a central structural question underlying linear programming.

importance.reason: The surviving fundamental diameter question after the original Hirsch bound failed; it separates geometric existence of short routes from algorithmic navigation and the newly resolved circuit analogue.

progress.text: Kalai–Kleitman establish a quasipolynomial general edge-diameter bound; Todd’s paper records and sharpens the recurrence-based result.
Santos disproves the original linear Hirsch conjecture with a 43-dimensional bounded polytope having 86 facets.
Todd proves the upper bound (n−d)^{log₂d}.
Sukegawa’s asymptotic improvement lowers the exponent by log₂log d up to an additive constant, still quasipolynomial.
The ETH geometry notes retain the polynomial problem; Wulf establishes Π₂^p-hardness of computing diameters even for bipartite perfect-matching polytopes.
Natura’s revised manuscript proves polynomial circuit diameter, including monotone circuit walks; ordinary edge diameter remains open.

cards.status_note: No polynomial upper bound or superpolynomial counterexample for the stated worst-case edge-diameter problem was found through 11 September 2026. Natura’s 2026 result resolves the circuit analogue and explicitly leaves the combinatorial problem open. The card includes bounded and pointed unbounded polyhedra, counts facets, and imposes neither monotonicity nor an efficient path-finding requirement.

context_blocks.text: The feasible region of a linear program is a polyhedron. Its vertices are candidate basic feasible solutions, and its edges describe elementary geometric moves between them. The diameter asks for the largest minimum number of such moves between any two vertices. It is therefore a question about the geometry of feasible solutions before one chooses a particular rule for navigating them.

The facet count is the relevant measure of description size here. A polyhedron described by a modest number of inequalities can have exponentially many vertices, so the trivial bound by the number of vertices is far too large. The d-dimensional cube illustrates the distinction: it has 2d facets and 2^d vertices, yet its diameter is only d because one can change differing coordinates one at a time.

Polynomial means a fixed exponent that works in every dimension. An n^d upper bound is polynomial in n when d is held fixed, but does not answer this question. Neither does a bound whose constant grows exponentially with d. The card includes pointed unbounded polyhedra, matching the saved formulation; pointedness removes polyhedra with no vertices, for which a vertex-graph diameter would not express the intended problem.

Hirsch originally proposed the much sharper n−d bound for bounded polytopes. Santos’s counterexample, announced in 2010 and published in 2012, has dimension 43 and 86 facets, with diameter exceeding 43. This refutes that linear expression, but it remains fully compatible with a bound such as Cn² or Cn¹⁰. The distinction between failure of one attractive formula and failure of every polynomial is the reason a major open question survived.

General upper bounds are quasipolynomial. Kalai and Kleitman’s 1992 argument gave n^{2+log₂d}; Todd improved it in 2014 to (n−d)^{log₂d}. For large d, Sukegawa’s later asymptotic refinement has the form (n−d)^{log₂d−log₂log d+O(1)}. The last exponent still grows with dimension. These are substantial structural bounds, but they do not reach one universal constant exponent.

The conjecture concerns shortest available paths, not the paths a chosen simplex pivot rule happens to take. A rule may visit exponentially many vertices even on a polytope whose graph has small diameter. Conversely, proving that short undirected paths exist would not tell a solver which edge to select efficiently, or ensure a short path that improves a specified linear objective at every step. Polynomial diameter is a geometric ingredient, not by itself a strongly polynomial linear-programming algorithm.

Recent complexity results make the distinction sharper. Wulf’s FOCS 2025 paper proves Π₂^p-hardness of computing the diameter of bipartite perfect-matching polytopes, and the corresponding decision problem is complete for that class. Such hardness is compatible with a polynomial upper bound on the value of the diameter. A small optimum can be difficult to compute exactly, just as short witnesses can be difficult to find.

Natura’s February 2026 paper proves a polynomial bound for a different geometric distance: circuit diameter. For a standard-form polyhedron {x∈R^N:Ax=b,x≥0}, with A having r rows, the stated bound is O(r²log r), and the construction also supplies monotone circuit walks. Circuit directions are support-minimal dependencies of A; a maximal feasible step in such a direction need not stay on an edge of the current polyhedron.

Every edge step is allowed among the circuit moves, but the converse fails. Consequently, a short circuit walk gives no automatic equally short edge walk: its intermediate points may lie inside higher-dimensional faces. The 2026 theorem settles the circuit analogue of the polynomial conjecture, while its introduction explicitly retains the ordinary combinatorial-diameter problem. The distinction is geometric, not a question of hiding logarithmic factors.

Other positive results exploit extra structure, such as totally unimodular constraint matrices or numerical bounds on subdeterminants. Those assumptions control features absent from the unrestricted statement. Random-polytope and smoothed analyses likewise describe particular distributions or perturbations; a worst-case theorem must include every allowed realization. This is why the model specifies arbitrary coefficients and requires constants independent of their encoding.

A positive resolution would reveal a universal short-route property of all polyhedral feasible regions, despite their potentially enormous vertex sets. A negative resolution would produce polyhedra on which every route between some vertices is intrinsically long. Both outcomes would identify a basic geometric limit underlying pivot-based optimization, independently of the performance of any individual implementation.

cards.title: Decidability of PL four-sphere recognition
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic Turing machine which, on every finite simplicial complex K promised to be a closed combinatorial 4-manifold, halts and decides whether K is piecewise-linearly homeomorphic to the boundary of a 5-simplex?
cards.definitions: A finite abstract simplicial complex is a finite family of finite vertex sets closed under taking subsets; its maximal sets are its facets. The input lists all facets with integer vertex labels in binary. K is pure of dimension 4 when all facets have five vertices. The link of a vertex v consists of the faces σ not containing v for which σ∪{v} is a face of K. A closed combinatorial 4-manifold here is a nonempty pure 4-dimensional complex in which each vertex link is a PL 3-sphere; connectedness is not promised. The standard PL d-sphere is the boundary complex of a (d+1)-simplex. Two complexes are PL homeomorphic when they admit finite simplicial subdivisions that are simplicially isomorphic, equivalently when their geometric realizations admit a homeomorphism affine on the simplices of suitable finite subdivisions. A simplicial subdivision triangulates the same realization by smaller simplices contained in the old simplices. Correctness and termination are required on every promised input; no behavior is required on other inputs. There is no time or space bound beyond termination.

cards.definitions: An input is a list of n≥0 closed boxes B_i=∏_{j=1}^d [a_i,j,b_i,j], specified by their 2dn finite real endpoints, with a_i,j≤b_i,j. Overlaps, coincident endpoints, duplicate boxes and zero side lengths are allowed. The output is the exact Lebesgue measure of ∪_i B_i, returned as a real number; the empty union has volume zero. For clarity, the real-RAM convention here is deterministic computation with exact real registers, unit-cost copying, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero values, comparisons and branching. Random access is through integer addresses. Control and address registers have O(log(n+2)) bits, with any fixed constant factor depending on the algorithm and d; standard arithmetic, comparison, Boolean and shift operations on these words cost one unit. Integers can be converted to real registers, but real values can affect integer control only through comparisons: no floor, bit extraction or arbitrary real-to-integer conversion is available. A program is finite and independent of n and the coordinates; any hard-coded real constants must be algebraic and finitely specified. Input reads, output writes, preprocessing, memory operations and control steps count. Worst-case time is the maximum over all endpoint lists of size n, regardless of coordinate magnitude. The requested precision is a Θ bound: logarithmic factors count, and constants may depend on d. No randomness, approximation tolerance, oracle or precomputed advice depending on n is supplied.
cards.answer_criterion: For each fixed d≥3, give a rate T_d(n), an exact algorithm with worst-case time O(T_d(n)), and an unconditional lower bound Ω(T_d(n)) for every correct algorithm in the same model. If no single rate is attainable within constant factors, establishing that failure of asymptotic optimality also answers the stated optimal-time request. An improved upper bound alone, a conditional lower bound, a restriction to particular box shapes, or a result only for approximate or dynamic volume does not complete the classification.

context_blocks.title: Overlap counts only once
context_blocks.text: Two boxes may cover the same region, so adding their individual volumes overcounts their intersection. In three dimensions, [0,2]³ and [1,3]×[0,2]² each have volume 8, but their union has volume 12. The task requests this single total volume; it does not request a full description of the union boundary. In higher dimensions a box is simply a product of intervals.

context_blocks.title: The known exact bound
context_blocks.text: Chan’s 2013 algorithm computes the union volume in O(n^(d/2)) time for every fixed d≥3. This gives n^(3/2) in dimension three and n² in dimension four. The unresolved target is a matching classification of the fastest possible exact computation. The known relationship with clique problems supplies conditional evidence for the exponent, rather than a matching unconditional lower bound for all algorithms.

context_blocks.title: Why numerical conventions matter
context_blocks.text: The real-RAM question counts an arithmetic operation on a coordinate as one step even when the coordinate would require many bits to encode. Chan also obtains logarithmic improvements for integer coordinates in a word-RAM setting. Those improvements do not automatically transfer to unrestricted real inputs, and the source explicitly discusses this distinction. The detailed primitive and worst-case conventions above make the inherited real-RAM target explicit.

context_blocks.title: Recent advances concern other guarantees
context_blocks.text: The SoCG 2025 work speeds up approximation of union volume and proves a lower bound for algorithms restricted to certain object queries. A small relative error is permitted there. The ICALP 2026 work maintains exact volume under insertions and deletions and measures amortized update time. Both are significant results, but neither determines the unconditional optimal time of a single exact static computation in this card’s model.

cards.definitions: The input gives n≥0, V={1,…,n}, and two symmetric zero-diagonal n×n binary adjacency matrices, with total bit length N; each graph is promised planar. No drawing, vertex coordinates or embedding is supplied. The common graph is H=(V,E₁∩E₂), which may be disconnected and have isolated vertices. A drawing assigns distinct points p(v)∈ℝ² to vertices and to each edge uv a simple continuous arc with endpoints p(u),p(v), whose interior contains no vertex point. Planarity means that arcs for distinct edges of the same graph meet only at a common endpoint, if there is one. A simultaneous drawing uses the same p(v) in both graphs and exactly the same arc image for every edge in E₁∩E₂. Edges exclusive to different graphs may cross each other. Arcs may bend freely; no grid, edge-length, area or bend bound is imposed. The requested output is only YES or NO. Polynomial time means one always-correct deterministic Turing machine and constants C,c≥1 with at most C(N+1)^c bit steps on every promised input, with no oracle or advice. “Fixed edges” means shared drawings agree on their common edges, not that any geometry is fixed in the input.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that a polynomial-time decider exists for all promised pairs, or prove that none exists. A positive answer must cover arbitrary disconnected common graphs and freely chosen embeddings. A nonembeddable pair is a NO instance, not a refutation of polynomial decidability. Hardness for three input graphs, straight-line drawings or an additional optimization objective does not answer this question.

context_blocks.title: Two compatible views of the same objects
context_blocks.text: Think of two network diagrams whose vertices denote the same objects and whose edges describe two relations. Each view must be crossing-free on its own. Shared edges must stay in place when switching views. This is why drawing each graph independently can fail to meet the simultaneous requirement.

context_blocks.title: The union need not be planar
context_blocks.text: Take G₁ to be K₅ with one edge deleted and G₂ to contain just that missing edge on the same five vertices. G₁ is planar, and G₂ can use the same vertex positions with its edge crossing edges exclusive to G₁. This is a valid simultaneous drawing, even though the union is the nonplanar graph K₅. Testing the union’s planarity would therefore reject valid instances.

context_blocks.title: The connected common case is solved
context_blocks.text: The checked 2025 papers report polynomial-time algorithms when H is connected. This is connectivity of the shared edges and vertices, not merely connectivity of each input graph. Allowing H to have multiple components introduces compatibility of their positions as well as choices of embeddings, and the unrestricted two-graph question remains open in those sources.

context_blocks.title: Which nearby results apply
context_blocks.text: Three-graph SEFE is NP-complete, but the number two is essential here. The March 2026 work on two paths studies straight-line grid drawings and optimizes geometric quantities. Its hardness result for edge length does not imply hardness of deciding whether unrestricted curved-edge drawings exist.

cards.definitions: A convex polyhedron here is a compact convex polytope K⊂ℝ³ with nonempty interior, whose boundary ∂K is a polyhedral sphere. Distances and angles are intrinsic to that boundary: neighboring faces may be unfolded into a plane along a shared edge. A simple closed curve is a continuous injective map γ:S¹→∂K, where S¹ is a circle; equivalently, a parametrization on [0,1] has equal endpoints and no other repetitions. The curve is nonconstant and locally polygonal. At a point away from a polyhedron vertex it must become a straight line after local unfolding. At a vertex on the curve, its two incident directions divide the total incident face angle into two surface angles, each required to be at most π. These angles are measured along the surface, not as angles of 3D chords. An ordinary geodesic has angle π on both sides everywhere; the relaxed condition allows a quasigeodesic to pass through a vertex with positive angular defect. The desired output is one curve satisfying all these conditions, not an approximate curve or an existence certificate without a specified curve. A doubled path that retraces itself is not injective and is excluded from this imported strict-simple target.
cards.answer_criterion: After the missing numerical and output conventions are fixed from the intended source model, exhibit one uniform algorithm with a polynomial worst-case bound in that model’s input size, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A finite but geometrically dependent exponential procedure, a possibly self-intersecting quasigeodesic or a weakly simple doubled path does not satisfy the stated strict polynomial-time target. The current card is not marked as a completed standalone computational formulation.

context_blocks.title: A straight route on a folded surface
context_blocks.text: A route can turn sharply in three-dimensional space when it crosses a polyhedron edge yet be straight after the two faces are unfolded. At an actual vertex, less than a full turn of surface may be available, so the two-sided angle condition replaces ordinary straightness. On a cube, the square loop halfway up the four vertical faces unfolds locally straight and is a simple closed geodesic.

context_blocks.title: Existence and finding a curve
context_blocks.text: Pogorelov’s classical theorem supplies simple closed quasigeodesics on convex polyhedra. Turning that existence statement into a fast construction requires controlling both the number of face segments and the exact geometry of their endpoints. A bound involving a ratio of geometric lengths can be enormous compared with the number of bits needed to describe those lengths.

Their convex-case discussion also permits a doubled path between two vertices as a degenerate simple case. That convention needs explicit attention when comparing the theorem with a request for an injective loop.

Turning that existence statement into a fast construction requires controlling both the number of face segments and the exact geometry of their endpoints. A bound involving a ratio of geometric lengths can be enormous compared with the number of bits needed to describe those lengths.

Chartier and de Mesmay give a finite algorithm for weakly simple closed quasigeodesics on polyhedral spheres, with running time exponential in the number of vertices and a length-to-altitude ratio. Their convex-case discussion also permits a doubled path between two vertices as a degenerate simple case. That convention needs explicit attention when comparing the theorem with a request for an injective loop.

The October 2025 revision by Demaine, Hesterberg and Ku corrects earlier details and separates real-RAM bounds from word-RAM bounds for radical-expression inputs. It also gives a pseudopolynomial bound on the number of face visits. The 2025 cube classification concerns one special polyhedron. Neither checked result supplies the general polynomial algorithm requested here.

The geometric request is now explicit. The source import still needs one precise convention for representing the polyhedron and the exact output curve, and for charging arithmetic operations. Those choices affect the meaning of polynomial time. This gap is recorded instead of treating a newly chosen numerical variant as the original question.

cards.definitions: The input lists n≥0 distinct points (x_i,y_i), and B, with every rational written as a signed binary integer numerator and a positive binary integer denominator. Let N be the total bit length. A triangulation is a maximal plane straight-line graph with vertex set exactly S: edges are segments joining pairs of distinct input points, no edge interior contains another input point, and two edges meet only at a shared endpoint. Maximal means that no further admissible segment can be added while preserving these conditions. This definition permits collinear points; in the entirely collinear case the graph is the path through consecutive points, and with fewer than two points it has no edges. No new vertices are permitted. Hull-boundary edges are included in the weight W(T)=∑_{ {i,j}∈E(T) }√((x_i−x_j)²+(y_i−y_j)²). Lengths are exact nonnegative square roots, with no rounding or tolerance, and equality W(T)=B is accepted. Malformed encodings and lists with duplicate points are rejected. Membership in NP means that there are a polynomial q and one deterministic Turing-machine verifier V, running in time polynomial in |x|+|y|, such that for every encoded instance x, x is a yes instance if and only if V(x,y) accepts for some binary certificate y of length at most q(|x|). Certificates may include auxiliary information beyond a list of edges; no exact-real arithmetic primitive has unit cost.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove NP membership by establishing a polynomial-length, polynomial-bit-time-verifiable certificate system for precisely these yes instances, or prove that this language is not in NP. Showing that one proposed verifier fails does not prove nonmembership. The certificate need only establish some triangulation below the threshold, not optimality of that triangulation.

context_blocks.title: The geometry is small; the lengths need not be rational
context_blocks.text: A triangulation can be described by listing its edges. Even with integer coordinates, their lengths can be irrational: the three points (0,0), (1,0), (0,1) have a single triangular boundary of total length 2+√2. A rational threshold must be compared with that exact value. With many edges, many different radicals appear in the sum.

context_blocks.title: What a certificate would have to establish
context_blocks.text: The edge list and its geometric validity have polynomial-size descriptions and can be checked using rational-coordinate operations. The remaining numerical comparison is why merely saying “guess the triangulation” does not establish an NP upper bound. The definition of NP also permits other short auxiliary certificates, so difficulty with direct numerical evaluation is not a proof that membership is impossible.

context_blocks.title: Hardness is already known
context_blocks.text: Mulzer and Rote prove strong NP-hardness of minimum-weight triangulation. Their paper explicitly distinguishes this lower bound from NP membership for exact Euclidean costs. Its rounded-cost variant is NP-complete, but replacing lengths by rounded values changes the language and the thresholds.

context_blocks.title: The related arithmetic frontier
context_blocks.text: An edge-length sum is a sum of square roots of rational numbers. After a common rational scaling, the threshold comparison is an instance of square-root sum with integer data. A polynomial-time method, or suitable NP certificates, for that general arithmetic comparison would supply the missing numerical verification. The 2025 ICALP paper still identifies an unresolved NP bound for square-root sum; the reverse implication from this triangulation question is not asserted.

context_blocks.title: Large solved instances and worst-case guarantees
context_blocks.text: Haas reports practical methods that solve very large triangulation instances to optimality. This is useful computational progress, but it does not establish a polynomial bound on verification resources for every possible binary-encoded input. The card asks for that uniform complexity guarantee.

cards.title: Linear-size sample compression
cards.formal: Is there a universal constant C such that every nonempty binary concept class H⊆{0,1}^X of finite VC dimension d≥1 admits a labeled sample compression scheme with kernel bound k and side-information bound b satisfying k+b≤Cd, in the model below? The same compressor and reconstructor must work for every finite H-realizable sample, independently of its size.
cards.definitions: The domain X is an arbitrary set, and a concept h∈H is a total function X→{0,1}. A finite set A⊆X is shattered if {h|_A:h∈H}={0,1}^A; d is the largest cardinality of a shattered set. A realizable sample is a finite set S⊆X×{0,1} agreeing with some h∈H. A scheme consists of deterministic maps κ and ρ, which may depend on H, and nonnegative integers k,b. For every realizable S, κ(S)=(T,z), where T⊆S is an unordered labeled subset with |T|≤k and z∈{0,1}^b. The reconstructor receives only T and z and produces a total predictor ρ(T,z):X→{0,1} agreeing with every pair in S. It does not receive S, its size, the omitted points, or their indices. The side string has fixed length b; padding shorter strings changes only constant-factor size conventions. Reconstruction need not lie in H, be stable under deleting unused examples, or have any prescribed computational complexity. No probability distribution, efficiency, or measurability condition is part of this combinatorial existence question. Dimension zero is harmless: a nonempty such class has one labeling and needs no stored examples.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A central question connecting the combinatorial complexity of prediction with how many observations suffice to represent all training decisions. Its universality across concept classes, and its links to learning, extremal set systems and graph geometry, make the linear-versus-exponential gap fundamental.

importance.reason: A longstanding general conjecture asking whether VC dimension controls sample representation up to a constant factor; it reaches far beyond any one learning algorithm or geometric example.

progress.text: The framework of Littlestone and Warmuth led to the conjecture that compression size can be linear in VC dimension; the general conjecture remains explicit in the 2025 survey of reductions.
Moran and Yehudayoff prove a general 2^{O(d)} bound for binary classes. The corrected arXiv v2 is the appropriate preprint; the journal version appeared in JACM in 2016.
Chase and coauthors prove an exponential dimension obstruction to embedding arbitrary VC classes in extremal classes, limiting a major proposed approach without refuting sample compression itself.
Bourneuf and coauthors obtain almost-linear proper compression in treewidth and cliquewidth for graph-ball classes, while retaining the general conjecture as open.

The latest version of arXiv:2603.23561, which had earlier claimed a compression breakthrough and later a no-clash teaching result, is withdrawn. Its authors identify an incorrect proof of Lemma 2. This is not a resolution.
