cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The general linear bound remains open in the primary sources checked. The 2026 graph-ball theorems concern structured classes. The claimed breakthrough at arXiv:2603.23561 is withdrawn and is included only to document its status. This card fixes labeled, possibly improper, unordered-subset compression with all side bits counted.

context_blocks.text: The stored object is a small selection of examples that lets a fixed decoding rule recover every training label. It need not identify the unknown target function on points never observed. For example, consider indicators of closed intervals on the real line. Retain the leftmost and rightmost positive examples, or the empty set if there are no positives. Decode to the interval between those retained points, or to the all-zero function in the empty case. Realizability ensures that no negative example lies between the extreme positives. Thus an arbitrarily large sample can be represented by at most two examples.

The distinction between examples and bits is essential. A real-valued example may itself require arbitrarily many bits to describe; sample compression charges one unit for retaining it. Conversely, permitting an arbitrary uncharged side message would trivialize the problem, because that message could encode the whole sample. The fixed reconstructor and the explicit bound b prevent this loophole. The question concerns the combinatorial information carried by selected observations, rather than ordinary lossless compression of their numerical representations.

Moran and Yehudayoff proved that every finite-VC binary class has a scheme of size 2^{O(d)}, settling the earlier existence question. Their argument combines learning with an approximate minimax principle. More precisely, their bound also involves the dual VC dimension: this reverses the roles of domain points and concepts, treating each point as its pattern of membership across the concepts. Since the dual dimension can be exponential in d, that result leaves a substantial quantitative gap. Their corrected 2015 version retains the binary theorem while withdrawing an erroneous multiclass extension.

A studied auxiliary question asks whether each class embeds in an extremal class of comparable VC dimension. Chase and coauthors show that such embeddings can require an exponential increase in dimension. Their COLT 2024 result rules out that general route to a linear bound; it does not show that the original class itself needs exponential compression. A failed intermediate representation is different from a lower bound against every compressor.

The problem also has concrete graph instances. Fix a graph and label sampled vertices according to membership in an unknown metric ball. Bourneuf and coauthors give proper schemes of size O(t log(t+1)) when the graph has treewidth at most t, and an analogous bound for cliquewidth. Proper means that decoding produces another ball, a stronger requirement than this card imposes. Their April 2026 work supplies structured examples and explicitly leaves the general linear-VC conjecture open.

Attias, Hanneke, and Ramaswami show how binary compression results transfer to multiclass, regression, and robust-learning settings, with additional factors or additional requirements on the binary scheme. Consequently, a solution could have consequences beyond binary prediction, but those transfers have hypotheses. In particular, their Open Problem 28 is about adversarially robust compression; the standard conjecture used here appears in their introduction.

cards.title: Learning parity with noise in polynomial time
cards.formal: For every fixed rational noise rate η with 0<η<1/2, does there exist a uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, for every n and every secret s∈{0,1}^n, recovers s with probability at least 2/3 from independent samples (a,⟨a,s⟩⊕e), where a is uniform in {0,1}^n and e is independently Bernoulli(η)?
cards.definitions: The inner product ⟨a,s⟩ is Σ_i a_i s_i modulo two, and ⊕ is addition modulo two. The unknown s is fixed throughout an execution. Each requested sample uses a fresh independent uniform vector a and an independent error bit e, with Pr[e=1]=η. The learner knows n and the fixed rate η, and receives only classical samples. It cannot choose a, request a noiseless label, identify which labels were corrupted, or make coherent quantum queries. For each fixed η the algorithm and its polynomial bound pη may depend on η, but they must be uniform in n, without advice. Every execution uses at most pη(n) bit operations and requests at most pη(n) samples; reading and storing samples is charged. Polynomially many stored bits and repeated access to stored samples are allowed. The success probability is over the example generator and the learner’s random coins, for each fixed s. The desired output is the entire secret vector, not merely a predictor with unspecified advantage. No sparsity promise is imposed on s or on a. The quantifier over fixed rational η does not demand a running-time bound uniform as η approaches 1/2 with n.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.

importance.reason: A fundamental boundary between information-theoretic learnability and efficient learning, with broad consequences for noise-tolerant algorithms and cryptographic assumptions.

context_blocks.text: A parity function is among the simplest algebraic classifiers: choose a hidden subset of coordinates and return their XOR. Without label noise, sufficiently many random examples give linear equations, and Gaussian elimination recovers the secret with high probability. Independent noise changes the task from solving a consistent system to identifying which apparent equations should be trusted. Ordinary elimination mixes error bits along with the equations, so its usual exactness argument no longer applies.

The difficulty is computational rather than a lack of information. For a fixed noise rate below one half, the true secret agrees with a fresh label with probability 1−η. Every other secret agrees with probability one half under the uniform distribution on inputs. With a sufficiently large constant multiple of n examples, concentration and a union bound over the 2^n candidates identify the true secret with high probability. Exhaustively testing those candidates takes exponential time, leaving open whether their search can be avoided.

At η=1/4, for example, the correct candidate has expected agreement 3/4, while every incorrect parity has expected agreement 1/2. A threshold strictly between these values separates them once enough independent samples have been collected. This simple gap explains why a polynomial sample bound alone is not the desired breakthrough. One must locate the exceptional candidate efficiently among exponentially many possibilities.

Writing the sample vectors as rows of a matrix A gives b=As+e over the binary field. The columns of A generate a random linear code, and the task becomes decoding a random noisy codeword. This connection explains the relevance to cryptography. It does not turn a worst-case NP-hardness theorem for decoding arbitrary codes into an average-case hardness theorem for the random distribution used here. Quantifiers over matrices, errors and sample counts have to survive the reduction.

Blum, Kalai and Wasserman give a 2^{O(n/log n)}-time algorithm using a comparable subexponential number of examples for constant noise. Combining examples cancels blocks of coordinates, while the analysis controls how the combined noise approaches a fair coin. Their work also separates noise-tolerant learning from the statistical-query framework in an appropriate restricted parity regime. Thus failure of statistical-query methods cannot simply be interpreted as failure of all algorithms with access to individual examples.

Lyubashevsky answers a different sample-efficiency question: subexponential computation is possible using only n^{1+ε} examples for each fixed ε>0. The resulting running time is 2^{O(n/log log n)}. This result is directly relevant to a learner that can collect only polynomially many samples, but its time bound is still superpolynomial. Keeping the two resources visible prevents the better exponent of the many-sample algorithm from being quoted as a polynomial-sample guarantee.

There are substantial unconditional lower bounds in restricted resource models. Garg, Kothari, Liu and Raz show that a streaming learner needs either Ω(n²/(1/2−η)) bits of memory or exponentially many samples, with a strong success-probability guarantee in their theorem. For fixed η, the memory alternative is quadratic, which is permitted by the polynomial-time question. This establishes a real storage cost without ruling out a general polynomial-time algorithm.

Aggarwal, Gupta and Zeyong’s May 2026 hardness amplification relates success on a small fraction of instances to success on almost all instances after changing the dimension and noise parameters. Aggarwal and coauthors’ September 8 revision gives low-noise LPN hardness under simultaneous worst-case assumptions concerning decoding a code and distinguishing noisy codewords of its dual. These strengthen the understanding of hardness assumptions; neither is an unconditional proof that this learner cannot exist.

The every-secret guarantee is not an artificial extra obstacle compared with a uniform random secret. A learner can choose a uniform mask r, replace each label b by b⊕⟨a,r⟩, learn the masked secret s⊕r and remove the mask. The transformed secret is uniform while the noise law is unchanged. The central uncertainty therefore persists even when randomness in the hidden parity itself is supplied for free.

At η=1/4, for example, the correct candidate has expected agreement 3/4, while every incorrect parity has expected agreement 1/2. A threshold strictly between these values separates them once enough independent samples have been collected. This simple gap explains why a polynomial sample bound alone is not the desired breakthrough. One must locate the exceptional candidate efficiently among exponentially many possibilities.

Writing the sample vectors as rows of a matrix A gives b=As+e over the binary field. The columns of A generate a random linear code, and the task becomes decoding a random noisy codeword. This connection explains the relevance to cryptography. It does not turn a worst-case NP-hardness theorem for decoding arbitrary codes into an average-case hardness theorem for the random distribution used here. Quantifiers over matrices, errors and sample counts have to survive the reduction.

Blum, Kalai and Wasserman give a 2^{O(n/log n)}-time algorithm using a comparable subexponential number of examples for constant noise. Combining examples cancels blocks of coordinates, while the analysis controls how the combined noise approaches a fair coin. Their work also separates noise-tolerant learning from the statistical-query framework in an appropriate restricted parity regime. Thus failure of statistical-query methods cannot simply be interpreted as failure of all algorithms with access to individual examples.

Lyubashevsky answers a different sample-efficiency question: subexponential computation is possible using only n^{1+ε} examples for each fixed ε>0. The resulting running time is 2^{O(n/log log n)}. This result is directly relevant to a learner that can collect only polynomially many samples, but its time bound is still superpolynomial. Keeping the two resources visible prevents the better exponent of the many-sample algorithm from being quoted as a polynomial-sample guarantee.

There are substantial unconditional lower bounds in restricted resource models. Garg, Kothari, Liu and Raz show that a streaming learner needs either Ω(n²/(1/2−η)) bits of memory or exponentially many samples, with a strong success-probability guarantee in their theorem. For fixed η, the memory alternative is quadratic, which is permitted by the polynomial-time question. This establishes a real storage cost without ruling out a general polynomial-time algorithm.

Aggarwal, Gupta and Zeyong’s May 2026 hardness amplification relates success on a small fraction of instances to success on almost all instances after changing the dimension and noise parameters. Aggarwal and coauthors’ September 8 revision gives low-noise LPN hardness under simultaneous worst-case assumptions concerning decoding a code and distinguishing noisy codewords of its dual. These strengthen the understanding of hardness assumptions; neither is an unconditional proof that this learner cannot exist.

The every-secret guarantee is not an artificial extra obstacle compared with a uniform random secret. A learner can choose a uniform mask r, replace each label b by b⊕⟨a,r⟩, learn the masked secret s⊕r and remove the mask. The transformed secret is uniform while the noise law is unchanged. The central uncertainty therefore persists even when randomness in the hidden parity itself is supplied for free.

benchmark_focus.reason: A fundamental boundary between information-theoretic learnability and efficient learning, with broad consequences for noise-tolerant algorithms and cryptographic assumptions.

cards.title: Public-key encryption from one-way functions
cards.formal: Does the existence of a classical cryptographic one-way function imply the existence of a classical public-key encryption scheme with negligible correctness error and security against uniform probabilistic polynomial-time chosen-plaintext adversaries? General constructions and security proofs may use the code of the one-way function; they need not be black-box.
cards.definitions: A one-way function is a deterministic polynomial-time map f:{0,1}*→{0,1}* such that every uniform classical PPT inverter I has negligible probability, for x uniform in {0,1}ⁿ, of outputting z∈{0,1}ⁿ with f(z)=f(x) on input (1ⁿ,f(x)). A function ν(n) is negligible if for every d>0 it is eventually at most n^{−d}. The scheme comprises uniform classical polynomial-time algorithms Gen, Enc, Dec. Gen(1ⁿ) randomly outputs public and secret bit strings (pk,sk); Enc(1ⁿ,pk,b) randomly encrypts a bit b; Dec(1ⁿ,sk,c) deterministically outputs a bit or failure. For each b, the probability over honest generation and encryption that decryption is wrong is negligible. Security means that for every uniform classical PPT adversary A, in the experiment (pk,sk)←Gen(1ⁿ), b←{0,1}, c←Enc(1ⁿ,pk,b), the advantage |Pr[A(1ⁿ,pk,c)=b]−1/2| is negligible. The adversary knows all algorithms and can encrypt arbitrary chosen bits itself with fresh randomness. This bit-message formulation extends to polynomially long messages by independent bit encryption and a hybrid argument. All runtime bounds are worst-case polynomial in the security parameter and appropriate input lengths. There is no shared secret before key generation, trusted setup, random oracle, quantum state, or auxiliary hardness assumption. Security is eventually negligible at all sufficiently large parameters, not merely infinitely often.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: This is the main unresolved boundary between the assumptions needed for private-key and public-key cryptography. It asks whether generic computational one-wayness already contains the structure needed to establish encrypted communication without a pre-shared secret.

importance.reason: A central minimal-assumption question in cryptographic foundations, separating the known reach of generic one-wayness from public-key communication.

progress.text: Impagliazzo and Rudich establish the fundamental oracle and black-box barriers to obtaining key agreement from one-way permutations; this also constrains public-key encryption constructions.
Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin, and Luby prove pseudorandom generators can be constructed from any OWF, establishing the generic route underlying private-key cryptography.
Barak and Mahmoody prove the quadratic-query attack on random-oracle key agreement. The result sharpens the oracle-model limitation without excluding arbitrary non-black-box constructions.
MIT’s foundations lecture explicitly presents PKE from OWFs as a major open question and distinguishes it from the established black-box separations.

Chatterjee, Mu, and Vasudevan construct PKE from planted MinRank hardness on random instances. The 2025 preprint appears at EUROCRYPT 2026; it adds a concrete foundation, not a reduction from an arbitrary OWF.

context_blocks.text: A one-way function creates an asymmetry between evaluating a map and finding a preimage of a random image. Public-key encryption needs a different asymmetry: anyone holding the public information can produce ciphertexts, yet a receiver possessing related secret information can recover their messages. The question is whether this additional structure is implicit in every possible source of one-wayness.

One-way functions already suffice for pseudorandom generators and, through the standard chain of constructions, private-key encryption. There the honest parties initially share a secret. Public-key encryption removes that initial shared secret, so the existence of symmetric cryptography is not already a construction of the desired public-key primitive.

The classical obstacle is the Impagliazzo–Rudich black-box separation. Roughly, an idealized one-way-function oracle can supply private-key cryptographic hardness without enabling the necessary key agreement. A construction allowed to inspect and reason about a concrete function’s program lies outside the oracle interface, which is why the general implication remains open despite this barrier.

Public-key encryption would give a two-message key-agreement protocol: send a public key, then send an encryption of a freshly chosen shared secret. Barak and Mahmoody show a quadratic-query attack on key agreement built from a random oracle, matching the limited query advantage of Merkle puzzles. The theorem counts oracle queries and allows extensive other computation; it is not an unconditional attack on every standard-model encryption scheme.

New constructions continue to broaden the available assumptions. Chatterjee, Mu, and Vasudevan base public-key encryption on a planted MinRank problem over random instances, equivalently a rank-metric decoding assumption, rather than hiding a specially structured efficiently decodable code. This is progress in the choice of concrete hardness assumptions. It still assumes that specific problem is hard, a property not supplied merely by the existence of some arbitrary OWF.

cards.title: Circuit obfuscation from polynomial-hard LWE
cards.formal: Does the decisional LWE assumption with the fixed polynomial parameters below imply the existence of indistinguishability obfuscation for all polynomial-size Boolean circuits, with no additional hardness, leakage-resilience, or circular-security assumption? The target is a classical polynomial-time obfuscator secure against classical polynomial-size adversaries.
cards.definitions: Fix q(n) to be the least prime at least n^4 for every integer n≥2. Let χ_n be the discrete Gaussian on Z with probability of e proportional to exp(−πe²/n²). The assumed LWE statement is: for every polynomial m(n), the ensembles (A,A s+e mod q) and (A,u) are computationally indistinguishable, where A is uniform in Z_q^(m×n), s is uniform in Z_q^n, the m coordinates of e are independent χ_n samples, and u is independent uniform in Z_q^m. Indistinguishable means every polynomial-size classical circuit family has negligible advantage in n; negligible means smaller than n^(−c) eventually for every constant c>0. No secret-dependent leakage is supplied. An obfuscator O is a uniform probabilistic algorithm running in time polynomial in λ+|C| that outputs a Boolean circuit O(1^λ,C) of polynomial size. Circuits are finite acyclic AND/OR/NOT circuits with fan-in at most two, a specified list of input and output bits, and explicit binary descriptions; |C| is description length. For every polynomial p, there is negligible μ_p such that for every |C|≤p(λ), with probability at least 1−μ_p(λ) over the obfuscator’s coins the output circuit agrees with C on ALL inputs. For every pair of circuit sequences C_0,λ and C_1,λ with polynomially bounded, equal description lengths, the same input/output lengths and identical functions, their obfuscations are computationally indistinguishable against all polynomial-size circuit families. Both functionality and security quantify over all such circuits, without requiring an efficiently checkable proof of equivalence. There is no oracle, trusted setup, quantum state, or restriction to a special circuit family. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: Asks whether a single basic noisy-linear-equation assumption supports general program obfuscation. Resolving the implication would clarify the strength of LWE and the assumption cost of a broad family of cryptographic constructions that currently use iO as a separate resource.

importance.reason: A central assumption-minimization problem for general obfuscation, with consequences throughout cryptography and a crucial distinction between ordinary LWE and strengthened LWE-based assumptions.

progress.text: Barak and coauthors establish impossibility for general virtual-black-box obfuscation while introducing weaker obfuscation notions, including the indistinguishability target.
Regev develops LWE, lattice-hardness connections and public-key encryption; these results supply the standard noisy-equation foundation, rather than general obfuscation.
Jain, Lin, and Sahai construct general iO from four well-founded assumptions with the quantitative security specified in their theorem. The JACM publication does not reduce the list to LWE.
Their follow-up removes LWE, obtaining iO from LPN over prime fields, DLIN, and local PRGs under subexponential security. It explicitly leaves minimal assumption sets open.

Brakerski and coauthors obtain iO from circular-security properties of LWE-based encryption, including randomness-leakage resilience. They also repair a limitation in a previous exponentially-efficient-obfuscation transformation.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. No construction from the plain polynomial-hard decisional-LWE assumption fixed here was identified. Existing multi-assumption and circular-security constructions do not settle it. Polynomial hardness, polynomial modulus/noise ratio, classical adversaries, arbitrary circuits and no auxiliary leakage are explicit choices that make the broad LWE-alone question unambiguous.

context_blocks.text: Indistinguishability obfuscation compares two implementations of exactly the same function. After obfuscation, an efficient observer should not tell which implementation was used. Equality of size prevents a trivial distinction from the amount of code supplied; padding can put implementations under a common size bound. This definition does not say that every secret written into an arbitrary program is hidden. A secret that the function itself reveals through its outputs remains visible.

That distinction is necessary. Barak and coauthors rule out general obfuscation under the stronger virtual-black-box requirement, which would make code reveal no more than oracle access to its function. Their impossibility theorem does not rule out indistinguishability obfuscation. The weaker comparison between equivalent implementations has therefore become a central target, rather than an informal promise to make arbitrary software unreadable.

LWE supplies a particularly concrete potential foundation. Its samples are linear equations modulo a public integer, perturbed by small independent errors. Exact equations would reveal the secret by linear algebra; the errors obstruct that approach. Regev introduced reductions connecting LWE to worst-case lattice problems and used it to build public-key encryption. This card fixes a particular ordinary decisional-LWE ensemble so that the noise distribution, modulus, number of samples, and adversarial resources cannot vary silently.

Jain, Lin, and Sahai established general-circuit iO from a combination of four assumptions: LWE, LPN over large fields, a local Boolean pseudorandom generator, and a bilinear-group assumption. Their theorem uses stronger quantitative security than mere polynomial hardness. Its Journal of the ACM version appeared in February 2026, following the STOC 2021 work. That publication is an important foundation for iO, but is not a 2026 construction from plain LWE alone.

A follow-up by the same authors removes LWE from that combination, leaving the other three assumptions. Eliminating LWE from a sufficient set is logically different from eliminating all the other assumptions while retaining LWE. The follow-up explicitly poses the possibility that LWE alone might suffice, without claiming a resolution.

Brakerski, Döttling, Garg, and Malavolta give another route using LWE-based encryption with circular randomness-leakage resilience. The construction uses that stronger assumption. Its security experiment exposes structured information related to keys and encryption randomness, whereas ordinary LWE supplies only the noisy linear samples defined above. Calling the construction LWE-based therefore does not remove the extra security hypothesis.

A solution would unify the assumptions behind many uses of obfuscation with an established lattice-learning problem. The specific target here is deliberately demanding: ordinary polynomial security and a polynomial modulus-to-noise ratio. Even a construction from plain LWE with stronger quantitative hardness would be substantial progress, but the security loss would still need attention before it established this exact implication. The question concerns mathematical feasibility; it does not impose practical code size or execution speed.

cards.definitions: The security parameter n≥1 is given in unary as 1ⁿ. A single deterministic Turing machine computes f on every finite binary string in time polynomial in its input length. Each inverter I is one classical randomized Turing machine with a worst-case polynomial running-time bound; its input contains 1ⁿ, so its running time and output length are polynomial in n. It receives f(X), not X, and has no advice, oracle or secret information. An output Y succeeds exactly when f(Y)=f(X); any preimage is accepted, even one of a different length from X. An explicit failure output is unsuccessful. No injectivity, permutation property or length preservation is imposed. A probability function is negligible if it is eventually at most n⁻ᵈ for each integer d≥1. The threshold n₀ can depend on I and d. Security is averaged over the uniformly sampled input and the inverter’s coins, and must hold for all sufficiently large n, not merely an infinite subsequence.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves, without an unproved computational hardness assumption, that at least one f satisfies the stated efficiency and inversion bound. A negative resolution proves that every polynomial-time f has a polynomial-time inverter whose success is non-negligible: for some d≥1 it exceeds n⁻ᵈ for infinitely many n. A conditional construction or a failure of one particular candidate does not decide existence.

context_blocks.title: What must be hard
context_blocks.text: Computing an output and finding an input that produces it are different tasks. The experiment first generates an ordinary random input, computes its image, and asks an efficient algorithm for any matching input. The difficulty must survive every polynomial-time inverter on this distribution. A few exceptional hard inputs, or a single unsuccessful attack, do not establish this average-case guarantee.

context_blocks.title: Forgetting information is not enough
context_blocks.text: Suppose f keeps the first ⌈n/2⌉ bits of an n-bit input and discards the rest. Recovering the exact original random string would usually be impossible because the discarded bits are missing. Inversion as defined here is easy: append enough zero bits to obtain an n-bit string with the given prefix. Its image is the required value. This example explains why the success condition accepts any preimage and why simple information loss is not cryptographic hardness.

context_blocks.title: How strong is negligible success?
context_blocks.text: An inverter that succeeds with probability 1/n¹⁰ still violates the requirement. A probability such as 2⁻ⁿ is negligible, while 1/n¹⁰ is not. The quantifiers allow a different eventual threshold for each algorithm and each requested exponent. They do not ask for a single finite input length at which every conceivable polynomial-time program is already defeated. The forward computation and all adversaries here are classical; a quantum primitive with different inputs or outputs is a separate model.

context_blocks.title: Relation to other open questions
context_blocks.text: One-way functions would imply P≠NP, since P=NP would permit efficient search for a polynomial-length preimage. Whether P≠NP alone implies their existence is separately recorded in TCS-0022. One-way functions are equivalent to several basic cryptographic primitives, including pseudorandom generators and suitable private-key encryption, but it is not known whether they suffice for public-key encryption; that implication is TCS-6545. The present question assumes neither P≠NP nor any candidate’s hardness.

context_blocks.title: What the existing theorems establish
context_blocks.text: Levin gives a concrete complete function whose one-wayness follows if any one-way function exists. Completeness identifies a universal candidate; it does not establish the premise. Liu and Pass characterize existence through an average-case hardness property of time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity, the length of a shortest program producing a string within a time bound. Their equivalence does not prove that hardness property. Hirahara and Nanashima’s June 2026 revision characterizes Pessiland, the hypothetical situation with average-case hard problems but no one-way functions. This is another structural theorem, not evidence that either hypothetical world actually occurs. The checked sources do not resolve unconditional existence.

cards.context:
Computing an output and finding an input that produces it are different tasks. The experiment first generates an ordinary random input, computes its image, and asks an efficient algorithm for any matching input. The difficulty must survive every polynomial-time inverter on this distribution. A few exceptional hard inputs, or a single unsuccessful attack, do not establish this average-case guarantee.

Suppose f keeps the first ⌈n/2⌉ bits of an n-bit input and discards the rest. Recovering the exact original random string would usually be impossible because the discarded bits are missing. Inversion as defined here is easy: append enough zero bits to obtain an n-bit string with the given prefix. Its image is the required value. This example explains why the success condition accepts any preimage and why simple information loss is not cryptographic hardness.

An inverter that succeeds with probability 1/n¹⁰ still violates the requirement. A probability such as 2⁻ⁿ is negligible, while 1/n¹⁰ is not. The quantifiers allow a different eventual threshold for each algorithm and each requested exponent. They do not ask for a single finite input length at which every conceivable polynomial-time program is already defeated. The forward computation and all adversaries here are classical; a quantum primitive with different inputs or outputs is a separate model.

One-way functions would imply P≠NP, since P=NP would permit efficient search for a polynomial-length preimage. Whether P≠NP alone implies their existence is separately recorded in TCS-0022. One-way functions are equivalent to several basic cryptographic primitives, including pseudorandom generators and suitable private-key encryption, but it is not known whether they suffice for public-key encryption; that implication is TCS-6545. The present question assumes neither P≠NP nor any candidate’s hardness.

Levin gives a concrete complete function whose one-wayness follows if any one-way function exists. Completeness identifies a universal candidate; it does not establish the premise. Liu and Pass characterize existence through an average-case hardness property of time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity, the length of a shortest program producing a string within a time bound. Their equivalence does not prove that hardness property. Hirahara and Nanashima’s June 2026 revision characterizes Pessiland, the hypothetical situation with average-case hard problems but no one-way functions. This is another structural theorem, not evidence that either hypothetical world actually occurs. The checked sources do not resolve unconditional existence.

cards.definitions: For security parameter n≥1, Gen(1ⁿ) samples a public key pk and a secret key sk. Enc(1ⁿ,pk,m) takes a bit m∈{0,1} and fresh independent coins and outputs a binary ciphertext; Dec(1ⁿ,sk,c) returns a bit or failure. All three algorithms have worst-case polynomial running time in their input length. Correctness means that max over m∈{0,1} of Pr[Dec(1ⁿ,sk,Enc(1ⁿ,pk,m))≠m] is negligible in n, with probability over key generation, encryption and any decryption coins. For IND-CPA, Gen runs first, and a uniform PPT adversary A₁ receives (1ⁿ,pk) and outputs bits m₀,m₁ and a state z. Independently choose a uniform bit b, generate c=Enc(1ⁿ,pk,m_b), and give (1ⁿ,pk,z,c) to its second stage A₂, which outputs a bit b′. For every pair (A₁,A₂), |Pr[b′=b]−1/2| must be negligible. A function η(n) is negligible if, for every integer d≥1, η(n)≤n⁻ᵈ for all sufficiently large n. Adversaries may run the public encryption algorithm themselves polynomially many times before and after seeing c; there is no decryption oracle. The model has no trusted correlated setup, ideal oracle, secret advice or quantum algorithms. The receiver’s public key is given authentically; its replacement by an active attacker is outside this confidentiality experiment. One-bit message space fixes an equivalent existence question: independent bit encryptions and the standard hybrid argument extend IND-CPA security to every polynomial message length.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves existence of a scheme satisfying the stated correctness and computational indistinguishability bounds with no unproved computational assumption. A negative resolution proves that every efficient correct scheme fails that security requirement. An assumed-hardness construction, experimental resistance to attacks, or an impossibility theorem only for unbounded attackers does not settle this question.

context_blocks.title: Public information, private recovery
context_blocks.text: A sender receives the public key and can encrypt a message without knowing the secret key. The receiver can decrypt with that secret key. An observer has the same public encryption capability as the sender, so secrecy must come from a limitation on computation rather than from hiding the encryption algorithm. The question asks whether such a limitation can be proved to exist for some efficient scheme.

context_blocks.title: Why the challenge compares two messages
context_blocks.text: The adversary chooses two messages after seeing the public key, then receives an encryption of a fair random choice between them. Guessing always gives success 1/2. Security requires every efficient adversary’s additional advantage to be negligible. This is stronger than merely failing to recover a long message exactly: learning one distinguishing bit can already violate the requirement. Restricting the displayed experiment to message bits keeps the existence question concrete without requiring a particular practical ciphertext format.

context_blocks.title: A simple failure of deterministic encryption
context_blocks.text: Imagine that encryption uses no fresh randomness and the two possible messages are 0 and 1. Anyone with the public key can compute both ciphertexts and compare the challenge with them. On keys for which both messages decrypt correctly, the two ciphertexts must differ, so the comparison reveals the challenge bit. Randomized encryption avoids this immediate comparison attack, but randomness by itself is not a proof of security.

context_blocks.title: Which assumptions are still missing?
context_blocks.text: Regev’s lattice-based construction gives classical public-key encryption from learning-with-errors hardness. This is a theorem relating two computational tasks; it does not prove the assumed task hard. In March 2026, Lu, Poremba, Quek and Ramkumar gave another conditional route based on average-case hardness of quantum stabilizer decoding, with classical cryptographic algorithms. A new candidate assumption broadens the foundations available for constructions while leaving unconditional existence unresolved. The word quantum in the underlying decoding problem does not itself make the encryption algorithms quantum.

context_blocks.title: The boundary of the question
context_blocks.text: Secure public-key encryption implies one-way functions and hence P≠NP. The converse implication from arbitrary one-way functions is a separate open question, TCS-6545; proving that implication alone would still leave their existence unproved. Computational security here permits an unbounded adversary to succeed. Consequently, the impossibility of information-theoretic secrecy from only public information does not answer the present question. Chosen-ciphertext security adds access to a decryption oracle and is also a different requirement. The requested theorem concerns precisely efficient classical attackers in the stated chosen-plaintext experiment.

cards.title: Key agreement from one-way functions
cards.formal: Does the existence of a classical one-way function imply the existence of a classical two-party key-agreement protocol with negligible disagreement and computationally secret shared keys, against passive probabilistic polynomial-time eavesdroppers, in the plain public-channel model defined below?
cards.definitions: All algorithms are uniform classical probabilistic Turing machines; security parameter λ is supplied in unary. A one-way function is a deterministic polynomial-time f:{0,1}*→{0,1}* such that, for every probabilistic polynomial-time I, Pr[f(Y)=f(X) and |Y|=λ] is negligible in λ, where X is uniform in {0,1}^λ and Y is the single output of I(1^λ,f(X)); probability also includes I’s private coins. A function μ:N→[0,1] is negligible if for every integer d≥1 there is λ₀ such that μ(λ)≤λ^(−d) for all λ≥λ₀. The protocol consists of two interactive machines A,B with independent private fair coins and total worst-case computation and communication polynomial in λ. They exchange classical messages on a noiseless public channel, with no correlated initial secrets, trusted setup, random oracle or quantum communication. At termination each outputs a λ-bit string K_A,K_B. Correctness requires Pr[K_A≠K_B] to be negligible. Let T be the full public transcript, and let U_λ be an independent uniform λ-bit string. For every probabilistic polynomial-time distinguisher D, |Pr[D(1^λ,T,K_A)=1]−Pr[D(1^λ,T,U_λ)=1]| must be negligible, over the honest coins, D’s coins and U_λ. The eavesdropper observes T but does not alter the messages. The target is the unrelativized existence implication; neither the construction nor its proof is required to treat f as a black box. Both premise and conclusion use the same uniform adversary convention.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.

context_blocks.text: A one-way function supplies a computational asymmetry: evaluating it is easy, while recovering a preimage of a random image is hard. Key agreement asks for a different capability. Two parties begin without a common secret and exchange visible messages, yet their final common key must remain hidden from an observer. The question is whether the first kind of asymmetry always suffices for the second.

The security definition concerns the entire transcript. Merely showing that a transcript has many possible explanations is insufficient if an efficient observer can identify the common key. Likewise, keeping each party’s private randomness hidden is weaker than hiding the particular string on which both parties agree. Comparing the actual key with an independent uniform key makes the secrecy requirement explicit.

Impagliazzo and Rudich established a black-box barrier between one-way functions and key agreement. Couteau, Farshim and Mahmoody’s 2021 work studies stronger notions of black-box uselessness and proves results for specified restricted settings. Such results delimit families of constructions; they do not refute the unrestricted existence implication on this card.

The existing TCS-6545 asks for public-key encryption from one-way functions. Public-key encryption would yield a key-agreement protocol by sending a fresh random key under the published encryption key. General interactive key agreement is a separate, weaker desired primitive. A negative conclusion about a restricted encryption construction cannot by itself rule out all interactive protocols.

The classical and passive conventions matter. Quantum key distribution uses an additional communication resource, while protection against an active man-in-the-middle requires an authentication model. Neither is part of this target. The card isolates the foundational question of creating a secret by classical public interaction from the minimal generic computational assumption.

cards.title: Oblivious transfer from public-key encryption
cards.formal: In the classical plain model, does the existence of an IND-CPA-secure public-key encryption scheme for bits imply the existence of a polynomial-time 1-out-of-2 bit oblivious-transfer protocol secure against static semi-honest corruption of either party? Both primitives have negligible error and computational security as defined below. The implication may use arbitrary non-black-box techniques and a polynomial number of communication rounds.
cards.definitions: The security parameter is λ, supplied in unary. Honest algorithms are uniform probabilistic polynomial-time Turing machines; adversarial distinguishers are polynomial-size classical circuit families. A function μ is negligible if for every c>0, μ(λ)<λ^(−c) for all sufficiently large λ. Public-key encryption consists of KeyGen(1^λ)=(pk,sk), Enc(pk,m;r), and Dec(sk,c), for m∈{0,1}; decryption fails with negligible probability over key generation and encryption coins, for each m. IND-CPA means that no such adversary given pk distinguishes Enc(pk,0) from Enc(pk,1) with nonnegligible advantage; public encryption is available to it. In OT, sender S has bits (m_0,m_1), receiver R has a choice bit c, and R must output m_c except with negligible probability for every input triple; S has no output. The parties follow their prescribed algorithms but keep their entire views, including inputs, random tapes, and messages. There must be uniform probabilistic polynomial-time simulators Sim_S(1^λ,m_0,m_1) and Sim_R(1^λ,c,m_c) whose outputs are computationally indistinguishable from the corresponding real views for every sequence of input triples. Thus S learns nothing about c and R learns nothing beyond (c,m_c). The parties have independent private randomness and exchange classical messages directly. There is no trusted setup, common reference string, random oracle, pre-shared correlated randomness, trusted hardware, or quantum resource.
cards.answer_criterion: Establish the stated existence implication without a second unproved hardness assumption, or refute that unrelativized implication. A construction may inspect and use the code of the encryption algorithms and use non-black-box security arguments. An oracle separation or a lower bound restricted to black-box reductions is a barrier, not a negative resolution of this question. A construction requiring an additional property of encryption must also derive that property from arbitrary IND-CPA encryption to settle the card.
cards.why: Determines whether the ability to send secrets to a designated receiver already suffices for general private computation between mutually distrustful parties. It is a basic boundary in the hierarchy of cryptographic assumptions, with a longstanding black-box barrier and no known unrestricted implication.

importance.reason: A foundational comparison between ordinary public-key confidentiality and a primitive complete for secure computation; resolving it would change which assumptions suffice for a broad range of protocols.

progress.text: Gertner and coauthors prove an oracle with PKE but no semi-honest OT, and give positive constructions when PKE has specified extra properties. Their oracle separations use uniform adversaries.
Haitner and coauthors give a fully black-box compiler from semi-honest to malicious OT and general secure computation, establishing the strength of even the passive-security target.
Maji and Wang prove limitations on optimal fair coin tossing from black-box PKE or key agreement; this is further evidence about restricted constructions, not an unrestricted separation.
Li, Zhang, and Lin construct OT from rerandomizable PKE, replacing oblivious sampling with a public ciphertext-rerandomization requirement.
The journal version of Tanishita and coauthors’ work derives OT from updatable encryption with additional sampling properties. It does not remove all extra assumptions on the starting primitive.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. No unrestricted classical implication from arbitrary IND-CPA public-key encryption to OT was identified. Known oracle/black-box separations and positive results for rerandomizable or suitably samplable encryption do not settle this formulation. The card fixes semi-honest standalone security with classical communication and no setup.

context_blocks.text: Ordinary encryption protects a message from someone who lacks the secret key. Oblivious transfer must arrange a more selective situation: the receiver can read one of two messages, cannot read the other, and does not disclose which one it selected. This combines privacy for both participants. Merely encrypting both messages under a key generated by the receiver fails, because that receiver can decrypt both ciphertexts. Asking the receiver to reveal which key it can decrypt would instead reveal its choice.

Some encryption schemes offer the missing structure. If a receiver can create two indistinguishable-looking public keys while knowing a decryption key for just one, it can place the decryptable key in position c. The sender encrypts the two messages under the corresponding keys. Such an argument needs a suitable oblivious-sampling property, including security even given the sampler’s retained randomness. Gertner and coauthors identify sufficient properties and also prove an oracle separation between general PKE and even semi-honest OT. Their historical separation uses uniform adversaries.

That result constrains a style of construction, rather than deciding the unrestricted implication. In an oracle argument all algorithms are given access to an additional idealized operation. A construction based on the actual implementation of an encryption scheme may use features that do not survive replacement by an arbitrary oracle. Consequently, the qualifier allowing non-black-box techniques is substantive; removing it would turn the card into a question already addressed by known barriers.

The semi-honest target is already powerful. Haitner, Ishai, Kushilevitz, Lindell, and Petrank show how to transform semi-honest OT into OT secure against malicious parties, and obtain general secure computation without an honest majority. Their result fixes static corruption and standalone security; it does not promise fairness or guaranteed output delivery against a party that aborts. This explains why the basic passive-security implication matters without building stronger composition or fairness requirements into the question.

Progress continues through additional algebraic or sampling structure. Li, Zhang, and Lin construct OT from rerandomizable PKE: anyone with the public key can turn a ciphertext into a fresh encryption of the same plaintext. This avoids their predecessors’ oblivious-sampling requirement but introduces a different hypothesis. Ordinary IND-CPA security alone does not include a public rerandomization algorithm.

A 2026 journal paper by Tanishita and coauthors studies updatable encryption, where update tokens let a third party transform ciphertexts across keys. With specified oblivious-sampling properties, it derives two- or three-round OT. Those theorems refine the boundary for a structured encryption primitive. They do not give a transformation starting with an arbitrary public-key encryption scheme.

A related barrier concerns fair coin tossing. Maji and Wang show limits for protocols using public-key encryption or key agreement as black boxes, whereas OT supports optimally fair constructions. This gives another operational way to see the distinction between ordinary encrypted communication and primitives complete for secure computation. The fairness result has its own model and does not constitute a proof against all non-black-box OT constructions.

Haitner, Ishai, Kushilevitz, Lindell, and Petrank show how to transform semi-honest OT into OT secure against malicious parties, and obtain general secure computation without an honest majority. Their result fixes static corruption and standalone security; it does not promise fairness or guaranteed output delivery against a party that aborts. This explains why the basic passive-security implication matters without building stronger composition or fairness requirements into the question.

Progress continues through additional algebraic or sampling structure. Li, Zhang, and Lin construct OT from rerandomizable PKE: anyone with the public key can turn a ciphertext into a fresh encryption of the same plaintext. This avoids their predecessors’ oblivious-sampling requirement but introduces a different hypothesis. Ordinary IND-CPA security alone does not include a public rerandomization algorithm.

A 2026 journal paper by Tanishita and coauthors studies updatable encryption, where update tokens let a third party transform ciphertexts across keys. With specified oblivious-sampling properties, it derives two- or three-round OT. Those theorems refine the boundary for a structured encryption primitive. They do not give a transformation starting with an arbitrary public-key encryption scheme.

A related barrier concerns fair coin tossing. Maji and Wang show limits for protocols using public-key encryption or key agreement as black boxes, whereas OT supports optimally fair constructions. This gives another operational way to see the distinction between ordinary encrypted communication and primitives complete for secure computation. The fairness result has its own model and does not constitute a proof against all non-black-box OT constructions.

cards.title: Collision-resistant hashing from one-way functions
cards.formal: In the ordinary classical computational model, does the existence of a polynomial-time computable one-way function secure against all polynomial-size circuit families imply the existence of a publicly keyed collision-resistant hash family H_k:{0,1}^{2λ}→{0,1}^λ secure against all polynomial-size circuit families?
cards.definitions: A one-way function is a deterministic uniformly polynomial-time computable map f on finite binary strings, with output length bounded by a polynomial in the input length, such that for every family of possibly randomized Boolean circuits A_n of size polynomial in n, Pr[f(A_n(1^n,f(X)))=f(X) and |A_n(1^n,f(X))|=n] is negligible in n, where X is uniform on {0,1}^n. The same invocation of A_n supplies the candidate preimage in both parts of this event. A function μ is negligible if for every c>0 there is N_c such that μ(n)≤n^{-c} for all n≥N_c. A hash family consists of a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time key generator Gen(1^λ) producing a polynomial-length public key k, and a uniform deterministic polynomial-time evaluator H(1^λ,k,x). For every key in the generator’s support, H_k maps every 2λ-bit input to a λ-bit output. Collision resistance means that for every polynomial-size possibly randomized circuit family B_λ, the probability that B_λ(1^λ,k) outputs distinct x,x′∈{0,1}^{2λ} with H_k(x)=H_k(x′) is negligible in λ, over k←Gen(1^λ) and the attacker’s coins. Both messages may be chosen after the attacker sees k. Circuit descriptions may depend on the security parameter, but not on the freshly sampled key. The implication permits arbitrary use of the description of f and arbitrary proof techniques; no random oracle, additional setup assumption, quantum resource, trapdoor, or stronger quantitative hardness assumption is supplied.
cards.answer_criterion: Establish the stated existence implication without additional assumptions, or refute it in the ordinary unrelativized model. A positive result may use non-black-box techniques. An oracle world where one-way functions exist but collision-resistant hashing fails proves only a relativizing barrier. Failure of a particular construction, even for a specific one-way function, is also insufficient to refute the existence implication. Producing only target-collision resistance, noncompressing injective functions, or a construction from stronger product-hardness assumptions does not settle the proposition.
cards.why: Determines whether a fundamental compressing cryptographic primitive needs assumptions beyond ordinary one-wayness, while exposing the gap between known black-box barriers and unrestricted constructions.

importance.reason: A central unresolved implication among cryptographic primitives, with consequences for authentication, data commitments and succinct verification.

cards.status_note: No unrestricted implication or refutation was found in the primary literature checked through 11 September 2026. Existing black-box separations do not settle this ordinary-model existence statement. The definitions explicitly use uniform honest algorithms, nonuniform classical adversaries, public fresh keys and factor-two compression.

context_blocks.text: A collision-resistant hash compresses its input while making it computationally difficult to find two distinct messages with the same digest. Collisions must exist by the pigeonhole principle: there are 2^{2λ} possible inputs and only 2^λ outputs. Security is therefore not a claim that collisions never occur, or that a digest uniquely identifies a message. It is a claim about what an efficient adversary can construct after learning the hash key.

A one-way function poses a different challenge. The attacker receives the image of a random input and must find any preimage. An injective one-way function can have no collisions at all, yet it is not a compressing hash. Conversely, a compressing map may have easily found collisions even if some inversion tasks look difficult. The question asks whether the minimal assumption of computationally hard inversion can always supply the more structured difficulty of finding collisions.

The public key matters to the asymptotic definition. If a single compressing function were fixed at each security parameter and security were required against nonuniform circuits, an attacker could hard-code one collision for each parameter. A fresh polynomial-length key prevents that pair from being selected in advance for the actual function used. The key is not secret: the adversary sees it before choosing either colliding message.

Target-collision resistance changes the order of moves. An attacker first commits to one message, then sees a random key and seeks a second message colliding with its committed target. Rompel constructs universal one-way hash functions of this kind from arbitrary one-way functions, as part of the route to secure signatures. That theorem does not give the present game, where both messages are chosen after the key is known. The order difference is small syntactically but central to the unresolved assumption gap.

Simon constructs an oracle setting with one-way permutations but no collision-resistant hash functions in the relevant relativized sense. It rules out building and proving the desired primitive by treating the assumed function purely as an oracle in the separated framework. The theorem does not rule out exploiting a function’s implementation or a proof that fails to relativize. The ordinary mathematical implication in this card therefore remains stronger than the black-box construction question already answered negatively.

Holmgren and Lombardi give a positive route under stronger assumptions about simultaneously inverting independent challenges. Their one-way product functions require quantitative batch hardness beyond ordinary one-wayness. They construct collision-resistant hashing from suitable such functions and connect the missing assumption to unusually strong parallel repetition. This identifies a concrete intermediate target without showing that every ordinary one-way function possesses the required batch security.

The separation also connects hashing to total search problems. Given a circuit for a compressing map, a collision is guaranteed to exist and can be checked efficiently. Folwarczný and coauthors study whether one-way functions can establish hardness for total NP search more generally, extending limitations for a class of single-query reductions. These are restrictions on reductions, not an unconditional proof that collision-resistant families cannot follow from one-wayness by any method.

Applications can sometimes avoid the full primitive. Rothblum’s July 2026 work constructs efficient interactive arguments for bounded-space computations from one-way functions. Communication depends on the space bound times a polynomial in log T and the security parameter, and the security loss depends polynomially on the computation time T. This weakens assumptions for that interactive application; it does not construct a publicly evaluable compressing hash that withstands arbitrary key-dependent collision attempts.

A resolution would clarify the foundations of many protocols that use short commitments to large data. It would either place full collision resistance on the same assumption level as ordinary one-wayness, or demonstrate a separation that survives beyond black-box barriers. The card asks for polynomial security only; requiring near-optimal exponential security or resistance to quantum attacks would introduce additional questions.

cards.title: Noninteractive SZK versus SZK
cards.formal: Does NISZK equal SZK for classical promise problems with an honestly generated common uniformly random reference string in the noninteractive model?
cards.definitions: SZK denotes statistical zero-knowledge interactive proofs; NISZK denotes their one-message analogue with public random setup. In both cases the verifier and simulator run in probabilistic polynomial time and the honest prover may be computationally unbounded. The comparison concerns promise problems, constant completeness-soundness gap and statistical simulation, not merely computational indistinguishability.

context_blocks.text: Zero knowledge restricts what a verifier learns while checking a mathematical claim. This question asks whether public randomness can replace the interaction needed for statistical zero knowledge.

The classic study of noninteractive statistical zero knowledge relates the two classes but does not establish equality. cards.title: Fully homomorphic encryption from public-key encryption
cards.formal: Does the existence of IND-CPA-secure public-key encryption imply compact fully homomorphic encryption for all polynomial-size Boolean circuits in the classical standard model?
cards.definitions: The security parameter λ is supplied in unary. Algorithms are uniform probabilistic polynomial-time machines; security is against nonuniform polynomial-size classical circuit families. A function ν(λ) is negligible if for every c>0, ν(λ)≤λ^(−c) for all sufficiently large λ. Probabilities include setup, algorithm and adversary coins. No ideal oracle or additional trusted setup is supplied unless explicitly stated; arbitrary non-black-box implications are allowed. Fully homomorphic encryption permits public evaluation of a Boolean circuit on encrypted inputs, producing an encryption of its output. Compactness requires the evaluated ciphertext length and decryption cost to be bounded by a polynomial in the security parameter and output length, independently of the evaluated circuit size. The intended scheme is unleveled: key generation receives no circuit-depth bound.

context_blocks.text: Public-key encryption permits confidential communication; fully homomorphic encryption additionally permits computation over ciphertexts. A general implication would make the stronger capability follow from the existence of the basic public-key primitive.

cards.title: PZK versus SZK
cards.formal: Does PZK=SZK for classical single-prover interactive proofs of promise problems, with polynomial-time verifiers and simulators, negligible proof error, and zero knowledge against every polynomial-time verifier?
cards.definitions: A promise problem is a pair (Y,N) of disjoint sets of finite binary strings. An interactive proof consists of a computationally unbounded prover P and a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time verifier V exchanging polynomially many bits on common input x. There is a negligible function ε such that on x∈Y the honest interaction accepts with probability at least 1−ε(|x|), and on x∈N every prover strategy is accepted with probability at most ε(|x|). Negligible means smaller than |x|^{−d} for every fixed d>0 at all sufficiently large lengths. No condition is imposed outside Y∪N. The view of a verifier consists of its random bits and exchanged messages. SZK requires that for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time verifier V* there is a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time simulator S* which, on x alone, produces a distribution within negligible total variation distance of the view of (P,V*)(x), for every x∈Y. Total variation distance is one half of the sum of absolute probability differences over possible views. PZK instead permits S* to output a failure symbol ⊥ with probability at most 1/2; conditioned on nonfailure, its output distribution must equal that view exactly. Every runtime bound is a strict polynomial bound over all random outcomes, with a polynomial allowed to depend on the fixed verifier or simulator. This is the ordinary input-only simulation convention of the cited definitions, without a shared random string, an oracle, a setup assumption, or a restriction to honest verifiers.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that every promise problem admitting the stated statistical proof also admits a perfect one in this model, or exhibit a promise problem in SZK and prove that it has no PZK proof. The protocol may change completely in a positive result. An oracle separation, a failure of one proposed compiler, a perfect-zero-knowledge PCP, or an honest-verifier-only theorem does not resolve this unrelativized class equality.

context_blocks.text: Zero knowledge formalizes the idea that a verifier can reproduce what it sees without receiving help from the prover. Statistical simulation permits a negligible discrepancy between distributions. Perfect simulation requires exact agreement after the allowed failure event. Goldreich’s textbook asks whether this difference changes which statements can be proved.

The failure convention is part of the model. A strict polynomial-time perfect simulator that never fails is a different requirement, often called super-perfect zero knowledge. Allowing an expected polynomial runtime is also a separate definitional issue discussed in the source. Neither convention is silently substituted here.

PZK is contained in SZK: repeat the bounded-failure perfect simulator polynomially many times until it succeeds, and use an arbitrary output if every attempt fails. The remaining probability of failure is negligible, while successful outputs retain the exact distribution. The open direction asks whether negligible simulation error can always be eliminated by some proof system.

Bouland, Chen, Holden, Thaler and Vasudevan construct an oracle relative to which SZK is not contained in PZK. This supplies evidence against equality and rules out a proof that relativizes in the corresponding way. It does not separate the classes in the ordinary model specified here.

Gur, O’Connor and Spooner explicitly retain PZK versus SZK as open in their 2024 paper. Their perfect-zero-knowledge construction is for probabilistically checkable proofs, where a verifier queries a proof oracle. That achievement concerns a different access model from ordinary interactive proofs and leaves this equality unresolved.

The target asks for a class equality, not a quantitative improvement in a particular cryptographic protocol. Its resolution would determine whether exact distributional privacy has an intrinsic expressive cost. TCS-1929 instead concerns zero knowledge for streaming interactive proofs with a memory restriction.

cards.title: Low-noise LPN hardness from Nearest Codeword hardness
cards.formal: Does the following implication hold? If binary Nearest Codeword is not in BPP, then no uniform probabilistic polynomial-time distinguisher D has advantage at least $n^{-c}$, for any fixed $c>0$ and all sufficiently large square n, between $(A,As+e)$ and $(A,u)$. Here $A\in\mathbb F_2^{n^2\times n}$, $s\in\mathbb F_2^n$, and $u\in\mathbb F_2^{n^2}$ are independent uniform random variables, and the coordinates of e are independent Bernoulli variables with rate $1/\sqrt n$. Advantage is the absolute difference of D’s acceptance probabilities in the two experiments.

progress.text: The revision gives a reduction for $\eta=n^{-\alpha}$, any constant $\alpha<1$, from simultaneous worst-case hardness of two tasks on a code and its dual. This advances beyond earlier near-half-noise reductions; the single-assumption target remains stronger.

cards.review_note: Editorial specialization of the NCP-only direction in Section 1.2 of the September 2026 revision. It fixes the starting problem, decision-LPN distribution, sample count, noise, uniformity, and asymptotic advantage, replacing the vague phrase natural worst-case problem. The source does not state this exact parameter specialization as a numbered conjecture.

context_blocks.text: LWE has strong connections to worst-case lattice problems. Establishing comparable foundations for LPN at cryptographically useful noise rates is more difficult.

Without noise, enough independent parity equations reveal the secret by linear algebra. Flipping some answers breaks that direct procedure: the learner must cope with equations whose right-hand sides may be wrong. At a low noise rate, most equations remain correct, which makes the precise source of hardness especially important.

A worst-case-to-average-case reduction would start with an arbitrary hard coding instance and turn it into the random samples used by LPN. It must preserve a usable noise regime and show how an LPN solver would solve the original task. Requiring two different coding tasks to be hard simultaneously is a stronger premise than deriving the guarantee from one standard worst-case problem.

cards.definitions: Binary Nearest Codeword receives a binary matrix G, a binary target y with the same number of rows, and an integer t, and asks whether $\min_z\operatorname{wt}(Gz-y)\le t$, with arithmetic over F_2 and Hamming weight wt. BPP means a uniform randomized polynomial-time decider correct with probability at least 2/3 on every instance. The LPN side here is a decision problem with n-squared samples, random secret, and inverse-square-root noise. Restricting n to squares makes the noise parameter an exact rational; this is an explicit specialization of the source’s broader low-noise direction.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed complexity-theoretic implication, for example by a reduction turning such an LPN distinguisher into a BPP algorithm for Nearest Codeword, or prove that the implication is false. Invoking simultaneous hardness of an additional problem on the dual code does not establish this implication.

cards.formal: Does the existence of a classical one-way function imply the existence of a classical one-way function computed by a polynomial-time uniform NC⁰ circuit family?
cards.definitions: The security parameter λ is supplied in unary. Algorithms are uniform probabilistic polynomial-time machines; security is against nonuniform polynomial-size classical circuit families. A function ν(λ) is negligible if for every c>0, ν(λ)≤λ^(−c) for all sufficiently large λ. Probabilities include setup, algorithm and adversary coins. No ideal oracle or additional trusted setup is supplied unless explicitly stated; arbitrary non-black-box implications are allowed. A one-way function is a deterministic polynomial-time map f:{0,1}*→{0,1}* of polynomially bounded, length-dependent output size, such that every allowed inverter on (1^n,f(U_n)) finds any n-bit preimage with negligible probability, for uniform U_n. A polynomial-time uniform NC⁰ family is generated from 1^n in poly(n) time, has polynomial size and a universal constant depth, and uses fan-in-two AND/OR and unary NOT gates. Inversion security quantifies over all polynomial-size adversaries, not just shallow ones.

context_blocks.text: Local evaluation and global inversion difficulty are strikingly different requirements. An NC⁰ one-way function has each output bit depend on only a constant number of input bits, while inverting the full output must defeat every polynomial-size adversary.

Known locality transformations start from stronger assumptions such as one-way functions in NC¹. Those constructions establish plausible NC⁰ cryptography, but they do not derive it from an arbitrary sequentially computable one-way function. The implication therefore asks whether cryptographic hardness can always be made local.

cards.why: Identify whether extreme locality is inherent in minimal cryptographic hardness or requires a stronger assumption.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.

cards.title: Non-tight verifiable delay functions from a random oracle alone
cards.formal: Historical question, resolved negatively: can a verifiable delay function with computational uniqueness be constructed in the parallel random oracle model alone when sequentiality is allowed to be substantially weaker than the honest evaluation time T, for example σ=T/2? The source’s tight impossibility theorem did not answer this question. The later general barrier shows that a perfectly complete candidate with polynomial query budgets either loses computational uniqueness or permits computation of its correct output in at most 6qᵥ online oracle rounds with constant success probability, after polynomial-query preprocessing. Here qᵥ is the verifier’s query bound. Thus even non-tight delay requirements exceeding this verification-scale depth cannot be obtained from the random oracle alone, whenever T is large enough relative to qᵥ.
cards.why: Determines whether ideal hash access alone can support both publicly verifiable uniqueness and a substantial sequential delay, a central assumptions question for timed cryptography.
cards.status_note: Read the original non-tight passage and ROM definitions, the current July 2026 major revision of the CRYPTO work, and the EUROCRYPT 2026 model and Corollary 1. Matched computational uniqueness, preprocessing and private-coin setup. The resolution is in the pure parallel query model; no ordinary polynomial-time attack or independent proof audit is claimed.

progress.text: Perfect-uniqueness and tight-sequentiality impossibility results leave general non-tight VDFs open.
CRYPTO result rules out computationally unique VDFs with public-coin setup.
EUROCRYPT result extends impossibility to private-coin setup, including expensive setup; Corollary 1 supplies the general query and round bounds.
The current ePrint of the CRYPTO work is labelled a major revision; the setup-general conclusion here is grounded in the separately published EUROCRYPT result.

cards.definitions: For security parameter λ, the shared oracle H maps finite binary strings to λ-bit strings, with independently uniform answers on new inputs and consistent answers on repetitions. A query round submits an arbitrary finite batch using only earlier answers; all answers in that batch arrive together. Total work counts oracle queries and sequential time counts rounds. Internal computation between queries is unrestricted in this model. A uniform scheme consists of Setupᴴ(λ,T), Evalᴴ(pp,x)=(y,π), and deterministic public Verifyᴴ(pp,x,y,π). Public parameters pp specify a finite uniformly samplable input set. For fixed H,pp,x the output y is fixed even if proof generation is randomized. Perfect completeness means every honestly generated output and proof is accepted. Setup, Eval and Verify have bounds qₛ,qₑ,qᵥ respectively; the source requires qₛ,qᵥ polynomial in λ and log T and qₑ≤T. The stronger 2026 model permits qₛ,qₑ polynomial in λ,T and evaluation in at most T rounds. Setup may hide its random coins; all verification information is public. Computational uniqueness forbids any adversary making polynomially many queries in λ,T from producing an accepted y′ different from the honest y, except with probability negligible in λ. Sequentiality at depth σ forbids a two-stage adversary, with the same polynomial total query budget, from outputting the honest y with non-negligible probability: the first stage sees pp and preprocesses, a fresh uniform x is then sampled, and the online stage receives x and has at most σ rounds. It need not output a proof. Negligible means smaller than λ^{−c} eventually for every fixed c>0. Probabilities include the oracle, setup, challenge and adversary coins. The later impossibility already holds with a random challenge in the uniqueness game; the 2020 source’s stronger adversarial-input and pointwise-oracle uniqueness cannot evade it. No algebraic or other hardness assumption is available in addition to H.
cards.answer_criterion: Establish existence or impossibility in the source’s general, computationally unique non-tight regime. The published 2026 Corollary 1 supplies impossibility: for perfect completeness, one of its two attacks succeeds with probability at least 1/3. The sequentiality attack uses at most 6qᵥ online rounds and polynomially many total queries, including preprocessing; the other attack breaks uniqueness with polynomially many queries. This is a query-model separation, not a claim that every ordinary implementation has a polynomial-time attack.

context_blocks.text: A proof of sequential work can have many valid outputs for one challenge. Such proofs exist in the random oracle model with non-tight sequentiality, so their existence did not answer the VDF question, which additionally requires a computationally unique output.

context_blocks.title: The two older barriers were restricted
context_blocks.text: The 2020 paper ruled out perfect uniqueness and separately ruled out delay requirements very close to T. Computational uniqueness allows incorrect accepted outputs to exist as long as bounded-query adversaries cannot find them. The extracted passage asks about that remaining non-tight setting.

context_blocks.title: Later results close the setup gap too
context_blocks.text: The CRYPTO 2025 result handles computational uniqueness with public-coin setup. The EUROCRYPT 2026 follow-up covers private-coin setup, even when its query budget grows polynomially with T. Its theorem therefore includes the source’s cheaper setup model.

context_blocks.title: The oracle model is part of the conclusion
context_blocks.text: The attacks may perform unrestricted local computation between bounded batches of oracle queries. Constructions using an additional repeated-squaring or other computational assumption are outside the pure oracle model and are not contradicted by this result.

cards.title: Quantum PCP conjecture
cards.formal: Do there exist integers k,d≥1 and a rational constant ε∈(0,1) such that the following promise problem is QMA-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? Input is a list of m≤(n+1)^d k-local Hermitian terms H_i on n≥1 qubits and rational a<b in [0,1], with 0⪯H_i⪯I and b−a≥ε. For H=(1/m)Σ_i H_i, distinguish λ_min(H)≤a from λ_min(H)≥b.
cards.why: This asks whether approximating a quantum system’s energy captures the full difficulty of quantum witness verification. It connects complexity, quantum codes, and local testing.

progress.text: The survey develops the Hamiltonian conjecture and obstacles to quantum PCP constructions.

Bafna–Vyas explicitly describe the general conjecture as open. Their classical private PCP uses $O(\sqrt n)$ queries; stronger parameters depend on a product-expansion conjecture. This does not prove Quantum PCP.
