context_blocks.text: The classical PCP theorem replaces full verification by inspecting a small part of a proof with a constant gap. Entanglement and local indistinguishability obstruct a direct quantum analogue.

Normalization makes the target meaningful. Multiplying a Hamiltonian by a large number could enlarge its energy gap, but would also violate the bound on individual terms. The conjecture asks for a constant gap in average local energy while every constraint retains bounded strength.

A useful way to read the two cases is that one input admits a low-energy global state, while in the other every state has appreciably higher average energy. The challenge is to preserve computational hardness at that coarse resolution. Checking a few local terms can detect a constant average discrepancy, but constructing a reduction with that discrepancy is the unresolved step.

cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.definitions: Here 1≤m; each term is specified by at most k distinct qubit indices and the complete matrix on those qubits, with rational real and imaginary parts encoded by signed binary numerators and positive denominators. It is tensored with identity on the other qubits. n is written in unary, thresholds in binary rational notation; N counts every supplied bit. λ_min is the smallest eigenvalue. M⪯N means that N−M is positive semidefinite, equivalently z*(N−M)z≥0 for every complex vector z. Inputs violating the matrix promises or with a<λ_min(H)<b are outside the promise. QMA consists of disjoint pairs (Y,N₀) of sets of binary strings with a polynomial-time uniform quantum verifier: on x it uses polynomially many qubits and gates over {H,T,CNOT}, an arbitrary polynomial-qubit witness, and auxiliary qubits initialized to |0⟩. H=2^(−1/2)((1,1),(1,−1)) is the Hadamard matrix, T=diag(1,exp(iπ/4)), and CNOT flips its target when its control is 1. A designated final qubit is measured. For x∈Y some witness gives acceptance probability ≥2/3; for x∈N₀ every witness gives probability ≤1/3. A deterministic machine produces the verifier circuit from x in polynomial time. QMA-hard means that for every such pair there is a deterministic polynomial-time map sending Y into the low-energy case and N₀ into the high-energy case, always producing legal instances on promised inputs. Constants k,d,ε are shared by the target problem; reduction polynomials may depend on the source promise problem.

cards.title: Area law for gapped two-dimensional Hamiltonians
cards.formal: For every fixed local dimension q≥2, interaction range r≥1, interaction incidence bound g≥1, norm bound J>0, and spectral gap Δ>0, is there a finite constant C=C(q,r,g,J,Δ) such that every Hamiltonian H described below, on every square lattice Λ_L, has unique ground state ψ satisfying S(ρ_A)≤C|∂A| for every A⊆Λ_L?
cards.definitions: Let L≥1 be an integer, Λ_L={1,…,L}² with open boundaries, and the Hilbert space be the tensor product of C^q over its sites. Write H=Σ_a h_a, where each h_a is Hermitian and acts only on a nonempty support X_a⊆Λ_L of diameter at most r in the maximum-coordinate metric. Each site belongs to at most g supports, counting terms with the same support separately, and the operator norm of every h_a is at most J. Suppose H has a unique normalized lowest-energy eigenvector ψ and its next eigenvalue is at least Δ above the lowest eigenvalue. This is a gap of the entire Hamiltonian; no spectral-gap condition is imposed on subregions or subsets of terms. For A⊆Λ_L, let A^c be its complement in Λ_L and ρ_A=Tr_(A^c)(|ψ⟩⟨ψ|) and S(ρ_A)=−Tr(ρ_A log_2 ρ_A), with 0 log_2 0=0. The boundary ∂A is the set of nearest-neighbor lattice edges with exactly one endpoint in A; its cardinality is the boundary length in lattice units. Empty and full regions have entropy zero. The local parameters and C must be independent of L, A, and the actual interaction matrices. Interactions may vary from site to site and with L. They need not commute or share a simultaneous minimum-energy state; translation invariance and frustration freeness are not assumed. No approximation or state-preparation algorithm is requested.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A central problem in quantum Hamiltonian complexity: whether locality plus a uniform gap controls the quantum information in ground states in two dimensions. It would sharpen the structural foundations of tensor-network methods and separate the task of bounding entanglement from the further task of computing the state.

importance.reason: A fundamental unresolved link between spectral gaps, geometric locality, entanglement, and the resources needed to describe quantum many-body ground states.

progress.text: Hastings proves the area law for gapped one-dimensional quantum systems; the bound depends on fixed local parameters.
Huang establishes QMA-completeness of two-dimensional local Hamiltonian problems even when ground states satisfy area laws, without claiming a uniform spectral gap.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The February and April 2026 results retain extra hypotheses; the general globally gapped 2D entropy area law remains unresolved. The formulation explicitly requires a size-independent constant and fixes the geometric boundary, interaction norms, local dimension, uniqueness, and global gap.

context_blocks.text: A region with m spins has enough Hilbert-space dimension for entropy m log_2 q. For a square block of side length ℓ, that is proportional to ℓ², whereas this conjecture allows only a constant times ℓ. The physical idea is that finite-range interactions and a gap should constrain how much quantum information crosses the boundary. Fixing both interaction strength and the gap prevents an artificial rescaling from making a gapless family appear uniformly gapped.

In one dimension, Hastings proves the corresponding entropy bound for gapped local systems. Since an interval has only a constant number of boundary points, its entropy remains bounded as the chain grows. Matrix-product-state approximations then connect this structure to classical numerical methods. Grouping columns of a two-dimensional lattice into single one-dimensional sites does not directly extend the theorem: each new site has dimension q^L, which grows exponentially with the width.

Anshu, Arad, and Gosset make major progress for frustration-free systems with a local gap. Frustration freeness means one state minimizes every local term; the local-gap assumption controls Hamiltonians obtained from subsets of terms, and is stronger than the global gap here. Their cited version proves a vertical-cut entropy bound n^(1+O((log n)^(−1/5))) for cut length n. It is asymptotically almost linear, but the remaining factor is not a constant and neither extra assumption follows from the statement in this card.

Anshu, Harrow, and Soleimanifar prove an area law for entanglement spread, a measure of variation among the Schmidt coefficients after an appropriate smoothing. This controls a different feature of entanglement from its entropy. For intuition, a maximally entangled state can have arbitrarily many equal Schmidt coefficients: its spread is zero while its entropy is the logarithm of their number. A spread bound therefore does not by itself answer the entropy question.

Arad, Firanko, and Jain’s February 2026 theorem treats mutual information of the maximally mixed ground state. It assumes a sufficiently accurate approximation to the ground-space projector whose operator Schmidt rank is suitably small. Constructing such an approximation for general gapped two-dimensional Hamiltonians remains a missing ingredient; the general wording of the title does not remove this hypothesis.

Garratt and Abanin’s April 2026 preprint provides thermodynamic upper bounds and proves area laws for frustration-free systems when ground-space degeneracies of the relevant subsystem Hamiltonians have suitable boundary scaling. A unique ground state for the full system does not impose that condition on each subsystem. These results retain additional assumptions.

The computational significance also needs care. Huang proves that two-dimensional local Hamiltonian instances whose ground states satisfy area laws can still be QMA-complete. Those instances are not claimed to have the uniform gap fixed here. The result nevertheless shows why an entropy bound alone should not be advertised as a general efficient classical algorithm for finding or manipulating two-dimensional ground states.

cards.title: NPT bound entanglement
cards.formal: Do there exist finite integers a,b≥2 and a bipartite density matrix ρ on ℂᵃ⊗ℂᵇ such that ρ has negative partial transpose, but ⟨ψ|(ρ^{Γ_B})^{⊗k}|ψ⟩≥0 for every integer k≥1 and every unit vector ψ of Schmidt rank at most two across (ℂᵃ)^{⊗k}:(ℂᵇ)^{⊗k}?
cards.definitions: A density matrix is a positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix with trace one. In fixed local orthonormal bases, partial transpose on B is defined by (ρ^{Γ_B})_{ij,kℓ}=ρ_{iℓ,kj}. Negative partial transpose (NPT) means that ρ^{Γ_B} has at least one negative eigenvalue; it does not mean that the whole matrix is negative semidefinite. Schmidt rank is the minimum number of product vectors whose sum is ψ. Tensor powers represent independent copies of the same fixed state. A state is k-copy distillable exactly when a Schmidt-rank-at-most-two vector makes the displayed expectation strictly negative. Thus the proposed state is undistillable for every finite number of copies. Operationally, Alice and Bob may use arbitrary local quantum operations, local auxiliary systems and unlimited classical communication in both directions, but no quantum communication or additional shared entanglement. Distillability means that they can asymptotically obtain Bell pairs (|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2 at a positive rate with error tending to zero. The finite-copy criterion above is equivalent to positive distillability in this model.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A defining question about whether partial-transpose negativity completely captures the possibility of converting bipartite entanglement into useful Bell pairs. Its precise all-copy quantifier connects quantum resource theory to tensor-stable matrix inequalities.

importance.reason: A central structural boundary in entanglement theory, with canonical finite-dimensional candidates and consequences for what quantum correlations can accomplish under local operations.

cards.status_note: The all-copy NPT bound-entanglement question remains explicitly open in the July 2026 primary sources. New two-copy solutions and restricted three-copy progress do not settle this formulation. Reviewed through 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: Entanglement is a property of a state, whereas distillation is an operational ability to turn many noisy shared states into nearly perfect Bell pairs. These pairs are useful because a pair, together with classical communication, can transfer an unknown qubit by teleportation. The question asks whether there is a form of entanglement that passes the necessary negative-partial-transpose test for distillation but is nevertheless permanently unusable for this particular conversion.

The Horodeckis established that entangled states with positive partial transpose can be bound entangled. Their obstruction survives every tensor power: a positive semidefinite partial transpose remains positive semidefinite after tensoring, so no test vector can have negative expectation. This card concerns the complementary regime, where some negative eigenvector exists already, but its Schmidt rank may be too large to provide the rank-two witness needed for a distillation protocol.

Low local dimension explains why a spectral test alone can be misleading in larger systems. If one party has dimension two, every vector has Schmidt rank at most two. A negative eigenvector then immediately certifies one-copy distillability. In higher dimensions, a negative eigenvector can require three or more product terms. Combining copies enlarges both local spaces and permits collective operations, creating additional opportunities to extract a useful two-dimensional entangled subsystem.

The systematic search for NPT bound entanglement dates at least to the families studied by DiVincenzo, Shor, Smolin, Terhal and Thapliyal. Their work provides evidence and reductions to structured states rather than a proof of an all-copy counterexample. Such reductions matter because the original statement quantifies over all finite dimensions and all density matrices; symmetry can expose a tractable algebraic problem inside that enormous search space.

A canonical family is ρ_W(d,α)=(I+αF)/(d²+αd), where d≥3, −1≤α≤1 and F swaps the two d-dimensional systems. These Werner states are NPT exactly when α<−1/d, and one-copy distillable exactly when α<−1/2. Consequently the interval −1/2≤α<−1/d consists of particularly important candidates. It is nonempty for d≥3. The endpoint α=−1/2 is NPT even though its minimum expectation on rank-two vectors is zero.

Several July 2026 papers prove that the one-copy and two-copy thresholds for Werner states coincide. Fraser and coauthors obtain this from a rank-constrained partial-trace inequality, with no Hermiticity or positivity assumption on the coefficient matrix. These results include the formerly open two-ququart example ρ_W(4,−1/2). They remove a major finite-copy obstacle, but do not prove that any particular NPT Werner state is undistillable for every number of copies.

A two-copy proof cannot simply be iterated. In the corresponding matrix formulation, taking a partial trace can increase rank; tensor products also need not preserve the relevant positivity property. Bharti, Gajjala and Haug make these obstacles explicit while giving restricted many-copy extensions. Likewise, a sequence of examples that resists progressively larger numbers of copies can approach the PPT boundary without yielding one fixed NPT state that resists all of them.

Wu and Zou’s subsequent three-copy analysis proves endpoint nonnegativity for the normal rank-two coefficient sector, among other restricted sectors, and studies genuinely nonnormal cases separately. It does not settle the unrestricted three-copy question, much less the all-copy target. sentences: Entangled states can sometimes be converted into nearly perfect shared Bell pairs using many copies and local operations with classical communication.
Bound entanglement means that this distillation remains impossible despite the presence of entanglement.
The question asks whether such states can have a negative partial transpose, a spectral property associated with distillability in simpler settings.
Failure of a protocol on one copy or any fixed number of copies does not establish the required obstruction for every number of copies.
Resolving the question would sharpen the distinction between entanglement as a property and entanglement as a usable communication resource.

cards.context:
Entanglement is a property of a state, whereas distillation is an operational ability to turn many noisy shared states into nearly perfect Bell pairs. These pairs are useful because a pair, together with classical communication, can transfer an unknown qubit by teleportation. The question asks whether there is a form of entanglement that passes the necessary negative-partial-transpose test for distillation but is nevertheless permanently unusable for this particular conversion.

The Horodeckis established that entangled states with positive partial transpose can be bound entangled. Their obstruction survives every tensor power: a positive semidefinite partial transpose remains positive semidefinite after tensoring, so no test vector can have negative expectation. This card concerns the complementary regime, where some negative eigenvector exists already, but its Schmidt rank may be too large to provide the rank-two witness needed for a distillation protocol.

Low local dimension explains why a spectral test alone can be misleading in larger systems. If one party has dimension two, every vector has Schmidt rank at most two. A negative eigenvector then immediately certifies one-copy distillability. In higher dimensions, a negative eigenvector can require three or more product terms. Combining copies enlarges both local spaces and permits collective operations, creating additional opportunities to extract a useful two-dimensional entangled subsystem.

The systematic search for NPT bound entanglement dates at least to the families studied by DiVincenzo, Shor, Smolin, Terhal and Thapliyal. Their work provides evidence and reductions to structured states rather than a proof of an all-copy counterexample. Such reductions matter because the original statement quantifies over all finite dimensions and all density matrices; symmetry can expose a tractable algebraic problem inside that enormous search space.

A canonical family is ρ_W(d,α)=(I+αF)/(d²+αd), where d≥3, −1≤α≤1 and F swaps the two d-dimensional systems. These Werner states are NPT exactly when α<−1/d, and one-copy distillable exactly when α<−1/2. Consequently the interval −1/2≤α<−1/d consists of particularly important candidates. It is nonempty for d≥3. The endpoint α=−1/2 is NPT even though its minimum expectation on rank-two vectors is zero.

Several July 2026 papers prove that the one-copy and two-copy thresholds for Werner states coincide. Fraser and coauthors obtain this from a rank-constrained partial-trace inequality, with no Hermiticity or positivity assumption on the coefficient matrix. These results include the formerly open two-ququart example ρ_W(4,−1/2). They remove a major finite-copy obstacle, but do not prove that any particular NPT Werner state is undistillable for every number of copies.

A two-copy proof cannot simply be iterated. In the corresponding matrix formulation, taking a partial trace can increase rank; tensor products also need not preserve the relevant positivity property. Bharti, Gajjala and Haug make these obstacles explicit while giving restricted many-copy extensions. Likewise, a sequence of examples that resists progressively larger numbers of copies can approach the PPT boundary without yielding one fixed NPT state that resists all of them.

Wu and Zou’s subsequent three-copy analysis proves endpoint nonnegativity for the normal rank-two coefficient sector, among other restricted sectors, and studies genuinely nonnormal cases separately. It does not settle the unrestricted three-copy question, much less the all-copy target. The distinction makes the remaining challenge concrete: control every admissible rank-two witness across the full collection of copies, rather than only witnesses with a convenient internal structure.

context_blocks.text: A quantum state may encode a proof that has no short classical description. Oracle separations test this idea but do not separate the standard classes.

The same quantum verifier is used on both sides of the comparison. What changes is the proof supplied by a prover: either a classical string or a quantum state. A classical proof is still allowed to instruct the verifier to perform a sophisticated quantum computation, so this is not simply a comparison between classical and quantum algorithms.

To prove a separation, one needs a verification task whose positive instances admit useful quantum proofs but no comparably short classical proofs for any efficient quantum verifier. Observing that a particular state has a long classical description is not sufficient: a different classical argument might certify the same claim without describing that state.

cards.definitions: Let G be a finite group with identity e and H≤G a subgroup. Its left cosets are gH={gh:h∈H}. A hiding function f:G→S is strictly H-periodic when f(g)=f(g′) if and only if gH=g′H, equivalently g⁻¹g′∈H. The codomain labels distinguish different cosets but have no promised algebraic meaning. The output is a finite list h₁,…,h_r whose generated subgroup equals H, not merely its order or a membership test. Every finite subgroup has a generating set of at most ⌈log₂|G|⌉ elements, so a short output is possible when group elements have short encodings. The standard hiding oracle coherently maps |g⟩|0⟩ to |g⟩|f(g)⟩; with a fixed binary output encoding it can be implemented as |g⟩|z⟩↦|g⟩|z XOR f(g)⟩. Bounded error means that the entire output generates exactly H with probability at least 2/3 on each promised instance. The desired resource bound concerns all computation, including classical preprocessing, group operations, non-oracle quantum gates, measurements and output processing, rather than just calls to f. The precise finite encoding and uniform access to arbitrary G remain unspecified in the source import, as recorded in statement_review.
cards.answer_criterion: The intended positive answer is a uniform bounded-error quantum algorithm with polynomial total cost in log|G|, valid for every group and hiding function in one specified efficient group-access model. A query upper bound alone does not qualify. A negative answer would exclude such algorithms in that same fixed model. The current card retains the missing group-representation specification instead of silently choosing a narrower group family or a stronger oracle.

context_blocks.title: A subgroup hidden by equal values
context_blocks.text: The oracle groups elements together by assigning the same label exactly on each coset of H. Consider addition modulo 12 and H={0,4,8}. The function f(x)=x mod 4 is constant on the four cosets and different between them. Outputting the single generator 4 identifies H; listing all twelve inputs or reconstructing the oracle’s labels is unnecessary. In a non-Abelian group, the distinction between left and right cosets matters, so the left-coset convention is explicit.

context_blocks.title: Easy membership does not give a short description
context_blocks.text: An element g belongs to H exactly when f(g)=f(e), so a single comparison with the identity’s label tests membership. That test does not by itself find generators quickly: a small hidden subgroup may contain only a tiny fraction of G. The objective is to recover its structure with cost polynomial in the number of bits needed to describe a group element, rather than by scanning every group element.

context_blocks.title: The query problem is already solved
context_blocks.text: Ettinger, Høyer and Knill prove that a polynomial number of hiding-function queries suffices for an arbitrary finite group. Their Theorem 1 gives an O((log|G|)^4) bound and also discusses an exact version with arbitrary one-qubit gates. The same paper explicitly says that its classical preprocessing and quantum networks are inefficient. Thus the title’s polynomial query complexity does not settle the total-running-time question. The bounded-error target here does not require the exact gate model from their additional exactness result.

context_blocks.title: Progress depends on the group family
context_blocks.text: Efficient quantum algorithms solve the Abelian hidden subgroup problem and explain several classic quantum speedups. In August 2026, Morales obtains additional non-Abelian cases: certain semidirect products under bounded-rank and exponent conditions, and quasi-Hamiltonian groups under an input-structure assumption. Those hypotheses do not cover arbitrary finite groups. The dihedral case remains an independently important specialization recorded elsewhere in the atlas.

context_blocks.title: What still needs specification
context_blocks.text: A multiplication table has roughly |G|² entries, far larger than a polynomial in log|G|. A short generating set with coherent group-operation access is a different input model. Unique element names, knowledge of the group order, and access to uniform superpositions can also change the available operations. The original import names a standard model without spelling these choices out, while its principal reference is designed to count only hiding-oracle queries. The common mathematical task and current research boundary are now stated, but the card remains unfinished until its group representation and cost conventions are fixed.

cards.title: Dihedral hidden subgroup problem in BQP
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform bounded-error quantum algorithm and constants C,c>0 such that, for every N≥2 and every oracle f hiding a subgroup H of D_N, the algorithm outputs generators of H with probability at least 2/3 using at most C(⌈log₂N⌉+ℓ+2)ᶜ total operations, where ℓ is the bit length of an oracle value?
cards.definitions: The dihedral group D_N has 2N elements represented as pairs (x,b) with x∈ℤ/Nℤ and b∈{0,1}, and multiplication (x,b)(y,d)=(x+(−1)ᵇy mod N,b+d mod 2). Its identity is (0,0). The classical input is N in binary and the positive integer ℓ specifying the output-register width. An arbitrary subgroup H≤D_N is hidden by f:D_N→{0,1}^ℓ when f(g)=f(g′) if and only if gH=g′H, equivalently g⁻¹g′∈H. Thus distinct left cosets have distinct labels, whose bit patterns carry no promised structure. Quantum access is the reversible XOR oracle U_f|g,z⟩=|g,z⊕f(g)⟩, usable on superpositions; it acts as the identity on invalid group encodings. Each call costs one oracle operation. Count all other elementary quantum gates, measurements and classical bit operations as well, using a fixed universal gate set such as Clifford+T. Uniformity requires an effective polynomial-time classical controller, with no advice depending on N, H or f. There is no input truth table for f and no additional subset-sum, state-preparation or memory-access oracle. The output is a finite list of encoded group elements whose generated subgroup equals H; the empty list is allowed for H={1}. The success probability is over the algorithm’s internal randomness and measurements, for every legal hiding function separately. The displayed bound is a worst-case bound on total work, not merely query count or parallel depth. When ℓ is polynomial in log N, as in the usual oracle model, the target is polynomial time in log N.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct and prove correct a quantum algorithm with the stated uniform polynomial total-work guarantee, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A polynomial number of oracle queries with superpolynomial postprocessing, a speedup using uncounted parallel hardware, or an algorithm requiring an additional subset-sum oracle does not suffice. Failure of one family of measurements or sieves is not a negative solution for all quantum algorithms.
cards.why: A central test for quantum algorithms beyond abelian Fourier sampling. The information can be acquired with few queries, but extracting the subgroup efficiently remains a fundamental computational challenge with lattice-related consequences under the appropriate reductions.

importance.reason: A basic nonabelian hidden-structure problem with a long-standing gap between polynomial information requirements and subexponential known algorithms.

Simon’s August 2026 coset-algorithm claim is disputed: the September 1 Gupte–Ragavan–Zhandry response proves failure of the proposed template, and Guo–Yang identify an unsupported independence hypothesis. context_blocks.text: Hidden subgroup problems ask a quantum algorithm to recover symmetry from equality patterns in a function. In an abelian group, Fourier sampling can turn those patterns into usable constraints, providing the framework for familiar quantum period-finding algorithms. The dihedral group adds a reflection to a cyclic rotation group and is among the simplest noncommutative settings in which the general polynomial-time method remains unresolved.

A representative hard case has H=H_s={(0,0),(s,1)}, with an unknown s∈ℤ/Nℤ. The hiding promise says f(x,0)=f(x+s,1), and each restriction to b=0 or b=1 is injective. Recovering the subgroup is therefore recovering a cyclic hidden shift. The unrestricted subgroup problem reduces to this reflection case after handling its rotational part; the inherited Kuperberg paper uses the hidden-shift formulation for its main algorithm.

A coherent oracle query followed by discarding the function value yields a coset state. In the reflection case it has the form (|0,x⟩+|1,x+s⟩)/√2 for an unknown random x. Fourier transformation of the cyclic coordinate produces a known random label k and a qubit with relative phase exp(2πiks/N). The phase contains information about s, but measuring that qubit does not simply reveal the modular product ks as a classical number.

This is already enough information in a statistical sense: polynomially many queries suffice if computationally expensive processing is allowed. The main obstacle is implementing an effective collective extraction of the hidden shift with polynomial total work. A bound on oracle calls therefore cannot be substituted for a bound on running time. The card deliberately counts both quantum gates and classical postprocessing.

Kuperberg’s first sieve gives time and query complexity 2^{O(√log N)}. It repeatedly combines phase states so that their labels become more useful for recovering the shift. This is a substantial speedup over generic classical approaches, yet it is superpolynomial in the input length n≈log N: the target here is n^{O(1)}, not 2^{O(√n)}.

The resource picture improved further. Regev obtains subexponential time with polynomial space, at a larger exponent involving √(log N log log N). Kuperberg’s later collimation sieve restores exp(O(√log N)) time while using only O(log N) quantum space, although classical storage remains subexponential. Small quantum memory and polynomial overall running time are different achievements.

The lattice connection is important but needs its access-model qualification. Regev reduces a unique-shortest-vector problem to solving dihedral coset samples. Thus a polynomial algorithm that works from those samples would have consequences for lattice algorithms. An arbitrary hiding-function oracle provides a different interface, so one should not silently claim that every conceivable oracle-HSP algorithm automatically implements the coset solver required by that reduction.

An older positive claim remains visible in search results. Moore and Young’s February 2022 preprint claimed polynomial time for dihedral groups of power-of-two size, but was withdrawn on February 23. The withdrawal states that Lemma 4.3 is wrong and that the main algorithm needs the states asserted by that lemma. It is retained here as a documented withdrawn attempt, not a known algorithm.

A much more recent claim requires a separate status entry. Daniel Simon’s August 2026 preprint claims a polynomial-time dihedral coset algorithm, replacing a subset-sum step with a different erasure procedure. Its latest listed revision is August 17 and acknowledges a correction to the analysis as well as a new critical response. A valid coset algorithm of the claimed generality would settle the reflection case, making this directly relevant to the present question.

Gupte, Ragavan and Zhandry’s response, revised September 1, gives an information-theoretic obstruction to the proposed algorithm. They show that its use of only a truncated portion of the classical Fourier labels leaves negligible advantage in guessing the secret’s least-significant bit. Their theorem covers a broader template containing the proposed procedure; it does not exclude all algorithms for the dihedral problem. The authors also supply a Lean formalization. This catalogue review checked the primary statements and repository description, but did not independently rerun that formalization.

Guo and Yang independently analyze the supporting lemmas. Their August 17 paper proves corrected statements while identifying a remaining independence assumption that the proposed choice of a partition does not supply. They explicitly conclude that establishing those lemmas does not establish correctness of the algorithm. The card therefore flags the recent claim as disputed rather than presenting polynomial time as established.

Positive results elsewhere among nonabelian groups continue to refine the boundary. Morales’ August 2026 algorithm handles certain scalar-action semidirect products with bounded generator rank and exponent-to-prime ratio polylogarithmic in group size, and another family with modular subgroup structure. For the ordinary dihedral family, the relevant ratio would be N/2, which does not meet that condition as N grows. These structural advances leave the unrestricted dihedral target intact.

A solution would identify a new way to convert nonabelian quantum information into efficiently recoverable classical structure. A negative result would be equally consequential because polynomial query complexity is already available: it would isolate a genuine computational obstruction in processing the information. The significance comes from that algorithmic boundary, alongside the precise reductions to coset and lattice problems.

The resource picture improved further. Regev obtains subexponential time with polynomial space, at a larger exponent involving √(log N log log N). Kuperberg’s later collimation sieve restores exp(O(√log N)) time while using only O(log N) quantum space, although classical storage remains subexponential. Small quantum memory and polynomial overall running time are different achievements.

The lattice connection is important but needs its access-model qualification. Regev reduces a unique-shortest-vector problem to solving dihedral coset samples. Thus a polynomial algorithm that works from those samples would have consequences for lattice algorithms. An arbitrary hiding-function oracle provides a different interface, so one should not silently claim that every conceivable oracle-HSP algorithm automatically implements the coset solver required by that reduction.

An older positive claim remains visible in search results. Moore and Young’s February 2022 preprint claimed polynomial time for dihedral groups of power-of-two size, but was withdrawn on February 23. The withdrawal states that Lemma 4.3 is wrong and that the main algorithm needs the states asserted by that lemma. It is retained here as a documented withdrawn attempt, not a known algorithm.

A much more recent claim requires a separate status entry. Daniel Simon’s August 2026 preprint claims a polynomial-time dihedral coset algorithm, replacing a subset-sum step with a different erasure procedure. Its latest listed revision is August 17 and acknowledges a correction to the analysis as well as a new critical response. A valid coset algorithm of the claimed generality would settle the reflection case, making this directly relevant to the present question.

Gupte, Ragavan and Zhandry’s response, revised September 1, gives an information-theoretic obstruction to the proposed algorithm. They show that its use of only a truncated portion of the classical Fourier labels leaves negligible advantage in guessing the secret’s least-significant bit. Their theorem covers a broader template containing the proposed procedure; it does not exclude all algorithms for the dihedral problem. The authors also supply a Lean formalization. This catalogue review checked the primary statements and repository description, but did not independently rerun that formalization.

Guo and Yang independently analyze the supporting lemmas. Their August 17 paper proves corrected statements while identifying a remaining independence assumption that the proposed choice of a partition does not supply. They explicitly conclude that establishing those lemmas does not establish correctness of the algorithm. The card therefore flags the recent claim as disputed rather than presenting polynomial time as established.

Positive results elsewhere among nonabelian groups continue to refine the boundary. Morales’ August 2026 algorithm handles certain scalar-action semidirect products with bounded generator rank and exponent-to-prime ratio polylogarithmic in group size, and another family with modular subgroup structure. For the ordinary dihedral family, the relevant ratio would be N/2, which does not meet that condition as N grows. These structural advances leave the unrestricted dihedral target intact.

A solution would identify a new way to convert nonabelian quantum information into efficiently recoverable classical structure. A negative result would be equally consequential because polynomial query complexity is already available: it would isolate a genuine computational obstruction in processing the information. The significance comes from that algorithmic boundary, alongside the precise reductions to coset and lattice problems.

cards.definitions: An n-qubit pure state is a unit vector u∈ℂ^(2^n), indexed by binary strings x∈{0,1}^n. A Hamiltonian is a Hermitian matrix; its energy in u is u†Hu, its ground energy λ_min(H) is its least eigenvalue, and ||H|| is its operator norm. A k-local Hamiltonian is a sum of polynomially many terms, each acting nontrivially on at most k qubits and as the identity on the rest. The constant k and the polynomial bound are independent of n. No geometric locality or efficient uniform construction of the Hamiltonian family is added to the source’s existence target. The norm bound fixes the energy scale, so multiplying all terms cannot create the required constant gap artificially. For a family F of nonzero finite complex vectors, a succinct representation consists of an injective map rep:F→{0,1}*, one polynomial q and one polynomial-time compiler A. Every u∈F has |rep(u)|≤q(log₂ dim u). On a valid representation A outputs descriptions of a coordinate-query procedure Q_u, a randomized sampler S_u, and m=||u||; on every string outside the image of rep it must reject. For any coordinate x, Q_u returns the complex amplitude u_x, including its phase, in time polynomial in log dim u. S_u produces x with probability exactly |u_x|²/||u||² in polynomial time. The resulting circuit descriptions have polynomial size in log dim u. This is the source’s perfect, ζ=0 access, with no approximation to the distribution or norm. The representation map itself need not be computable from an explicitly listed vector. The same polynomial bounds and compiler apply throughout F; the eventual threshold n₀ may depend on this entire representation family. The assertion tests every unit vector in F_n, not one preselected sequence of easy states. The source counts exact complex additions, subtractions, multiplications and divisions at unit cost; this is not automatically a bit-cost sampling model.
cards.answer_criterion: Resolve the stated source-model existence proposition with its ∃Hamiltonian family, ∃ε, ∀representation family, ∃n₀ quantifiers and perfect-sampling plus amplitude-query requirements. Before treating the card as a standalone machine-level benchmark, resolve the numerical conventions recorded in statement_review. Excluding only stabilizer states, Gaussian states or constant-depth quantum preparation does not exclude every family allowed by Definition 5.1.

context_blocks.title: Sampling outcomes loses phase information
context_blocks.text: The states |+⟩=(|0⟩+|1⟩)/√2 and |−⟩=(|0⟩−|1⟩)/√2 both produce a uniformly random bit when measured in the computational basis. Yet for H=(I−X)/2, where X exchanges |0⟩ and |1⟩, their energies are 0 and 1. Their measurement distributions agree while their energies differ. This is why the source also requires access to each complex amplitude.

context_blocks.title: What a succinct description must do
context_blocks.text: Listing all 2^n amplitudes would be exponentially long. A permitted description instead has length polynomial in n and supports the prescribed efficient queries and samples. The source further requires a common compiler that rejects invalid descriptions; it is not enough to assert that some sampler exists for each isolated state.

cards.title: Permanent-of-Gaussians conjecture
cards.formal: Is multiplicative approximation of the permanent of an independent complex Gaussian matrix, on a sufficiently large fraction of instances, #P-hard under randomized polynomial-time reductions as in the Permanent-of-Gaussians Conjecture?
cards.definitions: For X∈ℂ^(n×n), Per(X)=Σ_{σ∈S_n}∏_i X_(i,σ(i)). The entries are independent standard complex Gaussians. This concerns the complex permanent itself; hardness of worst-case permanent evaluation or additive approximation alone does not give this claim.

cards.title: Martin’s conjecture
cards.formal: Assume ZF+DC+AD. Do both assertions hold? (I) Every Turing-invariant function f:2^ω→2^ω is either constant in Turing degree on a cone or satisfies x≤_T f(x) on a cone. (II) Cone-wise Turing reducibility prewellorders all such functions that are above the identity on a cone, and the pointwise jump f′ has rank exactly rank(f)+1 in this prewellorder.
cards.definitions: A real x∈2^ω is an infinite binary sequence, identified with a subset of the natural numbers. Write x≤_T y if an oracle Turing machine with oracle y computes x, and x≡_T y for mutual reducibility. A function f is Turing-invariant when x≡_T y implies f(x)≡_T f(y). A cone above a real a is {x:a≤_T x}. Being constant on a cone means ∃a,b ∀x≥_T a, f(x)≡_T b; the output sequences need not be literally equal. Define f≤_M g by ∃a ∀x≥_T a, f(x)≤_T g(x), and f≡_M g by mutual ≤_M. Let F be the set of all Turing-invariant f for which id≤_M f, where id(x)=x. The prewellorder assertion says that ≤_M is total on F and its quotient by ≡_M is well-ordered. The rank of f is the ordinal order type of the quotient classes strictly preceding [f]. The jump of a real y is y′={e: the e-th oracle program with oracle y halts on input e}; f′(x)=f(x)′. ZF is Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory without the axiom of choice. DC is dependent choice: every serial binary relation on a nonempty set admits an infinite successive chain. AD says every infinite game in which two players alternately choose natural numbers, with an arbitrary specified set of winning sequences, is determined. Functions are not assumed computable, Borel, order-preserving, or uniformly Turing-invariant. Cone bases may depend on the functions being compared.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A central structural problem in computability theory: whether invariance alone, under determinacy, forces nontrivial operations on computational degrees into a well-ordered hierarchy. It connects relative computability, definability, descriptive set theory, and analogies with hierarchies of proof-theoretic strength.

cards.status_note: Explicitly open in Walsh’s March 2026 survey; checked through 10 September 2026. The saved draft’s already-settled regressive subcase has been replaced by the full quantified Part I, together with Part II. Determinacy, degree-wise constancy, and restrictions in the partial results are stated explicitly.

context_blocks.text: The Turing degrees form a complicated partial order, with many incomparable and specially constructed degrees. Yet operations arising naturally by relativizing mathematical definitions often produce a much more organized hierarchy. Martin’s conjecture attempts to make that phenomenon precise through invariance under Turing equivalence and comparison on cones, rather than through an undefined requirement that a construction be “natural.”

The two parts have different jobs. Part I rules out a function that remains nonconstant on every cone but never uniformly reaches the input degree on any cone. Part II concerns functions already above the identity. It asserts comparability and well-foundedness of their cone-equivalence classes, and says that taking an oracle halting problem moves exactly one level up, leaving no intervening class.

Cone-wise comparison ignores behaviour below a fixed computational base. This is meaningful under determinacy: every Turing-invariant set either contains a cone or is disjoint from one, giving Martin’s zero-one measure on degree-invariant sets. Thus “almost everywhere” in the literature means on a cone, not outside a null set for ordinary Lebesgue measure on binary sequences.

Restricting to functions below the identity gives a strictly narrower case with a known theorem: Slaman and Steel show that a Turing-invariant function satisfying f(x)≤_T x on a cone must be constant there or equivalent to the identity on a smaller cone. The unresolved Part I quantifies over all invariant functions, including ones not initially comparable with the identity.

Uniform invariance is another substantial restriction. It requires a single map that turns indices witnessing x≡_T y into indices witnessing f(x)≡_T f(y), independently of the actual reals. Steel and Slaman–Steel establish the conjecture for this subclass. Merely preserving equivalence classes, as the question requires, does not supply that uniform map.

Lutz and Siskind prove Part I for all order-preserving functions and more generally for measure-preserving invariant functions. Here measure-preserving means that for every fixed degree a there is a cone on which f(x) computes a. Their theorem supplies major new cases.
The March 2026 survey by Walsh still presents the full conjecture as open and keeps the Borel restriction on the earlier Part II result for order-preserving functions.

cards.title: Busy Beaver BB(6)
cards.formal: Determine the exact value of $BB(6)=S(6)$, the maximum number of steps taken before halting by a deterministic Turing machine with six nonhalting states, two tape symbols, and one initially all-zero, bi-infinite tape. The transition into a separate halting state counts as one step. Thus $BB(6)=\max\{T(M):M\in\mathcal{M}_6\text{ halts on the blank tape}\}$, where $T(M)$ counts executed transitions and the machine class is fixed below.
cards.definitions: The states are A, B, C, D, E, F and a separate halting state Z; Z is not one of the six states being counted. Tape cells are indexed by the integers and contain 0 or 1. Initially every cell contains 0, the head is at cell 0, and the state is A. For each nonhalting state and scanned symbol, the transition table specifies a symbol to write, a move by exactly one cell left or right, and a next state. Execution stops on entering Z, including that final write-and-move transition in T(M). Unreachable states are allowed. The finite set of these transition tables is $\mathcal{M}_6$. Here BB is the runtime (maximum-shift) function S, not the function $\Sigma$ that maximizes the number of 1s left on the tape. In the progress note, $2\uparrow\uparrow k$ is a tower of k twos, and $2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow 1=2$, $2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow(k+1)=2\uparrow\uparrow(2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow k)$.
cards.answer_criterion: Give an explicit positive integer N and prove BB(6)=N: exhibit a machine in the stated class that halts after exactly N transitions, and prove that every halting machine in this class takes at most N transitions. A finite, unambiguous expression using explicitly defined total operations is sufficient to specify N; its decimal expansion is not required. A larger lower bound or the analysis of only some remaining machines does not settle the question.
cards.why: This is a defining concrete problem in computability: identify the longest finite computation possible in a fixed, exceptionally small universal machine formalism. A proof would advance the boundary of complete mathematical understanding of small programs and test methods for nontermination proofs, recurrence analysis, and formal verification. The significance lies in establishing the exact boundary, not merely constructing a machine with an enormous runtime.

importance.reason: A landmark finite problem at the frontier of computability and formal verification, asking for the next binary Busy Beaver runtime value after the resolved five-state case.

context_blocks.text: Fixing the number of states leaves finitely many machines, so a maximum halting time exists. Nevertheless, enumerating their transition tables does not tell us when to stop waiting for the machines that never halt. The Busy Beaver function packages that obstruction into a sequence of finite integers. Noncomputability of the whole sequence does not prevent individual values from being established.

The five-state case provides a concrete precedent: the bbchallenge collaboration proved S(5)=47,176,870 with the Coq proof assistant. Its proof combines a complete enumeration after symmetry reductions with methods that certify halting or nonhalting. The paper makes precise how a finite search can be accompanied by a universal proof.

Six states introduce obstacles beyond running a larger search. The Antihydra machine has a halting question expressed through an integer recurrence whose parity behavior is still unresolved. A probabilistic heuristic about that behavior is not a proof that the machine runs forever. An exact Busy Beaver bound would also decide its halting behavior in principle, even if the required finite computation were physically infeasible.

The target is the exact six-state runtime maximum. Runtime and final tape output are different extremal quantities, and machine conventions matter. Existing catalogue questions about Busy Beaver growth, logical thresholds, or population protocols therefore remain separate problems.

Finding a long-running halting machine supplies only a lower bound; every remaining machine must also be shown to halt within the claimed maximum or never halt.
The problem turns the general undecidability of halting into an exceptionally concrete finite classification challenge.
The saved review records large candidate runtimes and unresolved holdouts, and distinguishes runtime from the separate Busy Beaver measure counting printed ones.

cards.context:
Fixing the number of states leaves finitely many machines, so a maximum halting time exists. Nevertheless, enumerating their transition tables does not tell us when to stop waiting for the machines that never halt. The Busy Beaver function packages that obstruction into a sequence of finite integers. Noncomputability of the whole sequence does not prevent individual values from being established.

The five-state case provides a concrete precedent: the bbchallenge collaboration proved S(5)=47,176,870 with the Coq proof assistant. Its proof combines a complete enumeration after symmetry reductions with methods that certify halting or nonhalting. The paper makes precise how a finite search can be accompanied by a universal proof.

Six states introduce obstacles beyond running a larger search. The Antihydra machine has a halting question expressed through an integer recurrence whose parity behavior is still unresolved. A probabilistic heuristic about that behavior is not a proof that the machine runs forever. An exact Busy Beaver bound would also decide its halting behavior in principle, even if the required finite computation were physically infeasible.

The target is the exact six-state runtime maximum. Runtime and final tape output are different extremal quantities, and machine conventions matter. Existing catalogue questions about Busy Beaver growth, logical thresholds, or population protocols therefore remain separate problems.

cards.title: Reversal of Hindman’s theorem to the ω-jump
cards.formal: Over RCA₀, does Hindman’s finite-sums theorem imply ACA₀⁺? Equivalently, does RCA₀+HT prove that every set X has an ω-th Turing jump?
cards.definitions: Work in classical two-sorted second-order arithmetic, with number variables and variables for sets of natural numbers. RCA₀ has the usual elementary arithmetic axioms, Σ⁰₁ induction and Δ⁰₁ comprehension, allowing set parameters. HT is the assertion that for every integer k≥1 and every coloring c of the positive integers into {0,…,k−1}, there exist an infinite set H of positive integers and a color i such that c(Σ_{h∈F}h)=i for every nonempty finite subset F of H. Terms in a sum are distinct; there is no fixed upper bound on their number and no additional sparsity requirement on H. For a set X, its Turing jump X′ is {e: the e-th oracle Turing machine with oracle X halts on input e}, using one fixed effective enumeration. The ω-jump existence axiom says ∀X∃Y [Y₀=X and ∀j(Y_{j+1}=Y_j′)], where Y_j={e:⟨j,e⟩∈Y} and ⟨·,·⟩ is a fixed primitive recursive pairing. ACA₀⁺ is RCA₀ plus that axiom. The question is formal provability of this implication over the stated base, not truth of Hindman’s theorem in ordinary set theory and not a single-instance computability claim.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the ω-jump existence axiom in RCA₀+HT, or prove nonimplication by constructing a model of RCA₀+HT in which some set has no coded ω-jump. A standard-natural-number model is sufficient for a separation but is not required. A lower bound of ACA₀ alone, an upper bound of ACA₀⁺, or a theorem about only bounded-length sums does not decide this implication. A negative answer need not show that HT is equivalent to ACA₀; an intermediate strength would also refute the implication.
cards.why: A longstanding gap in the computational and axiomatic strength of a central infinite combinatorial theorem, with a precise target at the ω-th Turing jump.

importance.reason: A landmark reverse-mathematical calibration problem connecting finite-sums combinatorics, oracle computation and the hierarchy of set-existence axioms.

progress.text: Blass–Hirst–Simpson establish ACA₀⁺⇒HT⇒ACA₀ over RCA₀, leaving the reversal in this card open.
Carlucci–Zdanowski characterize ACA₀⁺ using Ramsey’s theorem for exactly large sets; this supplies a comparison principle rather than an HT reversal.
Carlucci–Kołodziejczyk–Lepore–Zdanowski reach the ACA₀ lower bound already for sums of at most two elements with four colors; conference precursor 2017, journal version 2020.
Csima and coauthors prove nontrivial computability and reverse-mathematical lower bounds for sums of exactly two elements, a weaker principle than full HT.
Liu–Patey prove new upper bounds and separations for variable-word and unordered Carlson–Simpson principles, without claiming a resolution of HT’s strength.
Le Houérou–Patey obtain a conservation theorem for a one-variable, two-color Carlson–Simpson principle.

context_blocks.text: Hindman’s theorem says that a finite coloring contains an infinite set whose entire collection of finite sums has one color. This is much more than finding an infinite monochromatic subset: the same color must work for single elements, pairs, triples and every larger finite selection. For parity coloring, the positive even numbers give an immediate example. The theorem must also handle colorings with no such simple arithmetic description.

The combinatorial statement is a theorem, not the unresolved claim on this card. Reverse mathematics asks which set-existence axioms are needed to prove it. One works over a deliberately weak base theory and compares stronger principles by implication. The inherited paper records the classical bounds ACA₀⁺⇒HT⇒ACA₀ and identifies closing this gap as a major open problem. This card asks specifically whether the upper implication reverses.

ACA₀ allows arithmetic comprehension; equivalently over the base theory, every set has its Turing jump. An individual jump supplies answers to halting questions relative to the given set. Repeating that operation a fixed finite number of times yields increasingly strong information. The ω-jump places every finite iterate into the sections of one set. Being able to discuss each fixed finite stage is not the same as having this whole sequence available as a single object.

The distinction is visible in the model consisting of the standard natural numbers together with all arithmetical sets. It is closed under the ordinary Turing jump, since jumping an arithmetical set still yields an arithmetical set. It does not contain the join of all finite jumps of the empty set. Thus ACA₀⁺ demands more set existence than ACA₀. Whether Hindman’s theorem already forces that additional existence is the precise issue here.

The computability bounds show why ordinary computable colorings already matter. The account by Csima and coauthors recalls a computable coloring for which every finite-sums solution computes the halting set, and an upper bound placing a solution in the (ω+1)-st jump of the coloring. These are bounds on information in solutions. Neither identifies the exact reverse-mathematical strength, and noncomputability alone falls far short of an ω-jump reversal.

Restricted sum lengths have provided substantial progress without closing the full gap. Carlucci–Kołodziejczyk–Lepore–Zdanowski prove that the version requiring monochromatic singletons and pairs already implies ACA₀; four colors suffice without an additional sparsity condition. Their results for sums of exactly n≥3 terms use an apartness condition on the binary supports of the chosen integers. These carefully specified variants should not be merged with unrestricted HT.

Even replacing “at most two” by “exactly two” changes the logical picture. Csima and coauthors construct a computable two-color instance of the exactly-two version with no Σ⁰₂ solution and prove a lower bound through diagonally noncomputable functions relative to the halting set. Yet exactly-two sums follow from Ramsey’s theorem for pairs, placing that principle strictly below full HT over the base. This is a useful warning that small wording changes can alter the problem.

There is a separate combinatorial principle known to capture the desired upper level exactly. Carlucci–Zdanowski prove that Ramsey’s theorem for exactly large finite sets is equivalent to ACA₀⁺. A finite set F is exactly large when |F|=min(F)+1, so its dimension varies with its elements. This yields a potential comparison target: an implication from HT to this precisely defined Ramsey principle would suffice. Its equivalence does not itself supply that missing implication.

Recent results in the neighboring theory of variable words require the same care. Liu–Patey’s June 2026 preprint, revised in July, gives low₂ solutions to the Ordered Variable Word theorem for colorings of ordinary words and proves each fixed-dimensional unordered Carlson–Simpson lemma in ACA₀. The paper distinguishes these principles from ordered higher-dimensional counterparts and still describes ACA₀⁺ as the weakest known system proving HT. Its new upper bounds should not be transferred to Hindman’s theorem.

Le Houérou–Patey’s July 2026 preprint obtains a conservation result for a one-variable Carlson–Simpson principle with two colors. It controls which arithmetical consequences that particular principle adds to a weak theory. This is a different assertion from constructing the ω-jump out of unrestricted finite-sums homogeneity. Together the recent papers sharpen nearby boundaries without answering the implication stated here.

A positive answer would make a concrete additive-combinatorial theorem a characterization of closure under all finite Turing jumps at once. A negative answer would show that known proofs use more set existence than the theorem itself entails. Either outcome would clarify the information content of an infinite combinatorial search principle, which is the reason for its place in the computability part of this catalogue.

cards.title: Superpolynomial Extended Frege lower bounds
cards.formal: Is Extended Frege not polynomially bounded? Precisely, for every constants C>0 and c≥1, is there a propositional tautology φ whose shortest Extended Frege proof has bit length greater than C(|φ|+2)ᶜ? Here |φ| is the bit length of the explicitly written formula.
cards.definitions: Fix Boolean formulas over ¬ and →, with → interpreted as material implication and variable indices encoded in binary. Use the Frege axiom schemes A→(B→A), (A→(B→C))→((A→B)→(A→C)), and (¬B→¬A)→(A→B), together with modus ponens from A and A→B to B. An Extended Frege proof of φ may additionally introduce an abbreviation variable e by the two extension axioms e→θ and θ→e. Here e is fresh, absent from φ, θ, and every preceding line; θ uses original variables of φ and previously introduced extension variables. Extensions are thus acyclic definitions. Other proof lines are axiom instances or applications of modus ponens, and the last line must be φ, with no extension variables. Lines may cite and reuse earlier lines arbitrarily: proofs are not required to be trees. Proof size is the full binary encoding length of all explicitly written formulas, extension definitions, and inference references; there is no depth or per-line-size restriction. A tautology is true under every assignment to its variables. This fixed presentation is polynomially equivalent to the usual Extended Frege systems, so changing a standard finite Frege basis does not change polynomial boundedness. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: Extended Frege captures a powerful form of efficient propositional reasoning with reusable definitions. A superpolynomial lower bound would cross one of the central barriers in proof complexity and clarify whether a standard, highly expressive certificate language necessarily fails on some short true statements.

importance.reason: A defining open lower-bound problem for strong propositional reasoning, closely connected to bounded arithmetic, circuit complexity, and the limits of efficiently checkable certificates.

progress.text: Cook and Reckhow formalize propositional proof systems, polynomial simulation, and Extended Frege, proving robustness under the choice of standard rules and connectives.
Strong lower bounds emerge for weaker systems, while even unrestricted Frege lower bounds remain open. EF adds the ability to abbreviate and share formulas.

Pich and Santhanam establish conditional routes from EF proof lower bounds to P≠NP. The assumptions include formally provable computational statements; the result is not an unconditional EF lower bound.
Hsieh, Jain, Li, and Mathialagan obtain SNARGs for NP from derandomization, LWE, SXDH, and a bounded-arithmetic unprovability assumption concerning certificates of EF-hard tautologies.

Alekseev’s journal paper proves an exponential bit-size lower bound for algebraic Binary Value Principle refutations in extended polynomial calculus with a square-root rule. Its Section 1 explicitly distinguishes this from propositional Frege and EF lower bounds.

cards.status_note: Explicitly open in the primary proof-complexity sources, including Alekseev’s June 2026 journal article. Research through 10 September 2026 found no unconditional resolution for unrestricted Extended Frege. The algebraic and conditional results cited here retain their stated scope.

context_blocks.text: Extension variables let a proof name a formula once and reuse its name. This can represent shared computations economically, as a Boolean circuit shares intermediate gates. Expanding all abbreviations into formula trees can cause an exponential increase in length, so a lower bound that counts only ordinary Frege proofs does not automatically survive the extension rule.

The question concerns the existence of short certificates, not the time required to discover them. A particular proof search method might take exponential time even though another method could find a short proof; conversely, a proof-size lower bound would constrain every method that outputs an EF derivation. The input length is the final tautology’s actual encoding length, so a lower bound exponential in a smaller hidden parameter may still be only polynomial in the input.

If NP≠coNP, every polynomial-time verifiable propositional proof system has hard tautologies, including EF. The converse for this particular system is unknown: showing that EF is inefficient does not rule out a different proof system that gives short certificates for all tautologies. This is why an EF lower bound would be a major advance without automatically constituting a proof of NP≠coNP.

Recent algebraic lower bounds illustrate an encoding issue. Alekseev proves exponential bit-size lower bounds for an extension of polynomial calculus that can simulate EF on suitable propositional translations. The hard Binary Value Principle instance is not the corresponding translation of a polynomial-size CNF. The paper explicitly explains that its result therefore does not yield a Frege or EF lower bound.

Pich and Santhanam give implications from EF lower bounds to P≠NP under additional bounded-arithmetic assumptions. This explores the consequences of proof-complexity hypotheses without proving an unconditional EF lower bound.

Hsieh and coauthors construct succinct arguments under derandomization, cryptographic, and formal unprovability assumptions. Their result connects the difficulty of certifying hard tautologies to cryptography; it does not establish the unconditional size lower bound asked for here.

cards.title: Frege versus Extended Frege
cards.formal: Do there exist constants C>0 and k≥1 such that every Extended Frege proof π of a propositional tautology φ has some ordinary Frege proof ρ of the same formula with |ρ|≤C(|π|+2)ᵏ? Equivalently, if sF(φ) and sEF(φ) are the minimum proof sizes in the two systems, is sF(φ) polynomially bounded in sEF(φ), uniformly over all tautologies?
cards.definitions: Fix formulas over negation ¬ and material implication →, with binary-encoded variable indices. Ordinary Frege uses the axiom schemes A→(B→A), (A→(B→C))→((A→B)→(A→C)), and (¬B→¬A)→(A→B), and modus ponens: infer B from A and A→B. A proof is a finite sequence ending with φ; earlier lines may be cited and reused without restriction. Extended Frege adds acyclic definitions, introducing the pair e→θ and θ→e, where e is a new variable absent from φ, θ and all preceding lines. θ may use variables of φ and earlier extension variables. The final formula contains no extension variables. Proof size is the complete binary encoding length of every explicitly written line, definition and inference reference. No formula-depth, proof-depth or tree-shape bound is imposed. These presentations are polynomially equivalent to the usual finite-basis Frege and Extended Frege systems. The target is existence of short translated proofs: it does not require a polynomial-time function that finds ρ from π. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: This asks whether reusable definitions fundamentally shorten mathematical proofs, beyond any polynomial factor. It is one of the central comparisons between strong propositional proof systems and captures the difficulty of reasoning with shared circuits versus explicit formulas.

importance.reason: A canonical strong-system simulation problem, directly tied to Frege lower bounds, finite consistency and circuit-based reasoning.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. No polynomial size simulation or superpolynomial separation of unrestricted Frege and EF was found in the primary literature. The newest checked simulation, TR26-166, concerns a restricted algebraic formula system and has quasipolynomial overhead.

context_blocks.text: The extension rule gives reusable names to intermediate computations. If a subformula is used many times, ordinary formula syntax writes out each occurrence; Extended Frege can define it once and refer to its name. A network of such definitions represents a Boolean circuit with shared gates. The rule does not permit a false final theorem: every assignment to the original variables uniquely extends through the definitions, and the conclusion uses only original variables.

Repeated substitution eliminates definitions, but can create exponentially large formula trees. This explains why the obvious simulation is expensive; it does not prove that all ordinary Frege proofs must be expensive. The challenge is to compare the shortest proofs, not one syntactic expansion procedure.

The distinction between proof size and proof-search time is essential. The quantifiers are “for every EF proof there exists a short Frege proof.” They do not supply an algorithm for locating that proof. The stronger notion usually called p-simulation requires a polynomial-time transformation. A size simulation alone can hold even if the available methods for finding the translated proof are much slower.

Buss connects the comparison to finite consistency statements. Frege has polynomial-size proofs of its own partial consistency, meaning the corresponding finite statements that no contradiction has a proof up to a specified length. His theorem characterizes Frege simulation of EF by polynomial-size Frege proofs of the analogous partial consistency statements for EF. This turns a comparison of all proofs into a canonical family of propositional statements; it is not a general proof of the desired simulation.

For example, Aisenberg and coauthors give polynomial-size EF proofs and quasipolynomial-size Frege proofs of propositional Kneser–Lovász coloring principles. It would also imply superpolynomial Frege lower bounds, since the final formula is part of every EF proof. cards.definitions: Fix an explicit binary syntax for Boolean formulas built from indexed variables, AND, OR and NOT. A tautology evaluates to true under every assignment to its variables; TAUT is the set of encodings of such formulas. A Cook–Reckhow proof system is a total function P:{0,1}*→TAUT, computed by one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine in time polynomial in its input length, whose range is all of TAUT. A string π proves formula F when P(π)=F. Soundness requires every output to be a tautology; completeness requires every tautology to occur as an output. There is no polynomial upper bound on the shortest proof of every formula. In this total-function presentation, strings that would be malformed proofs in a conventional calculus may instead produce a fixed tautology such as x₁∨¬x₁. A simulation translation is total and satisfies the equality on all strings, preserving the exact output formula. Its program, polynomial exponent and constants may depend on Q and P, but not on π. The order is ∃P ∀Q ∃t_Q ∀π. No algorithm taking an arbitrary program for Q and producing its translator is required. Neither advice, randomization nor an oracle is allowed in the systems or translations. Polynomial translation time also bounds the translated proof length polynomially in |π|.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that one sound and complete polynomial-time proof system admits the required polynomial-time translations from every other such system, or prove that for every candidate P some sound and complete Q has no such translation. A proof-length comparison without an efficient translation proves only ordinary optimality. Refuting a particular named proof system’s p-optimality does not exclude all systems.

context_blocks.title: One common format for efficiently checked proofs
context_blocks.text: Different proof calculi can establish the same tautology with very different amounts of work. The question asks whether one format can accept a polynomial-time translation of any already-given proof in any other efficiently checkable format. The translator receives the proof; it is not being asked to discover a proof from the formula alone.

context_blocks.title: A simple simulation
context_blocks.text: Suppose Q is a proof system and another system merely adds a leading marker to each Q-proof. Removing the marker translates those proofs back with linear overhead. More generally, any fixed finite collection of sound systems can be combined using a system tag. The question quantifies over every sound polynomial-time system, so combining a predetermined finite list does not finish it.

context_blocks.title: Three distinct notions
context_blocks.text: Ordinary optimality asks only that comparably short proofs exist in the common system. P-optimality additionally asks for efficient translations of the given proofs. Polynomial boundedness instead asks that every tautology have a proof polynomial in the formula’s own length. A p-optimal system could still have very long proofs of some tautologies, so this target does not by itself say NP=coNP.

context_blocks.title: Known connections and current limits
context_blocks.text: Krajíček and Pudlák connect p-optimality with a tautology recognizer that is optimal up to polynomial overhead on positive inputs, compared with each other correct recognizer. Their theorem also gives the conditional implication from P=NP. Egidy’s February 2026 paper retains the question as open and proves limitations of relativizing arguments; the oracle supplied to those machines is extra computational power, absent from this card.

context_blocks.title: Later work on improving proof systems
context_blocks.text: The ICALP 2026 paper studies when the absence of an ordinary optimal system entails an effective procedure producing stronger systems. Its oracle and other-language results leave p-optimal propositional proof systems unresolved. Ordinary optimality, a procedure for improving systems, and efficient proof translation are related but separately quantified properties.

cards.title: Log-rank conjecture
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Do there exist universal constants C>0 and k≥1 such that every total Boolean function f:X×Y→{0,1}, on arbitrary nonempty finite sets X,Y, satisfies $D(f)\le C(\log_2(r(f)+2))^k$, where r(f) is the real rank of its 0/1 communication matrix and D(f) is its deterministic communication complexity?
cards.definitions: Alice receives x∈X and Bob receives y∈Y. Both know the complete function f and the protocol. They exchange bits interactively; each next transmitted bit is a deterministic function of the sender’s own input and the previous transcript. A binary protocol tree specifies whose turn it is, and every leaf has a Boolean output that must equal f(x,y) for every input pair reaching it. D(f) is the minimum, over all such exact protocols, of the maximum number of transmitted bits on an input pair. The number of rounds and the local computation are unrestricted; protocol description length is not charged. The communication matrix M_f has rows X, columns Y, and entry f(x,y); r(f)=rank_R(M_f) is ordinary matrix rank over the real numbers. The +2 makes the statement unambiguous for rank zero or one. The same constants C,k must work for all matrix dimensions and all functions. There are no undefined entries, input promises, random bits, quantum messages, approximation errors, or restrictions to one-way protocols. Sign rank and approximate rank are different parameters.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: One of the central organizing conjectures of communication complexity. It asks whether a basic linear-algebraic quantity characterizes efficient exact communication, and connects protocols to rectangle partitions, discrepancy, graph structure, and cancellation in matrix decompositions.

importance.reason: A flagship structural conjecture linking deterministic protocols and matrix rank, with many equivalent combinatorial formulations and a large quantitative gap.

progress.text: Lovász and Saks formulate the conjecture relating real rank and deterministic communication; the 2026 equivalent-formulations paper gives the original attribution and related graph versions.
Lovett proves D(f)=O(√r log r), the first general sublinear-in-rank upper bound; the later discrepancy paper explains and improves this step.
Göös, Pitassi, and Watson establish nearly quadratic lower bounds in log-rank, along with separations involving communication partition number.
Sudakov and Tomon improve the universal upper bound to O(√r). The 2023 preprint is published online in 2024 and in Mathematical Programming volume 212 in 2025.

Song reports an explicit lower bound Ω((log r)²/log log r) via alphabet-preserving lifting. The card records this as a preprint refinement, not an independently certified new universal separation record.
The CCC 2026 version of Hambardzumyan–Lovett–Shirley gives the O(r log r) signed-rectangle decomposition and equivalent formulations. It explicitly leaves the general conjecture open.
