cards.context:
The strings 0101 and 1010 disagree at all four positions, but their edit distance is 2: delete the first 0 and append a 0. One edit cannot suffice, because the lengths are equal and a single substitution would leave other disagreements. Edit distance therefore measures more than the number of mismatched positions. Insertions and deletions let long portions of the two strings line up at different offsets.

The classical dynamic-programming computation compares prefixes of the two strings and takes O(n²) time. The question concerns the best possible algorithm, not the necessity of evaluating every entry in that particular computation. A bound such as n²/log n is smaller than n² but does not give a fixed positive saving in the exponent. The target asks for n^(2−ε) with one ε>0 that remains valid for arbitrarily long strings.

The Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis, SETH, states that for every δ>0 there is a clause width k for which Boolean k-SAT on N variables cannot be decided deterministically in O(2^((1−δ)N) poly(L)) time, where L is the formula length. Backurs and Indyk relate a truly subquadratic exact edit-distance algorithm to a faster satisfiability algorithm. Bringmann and Künnemann establish the conditional obstruction even for binary strings. This is strong evidence for a barrier, but SETH is an assumption. The reduction does not prove unconditionally that the requested algorithm is impossible.

Mao and Rubinstein’s March 2026 result gives a randomized (1+η)-approximation for each fixed η>0, with running time n²/2^(log^Ω(1) n). A multiplicative approximation can return a nearby value rather than the exact minimum. Its error guarantee and its dependence on η cannot simply be replaced by exact correctness at no cost. Thus this progress does not supply the deterministic exact algorithm requested here.

The alphabet is explicitly binary, the edit costs are all one, and the guarantee is for every input pair. Results for typical strings, a bounded number of edits, weighted substitution schemes, or a supplied good alignment may have different complexity. Computing the distance is already a polynomial-time task. The unresolved issue is the finer rate within polynomial time and its connection to the exponential-time cost of satisfiability.

cards.title: Online matrix–vector multiplication conjecture
cards.formal: Given a Boolean matrix $M\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}$, receive vectors $v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\{0,1\}^n$ one at a time. Output each Boolean product $(Mv_t)_i=\bigvee_{j=1}^{n}(M_{ij}\wedge(v_t)_j)$ before receiving $v_{t+1}$. Is there any constant $\varepsilon>0$ and randomized algorithm with total running time $O(n^{3-\varepsilon})$ and error probability at most $1/3$? The OMv conjecture asserts that there is no such algorithm. In this formulation the total includes preprocessing of $M$.
cards.why: I include this because it is one of the central assumptions used to explain why many dynamic data structures resist fast updates and queries simultaneously. Refuting it would invalidate a large collection of conditional barriers; proving it would give a major unconditional lower bound for an explicit polynomial-time problem.
cards.definitions: The product uses OR and AND, not addition modulo two. The matrix remains fixed throughout the sequence. The word-RAM has logarithmic-size words. Success concerns the complete online computation. This is distinct from multiplying over a field, updating the matrix itself, or answering one query after an uncharged preprocessing phase.

progress.text: Henzinger, Krinninger, Nanongkai, and Saranurak formulate OMv and derive conditional lower bounds for dynamic problems, including reachability and variants of connectivity.
Larsen and Williams give randomized online multiplication in total time $n^3/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}$. This improves the algorithmic baseline without refuting the conjecture.

Hu and Polak show fine-grained equivalences between Boolean OMv and several online non-Boolean products, including min-max, dominance, and equality. These broaden the supporting connections; they do not prove the conjecture.

context_blocks.text: If all vectors were available together, they would form another matrix and fast matrix multiplication could batch the work. The online requirement forbids waiting for future columns. A data structure can learn and preprocess the fixed matrix, but it must answer a sequence of queries whose later values have not yet arrived.

A small graph construction explains the relevance to dynamic algorithms. Make one vertex for each matrix column and one for each row; put a directed edge from column j to row i exactly when the matrix entry is one. Add a source with edges to the columns activated by the current query vector. The rows reachable from the source are exactly the one-entries of the answer vector. Changing the active columns turns each matrix query into a sequence of graph updates followed by reachability questions.

The conjecture is about a polynomial saving in the exponent. An improvement from $n^3$ to $n^3/\log n$ is significant but compatible with it. Even the stronger documented saving $2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}$ is only $n^{o(1)}$, so it leaves the total time in the $n^{3-o(1)}$ range.

The graph reduction gives intuition, not a universal update-time theorem by itself. To derive a particular data-structure lower bound, one must account for preprocessing, the number of updates and queries, and how the graph size relates to the matrix dimension. These are precisely the parameters handled in the original reductions.

cards.title: ETH versus Gap-ETH
cards.formal: Does the deterministic Exponential Time Hypothesis imply the deterministic Gap Exponential Time Hypothesis for sparse 3-CNF formulas?
cards.definitions: For a 3-CNF formula F with n variables, let val(F) be the maximum fraction of clauses simultaneously satisfiable. The ETH convention here asserts that there is c>0 for which no deterministic algorithm decides satisfiability of all 3-CNF formulas in time O(2^(cn) poly(L)), where L is the binary encoding length. Gap-ETH asserts that there exist constants B≥1, δ∈(0,1) and c′>0 for which no deterministic algorithm in time O(2^(c′n) poly(L)) distinguishes val(F)=1 from val(F)≤1−δ on formulas with at most Bn clauses. Its inputs are promised to satisfy one of those two alternatives. Empty formulas are satisfiable. All constants are fixed independently of F; randomized versions are not asserted.

context_blocks.text: ETH concerns exact satisfiability, while Gap-ETH postulates comparable exponential hardness even when unsatisfiable inputs violate a fixed fraction of clauses. Their equivalence would unify many exact and approximation lower-bound assumptions.

Bitansky and coauthors distinguish ETH from the stronger gap hypothesis while obtaining exponential hardness for particular approximation tasks. Hardness for those tasks does not imply a gap-preserving sparse 3-CNF statement. This implication is distinct from asking whether either hypothesis is true.

cards.why: Clarify whether a major approximation-hardness assumption adds strength to the standard exact exponential-time hypothesis.

cards.title: FPT versus W[1]
cards.formal: Do there exist a total computable function f:ℕ→ℕ, a constant c, and one deterministic algorithm that decides whether an n-vertex graph contains a k-clique in time at most f(k)(n+2)ᶜ on every input? Equivalently, is FPT=W[1]?
cards.definitions: An instance is a finite simple undirected graph G on [n], encoded by its adjacency matrix, and an integer k with 0≤k≤n, encoded in binary. A k-clique is a set of k distinct vertices for which every pair is an edge; k=0 is a yes-instance. Inputs with k>n are rejected immediately, and other malformed inputs are rejected. The parameter is k, not treewidth, degree, or the size of a supplied decomposition. Running time counts deterministic Turing-machine steps on the full input. Constants and the function f may be arbitrary but must be fixed independently of n; the exponent c must also be independent of k. FPT comprises parameterized decision problems solvable in f(k)Nᶜ time, where N is their input encoding length. One equivalent definition of W[1] is the class of parameterized problems reducible to k-Clique by a deterministic f(k)Nᶜ-time many-one reduction whose output parameter is bounded by a computable function of k alone. This is the standard parameterized reduction convention under which Clique is W[1]-complete. No randomness, advice, or promise about G is allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: This is the principal boundary question for algorithms whose exponential difficulty is confined to a small parameter. It determines the force of thousands of parameterized hardness reductions and separates efficient small-solution search from algorithms whose input-size exponent grows with the solution size.

importance.reason: The defining unresolved tractability separation of parameterized complexity, with Clique as a precise and widely used complete problem.

progress.text: Downey and Fellows develop the W-hierarchy and the completeness framework that makes parameterized Clique a canonical target for the FPT-versus-W[1] question.
ETH-based reductions establish the stronger conditional obstruction to f(k)n^{o(k)} Clique algorithms; the textbook develops this in its parameterized lower-bound chapters.
Bottesch studies structural and relativization evidence concerning FPT and W[1], explicitly distinguishing this conjecture from P≠NP. No unrelativized separation is proved.
Lin proves constant-factor FPT approximation of Clique W[1]-hard, transferring the same central assumption to approximate search.
Chen, Feng, Laekhanukit, and Liu give a simpler combinatorial construction for the k^{o(1)} parameterized Clique inapproximability bound.
Abboud, Fischer, and Shechter improve combinatorial fixed-k Clique running times by logarithmic factors. The Algorithmica publication of 22 May 2026 retains dependence on k in the exponent of n.

cards.status_note: Explicitly presented as the central open conjecture in Bottesch’s primary paper and the parameterized-algorithms textbook. Research through 10 September 2026 located no proof of equality or separation. Conditional lower bounds and improved fixed-k algorithms are recorded with their distinct quantifiers.

context_blocks.text: For each fixed k, exhaustive search over vertex subsets decides Clique in polynomial time. The exponent grows with k, so this observation gives a different kind of tractability: increasing the target clique size can increase the power of n in the running time. The question asks whether all dependence on k can instead be moved into one multiplicative function. For example, 2^{2^k}n³ meets the requested form, while n^{k/10} does not.

The unrestricted Clique problem is NP-complete, but this alone cannot rule out fixed-parameter tractability. The permitted function f can grow much faster than any polynomial when k grows with n. If P=NP then Clique is certainly FPT; the converse implication is not known. Thus FPT≠W[1] is a stronger separation conjecture than P≠NP in the direction currently proved.

Parameterized reductions keep the output parameter controlled solely by the original parameter. Since Clique is complete under these reductions, an FPT Clique algorithm would solve every W[1] problem in FPT time. This is why a W[1]-hardness proof is useful evidence against a parameterized algorithm for another problem. The evidence is conditional on the separation being true, even when the reduction theorem itself is unconditional.

The Exponential Time Hypothesis supplies a stronger quantitative barrier: it rules out f(k)n^{o(k)} algorithms for Clique. That conclusion excludes FPT, but uses an assumption that is itself open. Matrix-multiplication methods and improved combinatorial methods accelerate Clique for fixed k while leaving an exponent that grows with the parameter. Their progress does not eliminate the central gap.

Approximation has become another way to measure the reach of the conjecture. Lin proves that even fixed-factor parameterized approximation of Clique is W[1]-hard. Later constructions strengthen the factor and simplify the reductions. These results enlarge the consequences of a separation; they do not prove FPT≠W[1].

The Exponential Time Hypothesis supplies a stronger quantitative barrier: it rules out f(k)n^{o(k)} algorithms for Clique. That conclusion excludes FPT, but uses an assumption that is itself open. Matrix-multiplication methods and improved combinatorial methods accelerate Clique for fixed k while leaving an exponent that grows with the parameter. Their progress does not eliminate the central gap.

Approximation has become another way to measure the reach of the conjecture. Lin proves that even fixed-factor parameterized approximation of Clique is W[1]-hard. Later constructions strengthen the factor and simplify the reductions. These results enlarge the consequences of a separation; they do not prove FPT≠W[1].

cards.title: Exponential Time Hypothesis
cards.formal: Is there a constant c>0 such that, for every deterministic algorithm A that correctly decides every 3-CNF satisfiability instance, and every constant d≥0, A does not have worst-case running time O(2^{cn}L^d)? Here n is the number of variables and L is the full binary input length. This is the deterministic Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH).
cards.definitions: A 3-CNF formula is a conjunction of explicitly listed clauses, each containing at most three literals xᵢ or ¬xᵢ. Satisfiability means existence of a Boolean assignment satisfying all clauses. Variables are relabeled consecutively; n counts the distinct variables actually present, and L includes all literal indices, signs, delimiters, and repetitions. An empty clause is unsatisfiable and an empty conjunction is satisfiable. Algorithms are uniform deterministic Turing machines with no advice or oracles; they must halt and answer exactly on all inputs, with no promise about density, solution count, or distribution. Define s₃=inf{α≥0 : some such algorithm runs in O(2^{αn}L^d) for a fixed d}. ETH asserts s₃>0. The excluded exponent c is a single constant independent of the algorithm. The polynomial exponent and hidden constant may depend on the algorithm, but not the instance. Polynomial input factors allow the complete formula to be read even if clauses are repeated many times. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: ETH is the central hypothesis for ruling out subexponential exact algorithms and many fixed-parameter speedups. It turns the qualitative P versus NP question into a quantitative claim that can be transferred through carefully sized reductions.

importance.reason: A foundational quantitative hardness hypothesis underlying exact, parameterized, graph, and geometric algorithm lower bounds.

progress.text: Impagliazzo and Paturi formalize the exponential rates of k-SAT and study their relations. These rates remain conjectural lower bounds against unrestricted algorithms.

Liu gives a deterministic 3-SAT upper bound with base 1.32793 using branching and generalized covering codes. The saving leaves a positive exponential rate.

Aggarwal, Gupta, Morolia, and Zhang obtain new lattice approximation hardness from ETH or randomized ETH, depending on the target problem and reduction. Their ICALP paper continues to treat these as hypotheses and separates them from Gap-ETH.

cards.status_note: The cited foundational and 2026 conference sources treat ETH as an open hypothesis. Checked through 10 September 2026. This formulation is uniform, deterministic, and a positive-infimum assertion; randomized, nonuniform, gap, and stronger all-width hypotheses are distinct.

context_blocks.text: NP-completeness describes the possibility of polynomial-time algorithms and does not itself impose a positive exponential rate. Even if P differs from NP, a running time such as 2^{√n} remains possible for 3-SAT. ETH asks for a stronger obstruction: some fixed amount of exponential work must remain unavoidable when complexity is measured by the number of Boolean choices.

That parameter must be preserved carefully by a reduction. An ordinary polynomial-time reduction may turn an n-variable formula into an instance of size n³, which can destroy a claimed exponential lower bound in the new parameter. Sparsification supplies a controlled disjunction of bounded-density formulas, allowing variables and clauses to be related without an arbitrary polynomial blowup. This is a main reason ETH can support sharp bounds across many problems.

The infimum over all algorithms matters. Excluding one 2^{o(n)} algorithm is the common informal wording, but the textbook explicitly keeps the stronger positive-infimum statement because the converse is unclear. ETH would be false if arbitrarily small constant exponents were attainable, even if the known algorithms depended on the desired exponent. A card that omitted this distinction would change the quantified question.

There are substantial deterministic improvements over trying all 2ⁿ assignments. Liu combines branching with derandomized local search to obtain a 1.32793ⁿ bound for 3-SAT, up to polynomial factors. Such an algorithm decreases an upper bound on s₃ while leaving it positive. Empirical solver success, promises of many solutions, and bounded-occurrence restrictions do not address worst-case unrestricted formulas.

ETH is weaker than SETH, whose optimal rates approach one as the fixed clause width grows. It also differs from randomized ETH and from Gap-ETH, which asks for hardness of distinguishing fully satisfiable formulas from formulas with a constant unsatisfied fraction. Recent lattice reductions illustrate the value of tracking these distinctions: some approximation hardness can be obtained from deterministic ETH, while other results use randomized ETH. They extend the consequences of assumptions without proving the assumptions.

cards.title: Breaking the 2ⁿ barrier for weighted TSP
cards.formal: Do there exist constants ε∈(0,1), c≥1 and a uniform classical randomized algorithm that, for every complete undirected graph on n≥3 labelled vertices with nonnegative binary-encoded integer edge weights of total encoding length L, outputs a minimum-weight Hamiltonian cycle with probability at least 2/3 in worst-case time O((2−ε)^n(n+L)^c)?
cards.definitions: Each unordered pair of distinct vertices has one explicitly listed weight. A Hamiltonian cycle visits each vertex exactly once before returning to its first vertex, and its weight is the sum of its n edge weights. Output the cyclic list of vertex labels. The input has no metric, bounded-weight, planarity or sparsity promise. Use a random-access word RAM with w=B⌈n+log₂(L+2)⌉ bits per word for one fixed sufficiently large integer B; unit-cost operations are reads/writes, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction, multiplication modulo 2^w and integer division by nonzero words. Integers occupying several words incur the cost of all word operations. This word size permits addressing exponential-space subset tables; its polynomial bit-operation overhead is already permitted by the polynomial factor in n+L. The running-time bound includes reading weights, preprocessing, random bits and output and holds on every execution. Only independent private fair random bits are allowed; there is no quantum access, advice or oracle. The constants ε,c,B and the implicit multiplicative constant are independent of n,L and the weights. A deterministic algorithm also qualifies. Dependence polynomial in the numerical maximum weight, rather than its binary length, does not qualify.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.

context_blocks.text: The exact travelling salesman problem asks for a cheapest tour through all vertices. In the general weighted setting, discovering a Hamiltonian cycle is not enough: the input is complete, so tours certainly exist, but their costs can vary greatly. The computational target is the minimum among them.

The classical subset dynamic program has a base-two dependence on the number of vertices. Stoian’s 2024 algorithm improves the familiar O(2^n n²) time by a factor 2^{Ω(√log n)}. Its bound retains the exponential base two and does not yield O*((2−ε)^n) for any fixed positive ε.

This distinction is substantial even though both bounds are exponential. A fixed base reduction saves an exponential factor on increasingly large instances, whereas savings in the polynomial or subexponential prefactor do not. The card asks about unrestricted classical algorithms, not about the optimality of the original dynamic-programming recurrence.

Weight encoding separates this target from several related exact questions. A method whose time is polynomial in the maximum integer weight can be very expensive when a large weight has a short binary representation. Likewise, faster algorithms for unweighted Hamiltonicity or for special weighted graph classes do not establish the general weighted guarantee.

No asserted reduction from SETH is built into the question. The desired algorithmic existence is itself the target; a conditional lower bound must state its assumption separately. The Parameterized and exact algorithms bucket is appropriate because the defining issue is the exponential dependence on n, rather than polynomial-time approximation of a tour.

cards.title: FPT approximation of twin-width
cards.formal: Do there exist total computable functions f,g:N→N and a constant c≥1, and one deterministic Turing machine A, such that for every finite nonempty simple graph G on n vertices and integer k≥0, A halts within f(k)(n+1)^c bit operations and either correctly reports tww(G)>k or outputs a contraction sequence of G of width at most g(k)? No order, decomposition or contraction sequence is supplied with G.
cards.definitions: The input gives n, the n×n adjacency matrix of G, and k in binary. A contraction sequence is a sequence of partitions of V(G), starting with the singleton partition and ending with {V(G)}, each obtained from its predecessor by merging two parts. For distinct parts X,Y, their pair is mixed if there exist both an adjacent pair x∈X,y∈Y and a nonadjacent pair x′∈X,y′∈Y in the original graph. The red degree of a part is the number of other parts with which it has a mixed pair. The sequence width is the maximum red degree over every part of every partition. Twin-width tww(G) is the minimum sequence width; a one-vertex graph has twin-width zero. The output lists the n−1 merges using integer part labels. Both f and g depend only on k, whereas c is independent of k and G. If tww(G)≤k, rejection is forbidden. If tww(G)>k, either a correct rejection or the stated bounded-width sequence is allowed.

cards.title: Independent set algorithms from tropical circuit size
cards.formal: Do there exist one deterministic Turing machine A and constants C,c≥1 such that for every finite simple graph G on n≥1 vertices and nonnegative integer weight vector w, A outputs the maximum independent-set weight within C(τ(G)+n+L+1)^c bit operations, where L is the total binary encoding length of w and τ(G) is the minimum size of a tropical MWIS circuit defined below? Only G and w are supplied; neither τ(G) nor a circuit is part of the input.
cards.definitions: G is given by its n×n adjacency matrix. The n nonnegative weights are binary integers with delimiters, all counted in L. A vertex set I is independent when no edge has both endpoints in I. MWIS(G,w)=max_{I independent}Σ_{v∈I}w_v, allowing I=∅ with weight zero. A tropical circuit for G is a finite acyclic circuit with one designated output, arbitrary fan-out, input gates labeled x_v or the constant 0, and binary internal gates labeled max or + with their ordinary real-number meanings. No other constants or operations are allowed. Size counts every gate, including input and constant gates. An MWIS circuit must output MWIS(G,x) for every vector x∈R_≥0^n, so its topology depends only on G. Define τ(G) as the minimum size of such a circuit. This minimum exists because finitely many independent sets can each be summed and their maximum computed. The output algorithm may use general deterministic computation, not only tropical operations. Constants C,c are uniform over all graphs and weight vectors.

cards.definitions: A parameterized decision problem Q is a subset of {0,1}*×N, with input (x,k), n=|x| and k supplied in binary. XNLP consists of those Q decided by one nondeterministic multitape Turing machine using time g(k)(n+2)^a and working space g(k)log₂(n+2) for some total computable g and constant a, simultaneously on every branch. An input is accepted exactly when some branch accepts; all branches halt within the bound. The input tape is read-only and excluded from working space, which counts visited cells on the fixed finite-alphabet work tapes. A parameterized logspace reduction Q₁≤Q₂ is a deterministic halting transducer mapping (x,k) to (y,k′), preserving the yes/no answer, with k′≤h(k) for a total computable h and space h(k)+C log₂(n+2) for an absolute C. Its output is write-only and is not counted as working space. Q is XNLP-hard when every problem in XNLP has such a reduction to Q. In the conjectured forbidden deterministic algorithm there is no randomness, oracle or advice, and a single program handles all parameters. Constants, including c and the code computing f, are fixed for that program; f may grow arbitrarily fast but must be computable. Using different computable functions in the time and space bounds is equivalent, since one common f can dominate both. Replacing n by n+2 only handles short inputs. Slice-wise polynomial time allows its exponent to depend on k; the conjectured space bound permits dependence on k only in a multiplicative factor.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the simultaneous resource obstruction for every XNLP-hard problem, or refute it by an XNLP-hard problem and one uniform deterministic algorithm satisfying both bounds for explicit computable f and fixed c. A space bound achieved by a different algorithm, a time bound with a superpolynomial exponent in n at fixed k, or a result for only bounded parameter values does not meet the criterion.

cards.title: Polylogarithmic approximation for Directed Steiner Tree
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Do there exist constants a≥1 and C≥1 and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, for every feasible Directed Steiner Tree instance with k terminals, outputs a feasible subgraph of cost at most a(log₂(k+2))^C times optimum with probability at least 2/3?
cards.definitions: An instance consists of a finite directed graph G=(V,E), a root r∈V, a nonempty terminal set T⊆V∖{r} with k=|T|, and nonnegative rational arc costs c_e given exactly in binary. Every terminal is promised reachable from r; this can also be checked in polynomial time, with infeasibility reported otherwise. A feasible solution is an arc subset F⊆E such that (V,F) contains a directed path from r to every t∈T. Its cost is Σ_{e∈F}c_e, counting an arc once even if many paths use it. OPT is the minimum such cost. The algorithm must output a feasible subset on every execution and satisfy the approximation guarantee on every instance with probability at least 2/3 over its internal randomness. Its bit running time on every execution is bounded by one fixed polynomial in the entire input encoding length, including cost bits. The constants a,C and the polynomial are independent of n=|V|, k and the costs. If OPT=0, the successful output must also have zero cost. Local computation is ordinary uniform classical computation without advice or free optimization oracles. There is no planarity, acyclicity, bounded depth, bounded treewidth, metric, or supplied fractional-solution promise. The word tree refers to the optimization problem: any feasible subgraph may be returned, and redundant edges can be removed.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct an algorithm and fixed constants satisfying these bounds, or prove that no such randomized polynomial-time algorithm exists. An O(k^ε)-approximation for every separately fixed ε>0, a polylogarithmic approximation taking quasipolynomial time, or a guarantee on a restricted graph class is partial progress. A gap for a particular LP relaxation limits that relaxation, not every algorithm. A hardness result ruling out only some smaller powers of log k does not exclude all fixed powers and therefore does not refute this proposition.
cards.why: A defining gap in directed network-design approximation: determine whether a shared directed connection network can be approximated within a polylogarithmic factor using only polynomial time.

importance.reason: A central approximation problem encompassing covering and rooted network design, with a persistent gap between polynomial and quasipolynomial algorithms.

context_blocks.text: The problem asks how cheaply a root can reach many destinations through one shared directed network. Buying a common initial segment can save cost across many root-to-terminal paths, but the directions restrict which branching structures are usable. With one terminal the problem is shortest path. With many terminals, selecting where the paths should share infrastructure becomes the central optimization challenge.

A simple reduction explains why ordinary reachability is insufficient. For a set-cover instance, create a vertex for each set and each element, an arc of cost one from the root to every set vertex, and zero-cost arcs from each set to its elements. Make all element vertices terminals. A feasible network must buy a collection of set arcs covering all elements, and its cost equals the number of chosen sets. The directed graph can thus encode a nontrivial covering problem even with only two layers after the root.

The familiar polynomial-time approximation frontier is O(k^ε) for every fixed ε>0, from the classical directed Steiner algorithms. The running-time exponent depends on the chosen accuracy parameter. Setting ε to a quantity that shrinks with k is not a free improvement: it changes that dependence and can produce quasipolynomial time. A power of k, however small and fixed, eventually exceeds every fixed power of log k.

Grandoni, Laekhanukit and Li obtain an O(log² k/log log k)-approximation in quasipolynomial time. Their techniques combine a structured reduction with a hierarchy of strengthened linear relaxations and dependent rounding. This establishes that a good approximation exists at a slower time scale. The requested advance is to achieve some polylogarithmic factor with a fixed polynomial running-time exponent; matching the sharper quasipolynomial factor is not required.

The same work gives near-matching quasipolynomial-time hardness under additional complexity assumptions, including the Projection Games Conjecture. This does not show that every polynomial-time polylogarithmic approximation is impossible: a larger fixed logarithmic power is allowed in this card. The issue is a gap between what can currently be computed in polynomial time and what is known with more time, rather than the already settled hardness of exact optimization.

A natural flow relaxation buys a fractional capacity x_e for each arc and, separately for each terminal, sends a unit flow from the root using at most x_e on that arc. Different terminals may reuse the same purchased capacity because a network edge is bought once. In general graphs this relaxation has polynomial-size integrality gaps, including Ω(√k) examples. Those examples explain why a straightforward LP-rounding strategy cannot guarantee a polylogarithmic factor against that relaxation on every instance. They do not rule out stronger relaxations or a different algorithm.

The inherited Laekhanukit reference requires careful version tracking. Its December 2024 general claim was withdrawn in version 2. Version 3, submitted in October 2025, presents itself as a rectification restricted to a relatively integral fractional solution: each terminal flow on an edge is either zero or the entire purchased capacity. The record still displays the earlier withdrawal comment about a reachability-proof error. This card treats the later restricted statement as a reported claim, not an established general approximation; finding an appropriate fractional solution is an additional requirement.

Planarity changes the picture substantially. Friggstad and Mousavi give a polynomial-time O(log k)-approximation for planar directed graphs, using shortest-path separators. Later work extends the structural approach to other rooted planar network-design problems and bounds a natural planar LP gap by O(log² k). These theorems show that directedness alone does not preclude the requested factor, but their separator arguments do not apply to arbitrary directed graphs.

Chekuri and Jain’s July 2026 work extends planar results to length-constrained network design. Its guarantees are bicriteria: they approximate cost while allowing an O(log k) multiplicative violation of the path-length constraint. The paper explicitly retains the general Directed Steiner Tree approximation question as open. Removing a length constraint or changing the objective does not remove the planarity hypothesis needed by those algorithms.

cards.title: Small-Set Expansion Hypothesis
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: For every rational constant η∈(0,1/2), is there a rational constant δ∈(0,1/2) such that the following promise problem is NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? Given a regular graph G on n vertices with δn an integer, distinguish YES: some S⊆V(G) with |S|=δn has Φ_G(S)≤η, from NO: every S⊆V(G) with |S|=δn has Φ_G(S)≥1−η.
cards.why: A major proposed basis for hardness of graph partitioning and layout problems, with connections to Unique Games.

cards.definitions: Use finite simple undirected d-regular graphs G=([n],E), n≥2 and d≥1, given explicitly by their adjacency matrices. Regular means that every vertex has exactly d neighbours; d is not a fixed constant or an extra promise. For nonempty S, ∂_G S is the set of edges with exactly one endpoint in S, and Φ_G(S)=|∂_G S|/(d|S|). Internal edges contribute twice to d|S| and zero to the boundary. This is normalized edge expansion, not the number of outside neighbours. The graph has no promised connectivity, geometry or spectral gap. The constants η,δ are chosen before the input; they are not parameters tending to zero with n. For δ=a/b in lowest terms, inputs have n a positive multiple of b, so exact set size has no rounding ambiguity. The YES and NO cases are disjoint since η<1/2; inputs meeting neither case have no required decision answer. NP-hardness means that for every language L with polynomially checkable witnesses, a deterministic polynomial-time map sends each x∈L to a YES graph and each x∉L to a NO graph. Equivalently, it suffices to supply such a reduction from Boolean satisfiability. Reduction constants and the polynomial exponent may depend on η and its chosen δ. The card fixes the unweighted regular-graph, exact-cardinality version of the imported question; weighted-volume, randomized-hardness and size-interval versions must be identified when cited.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves the stated NP-hardness for every η by choosing δ and giving a valid promise-preserving reduction. A negative resolution refutes this quantified hardness statement for some fixed η. Polynomial-time algorithms for every fixed δ at that η would refute the hardness claim under P≠NP; an algorithm alone must not be called an unconditional disproof of NP-hardness. Results restricted to special graph classes or allowing a different output set size do not automatically settle this formulation.

context_blocks.title: What expansion measures
context_blocks.text: Choose a vertex uniformly from S, then choose one of its neighbours uniformly. The probability of leaving S is exactly Φ_G(S). A set with expansion near zero is a group whose connections mostly remain inside it. Expansion near one means that almost every connection goes out. The promise asks whether one unusually insulated set exists at the specified size, or whether every set of that size is almost completely exposed.

context_blocks.title: Small means a fixed fraction
context_blocks.text: If δ=1/1000, the target has one thousand vertices in a million-vertex graph and one million vertices in a billion-vertex graph. Its size still grows linearly with n. Enumerating all sets of a fixed number of vertices therefore does not give a polynomial-time algorithm for the question. The order of constants also matters: δ may depend on the desired expansion gap η, and an algorithm for one convenient pair of constants would not refute the full hypothesis.

context_blocks.title: A sparse large cut can miss the issue
context_blocks.text: Take the disjoint union of two complete graphs on 50 vertices. Either whole component has expansion zero. Yet a two-vertex set contained in one component has expansion 48/49, and a two-vertex set split between the components has expansion one. Thus every set of the specified small size expands very well even though a larger zero-expansion cut exists. Optimizing over all sets up to half the graph can answer a different question from the exact small-size promise.

context_blocks.title: Why a large gap remains difficult
context_blocks.text: For a proposed set, its size and edge boundary are easy to count. The universal NO condition ranges over all sets of that size. The hypothesis asserts hardness even though YES and NO graphs are separated by a wide gap, with many intermediate graphs excluded by the promise. A graph expansion construction, a bound on one spectral parameter, or an algorithm with an uncontrolled change in set size is not automatically a distinguisher for this promise.

context_blocks.title: Connections and current boundary
context_blocks.text: Raghavendra and Steurer reduce small-set expansion to Unique Games, making this hypothesis a sufficient foundation for Unique Games hardness. Raghavendra, Steurer and Tulsiani relate it to a version of Unique Games with an additional expansion requirement and derive conditional hardness for graph partitioning and arrangement problems. This does not establish equivalence to unrestricted Unique Games in both directions. In August 2026, Lin, Mirrokni and Woodruff use a randomized, weighted, exact-volume variant to prove a sparse least-squares hardness result. Such an application assumes an SSE statement; it does not prove the statement itself, and its modeling conventions should not be silently transferred to this card. The checked sources leave the hypothesis unresolved.

Enumerating all sets of a fixed number of vertices therefore does not give a polynomial-time algorithm for the question. The order of constants also matters: δ may depend on the desired expansion gap η, and an algorithm for one convenient pair of constants would not refute the full hypothesis.

Take the disjoint union of two complete graphs on 50 vertices. Either whole component has expansion zero. Yet a two-vertex set contained in one component has expansion 48/49, and a two-vertex set split between the components has expansion one. Thus every set of the specified small size expands very well even though a larger zero-expansion cut exists. Optimizing over all sets up to half the graph can answer a different question from the exact small-size promise.

For a proposed set, its size and edge boundary are easy to count. The universal NO condition ranges over all sets of that size. The hypothesis asserts hardness even though YES and NO graphs are separated by a wide gap, with many intermediate graphs excluded by the promise. A graph expansion construction, a bound on one spectral parameter, or an algorithm with an uncontrolled change in set size is not automatically a distinguisher for this promise.

Raghavendra and Steurer reduce small-set expansion to Unique Games, making this hypothesis a sufficient foundation for Unique Games hardness. Raghavendra, Steurer and Tulsiani relate it to a version of Unique Games with an additional expansion requirement and derive conditional hardness for graph partitioning and arrangement problems. This does not establish equivalence to unrestricted Unique Games in both directions. In August 2026, Lin, Mirrokni and Woodruff use a randomized, weighted, exact-volume variant to prove a sparse least-squares hardness result. Such an application assumes an SSE statement; it does not prove the statement itself, and its modeling conventions should not be silently transferred to this card. The checked sources leave the hypothesis unresolved.

cards.title: 4/3 conjecture for metric TSP
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Let Γ=sup_{n≥3,c} OPT_TSP(c)/OPT_LP(c), where c ranges over all metrics on n labeled points and OPT_LP is the subtour relaxation defined below. Is Γ=4/3?
cards.definitions: For V={1,…,n} and E={{u,v}:u≠v}, a metric has c_uu=0, c_uv=c_vu>0 for u≠v, and c_uv≤c_uw+c_wv. Costs are arbitrary real numbers; no Euclidean embedding is assumed. OPT_TSP is the minimum sum of edge costs on a Hamiltonian cycle of the complete undirected graph. For S⊆V, δ(S) contains edges with exactly one endpoint in S, and x(F)=Σ_{e∈F}x_e. Define OPT_LP=min Σ_e c_e x_e subject to x(δ({v}))=2 for every v, x(δ(S))≥2 for every nonempty proper S⊊V, and 0≤x_e≤1 for every e. The LP is feasible and has positive optimum. The supremum ranges over every finite size, not one fixed n. This is the symmetric metric subtour-LP integrality gap, not an approximation ratio measured only against OPT_TSP, an asymmetric TSP relaxation, or a restricted geometric metric.
cards.answer_criterion: Known constructions establish Γ≥4/3. Thus an affirmative resolution proves OPT_TSP(c)≤(4/3)OPT_LP(c) for every finite metric instance. A negative resolution gives an instance with ratio strictly greater than 4/3, or proves such an instance exists. A supremum need not be attained to make the question meaningful. Improving an algorithm’s upper bound while it remains above 4/3 is progress, not a resolution.
cards.why: The exact strength of the principal relaxation for a canonical optimization problem, joining polyhedral structure, probabilistic rounding and approximation. A resolution would explain a longstanding gap between fractional connectivity and integral tours.

importance.reason: A defining integrality-gap conjecture in combinatorial optimization with consequences for LP rounding and the limits of metric TSP approximation methods.

cards.status_note: The general 4/3 equality remains open through the primary-source review of 11 September 2026. The established explicit upper bound recorded here is 3/2−2.18·10^{−34}; a September 2 preprint claims a further small improvement, clearly separated from verified literature. Restricted-class theorems and finite-size verification do not resolve the universal conjecture.

context_blocks.text: The relaxation allows fractional edge purchases while retaining two elementary properties of every tour: each vertex has degree two, and every nontrivial cut is crossed at least twice. It therefore knows much more than a disconnected cycle-cover relaxation, but its feasible points need not be convex combinations of Hamiltonian cycles. The conjecture asks for the exact worst loss caused by that remaining freedom.

For example, a feasible fractional vector may put positive weight on several alternative connections at one vertex without choosing a single predecessor and successor. The cut inequalities ensure aggregate connectivity, yet they do not force these local choices to assemble into one integral cycle. The proposed factor 4/3 says that, in a metric, repairing all such inconsistencies never costs more than one third of the fractional optimum.

The metric assumption is what makes shortcutting possible. If a connected Eulerian multigraph visits a vertex several times, replacing a detour by the direct edge between its endpoints does not increase cost. One can consequently search for a suitably cheap Eulerian structure rather than construct a Hamiltonian cycle at every intermediate step. This observation explains why spanning trees and parity correction recur in approximation algorithms for the problem.

A minimum spanning tree followed by a minimum-cost matching on its odd-degree vertices yields the classical 3/2 guarantee. Wolsey’s analysis measures both components against the LP: the tree costs at most the fractional optimum, and the matching at most half that value. The inherited July 2026 paper recalls this argument before studying a particular randomized refinement.

An algorithmic ratio and an integrality-gap ratio must use the correct denominator. A guarantee cost≤α·OPT_TSP does not establish OPT_TSP≤α·OPT_LP, since the fractional optimum can be smaller. Karlin–Klein–Oveis Gharan’s FOCS 2022 result explicitly supplies an LP-relative guarantee below 3/2, extending the earlier approximation breakthrough. It is this later theorem that directly improves the general gap bound.

The modern approach samples a spanning tree from a distribution constrained by fractional edge marginals, then corrects its parity. Tree cost and parity-repair cost interact, so treating the two separately can lose the desired saving. Gurvits–Klein–Leake strengthen probability estimates using capacities of real stable polynomials. Their Lemma 4.5 is explicitly LP-relative and yields the certified bound Γ≤3/2−2.18·10^{−34}. The small constant reflects a worst-case proof, not a claim that practical tours are that close to 3/2.

A class can have a better integrality gap than the worst ratio of a particular algorithm on it. Jin–Klein–Williamson prove the 4/3 bound for half-integral cycle-cut instances using a specialized construction. Half-integral means that nonzero fractional coordinates are 1/2 or 1, with an additional restriction on the hierarchy of tight cuts. This result does not cover every half-integral instance, still less every subtour solution.

Their July 2026 paper, which supplied the inherited reference, proves a 10/7 guarantee for the maximum-entropy algorithm on that same restricted class. Since 10/7 exceeds 4/3, it improves understanding of the chosen algorithm rather than improving the already-known class gap. The authors also identify examples giving a lower bound of 11/8 on the algorithm’s performance. Such an algorithm-specific obstruction cannot refute the conjecture about the cheapest possible tour.

Two complementary approaches restrict the fractional solution in other ways. Villa–Vercesi–Barta–Mastrolilli prove the 4/3 bound when an optimal solution has at most n+6 nonzero components, combining structural reasoning and computation. This is a support-size condition, not a theorem for every instance on at most n+6 vertices. Larger support remains outside its stated guarantee.

Cook–Hougardy–Petrich’s September 8, 2026 revision reports exact verification for all metric instances through n=16 and for half-integral extreme points through n=18. It also repairs omissions in earlier extreme-point lists. This is stronger evidence than sampling finitely many random metrics, because the computation organizes the relevant polyhedral cases. It still leaves unbounded n, and the catalogue has not rerun that enumeration.

A September 2 preprint by Zhao Song claims a larger universal saving, ε★>2.05522·10^{−30}, through a refined maximum-entropy analysis. Its main theorem is explicitly relative to OPT_LP. The statement was checked, but the lengthy proof and numerical certificate were not independently verified here, so the value is recorded as a recent claim rather than silently replacing the established bound. Even if confirmed, it would remain far above the requested ratio 4/3.

cards.title: Metric k-Median at the 1+2/e threshold
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: For every fixed rational ε∈(0,1), does a randomized polynomial-time (1+2/e+ε)-approximation algorithm exist for general metric k-Median that always opens at most k facilities?
cards.definitions: An input consists of a finite set V, a full table of nonnegative rational distances d on V encoded in binary, nonempty subsets C,F⊆V of clients and allowable facilities with C∪F=V, and an integer 1≤k≤|F|. The table is promised to satisfy d(u,v)=d(v,u), d(u,v)=0 exactly when u=v, and the triangle inequality. Each client has unit demand. For nonempty S⊆F define cost(S)=Σ_{c∈C}min_{s∈S}d(c,s), and OPT=min{cost(S):S⊆F,1≤|S|≤k}. L is the total bit length of the input. For each fixed ε the target is one uniform classical randomized algorithm A_ε, with constants K_ε,d_ε such that every execution takes at most K_ε L^{d_ε} bit operations. It always returns an explicit nonempty S⊆F with |S|≤k, and on each input Pr[cost(S)≤(1+2/e+ε)OPT]≥2/3. Here e is the base of the natural logarithm. The constants may depend on ε but not on k, |C|, |F| or distance precision. No Euclidean, low-dimensional, stability, capacity or input-distribution promise is made. Candidate facilities are part of the input and cannot be enlarged. The guarantee also covers OPT=0.
cards.answer_criterion: Give the stated algorithms for every fixed ε>0, or rule them out for at least one fixed ε, explicitly identifying any complexity assumption used. This card fixes the yes/no question of approaching the known hardness threshold; it does not additionally require finding a different exact threshold after a negative answer. An algorithm opening k facilities only in expectation, one allowing k+o(k) facilities, or an FPT algorithm with unrestricted dependence on k does not prove the claim.
cards.why: A central unresolved approximation threshold for metric clustering, separating known coverage hardness from the best algorithms with a strict facility budget.

importance.reason: A major optimization problem with a substantial remaining algorithm–hardness gap and connections to coverage, facility location, LP rounding and parameterized approximation.

progress.text: Feige proves the 1−1/e hardness threshold for Max k-Cover, which yields the 1+2/e metric k-Median gap through a client–facility metric construction.

Cohen-Addad–Gupta–Kumar–Lee–Li reach 1+2/e+ε in fixed-parameter time with respect to k, not unrestricted polynomial time.
Cohen-Addad–Grandoni–Lee–Schwiegelshohn–Svensson obtain a randomized polynomial-time 2+ε approximation with at most k facilities; the May 2026 full-version revision retains the theorem.
Improved approximation-scheme runtimes apply to low-dimensional Euclidean clustering, a restricted metric setting.
Spectral dual fitting improves k-Means approximation; squared-distance clustering is a different objective.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The checked general-metric result remains 2+ε with a strict budget, while the classical hardness threshold is 1+2/e. The FPT algorithm, Euclidean schemes and 2026 k-Means results do not settle the polynomial-time target here.

context_blocks.text: Metric k-Median selects a limited number of service locations and minimizes total distance to the nearest selected location. The number of clients and the number of candidate facilities may differ, and the distance table need not come from a Euclidean embedding. The same formulation models representative selection for clustering and placement of facilities. Its simplicity makes the unresolved approximation threshold a central benchmark for algorithm design.

The two endpoint numbers are approximately 1.73576 and 2. The lower endpoint is the classical hardness threshold 1+2/e; the best general feasible guarantee in the checked literature is 2+ε. The inherited STOC 2025 paper explicitly asks for a tight approximation result after obtaining that upper bound. Asking for 1+2/e+ε for every fixed ε avoids requiring that an infimum approximation ratio be achieved exactly.

The coverage origin of the lower endpoint can be seen directly. Represent each set as a candidate facility and each universe element as a client. Give a client–facility pair distance one when the set contains the element and distance three otherwise, and give distinct pairs on the same side distance two. These distances satisfy the triangle inequality. A collection of k sets covering a fraction p of the elements then has clustering cost (3−2p) times the universe size.

Feige’s Max k-Cover gap distinguishes complete coverage from coverage of at most 1−1/e+η, for any fixed η>0. Under the preceding metric construction this becomes a gap between cost one per client and cost at least 1+2/e−2η per client. This is why the constant is not an arbitrary numerical target. A randomized algorithm beating that gap on every input would yield randomized algorithms for the underlying NP-hard decision problem; the appropriate exclusion is NP≠RP for this card’s success convention.

Jain–Mahdian–Saberi’s 2002 paper gives the classical metric k-Median lower bound through a reduction to approximating Set Cover. Its historical statement uses the then-known slightly-superpolynomial-time assumption for Set Cover hardness. The coverage reduction above explains the stronger ordinary NP-hardness formulation without silently changing the assumption in the original theorem. Neither lower-bound route excludes approximation from just above 1+2/e.

The 2025 algorithm combines two components. One permits a logarithmic number of extra centers while retaining a 2+ε cost bound; another handles instances where deleting one optimal center increases the optimum substantially. Combining them returns a feasible solution opening at most k centers. The full paper’s May 2026 revision retains this result. It is therefore incorrect to describe the headline 2+ε theorem as only a bicriteria approximation.

The usual linear relaxation has a separate barrier near two. It uses fractional openings y_s, assignments x_{c,s}≤y_s, unit total assignment for each client, and Σ_s y_s≤k. For a star with q≥3 leaves, all vertices available as facilities, clients at the leaves and k=q−1, every integral optimum has cost two. Set the central opening to 1/(q−1), each leaf opening to (q−2)/(q−1), and assign each client’s remaining fraction to the center. This feasible LP solution costs q/(q−1), giving an integrality gap approaching two.

That explicit example limits a guarantee measured against this relaxation, not every polynomial algorithm measured against OPT. A sharper algorithm might use additional constraints, a different relaxation, or another method. Likewise, a lower bound for one rounding framework is not a computational impossibility theorem for the original optimization problem. The card’s target is deliberately stated using the true integral optimum.

There is already a matching-threshold algorithm in a different runtime regime. Cohen-Addad–Gupta–Kumar–Lee–Li’s ICALP 2019 work achieves 1+2/e+ε in fixed-parameter time with respect to k. The potentially large dependence on the number of opened facilities is permitted there. This does not supply a polynomial-time algorithm when k grows as part of the input, but it shows that the target ratio has meaningful algorithmic support.

A 2026 development concerns geometric input. Cohen-Addad and coauthors improve approximation-scheme runtimes in low-dimensional Euclidean spaces, where additional structure is available. Such a scheme does not apply to arbitrary distance tables.

Anand and coauthors’ July 2026 spectral dual-fitting paper improves k-Means guarantees, including in general metrics. That objective sums squared distances; squaring changes both the analysis and the hardness constants. It does not establish the stated k-Median ratio.

Resolving this question would determine whether the coverage obstruction captures the full cost of efficient metric clustering. A positive answer would bridge the remaining gap beyond the familiar LP benchmark. A stronger hardness threshold would reveal an obstruction not expressed by coverage alone. The exact facility budget is essential to either conclusion: averaging an excessive number of facilities over random choices changes the feasible problem.

upgraded_from.title: The factor-2 integrality-gap conjecture for the ATSP subtour LP

cards.definitions: A directed metric is a function c:V×V→R≥0 with c(i,i)=0 and c(i,k)≤c(i,j)+c(j,k) for all i,j,k. Symmetry is not required, and distinct vertices may have zero distance. The complete directed graph has one arc (i,j) for each i≠j and no loops. A Hamiltonian cycle visits every vertex once before returning to its start; its cost is the sum of its n arc costs. OPT_ATSP(c) is the minimum over all such cycles. For S⊆V, δ⁺(S)={(i,j):i∈S,j∉S} and δ⁻(S)={(i,j):i∉S,j∈S}; for a set of arcs F write x(F)=Σ_(i,j)∈F x_ij. LP_ATSP(c) minimizes Σ_i≠j c(i,j)x_ij over real variables x_ij≥0 subject to x(δ⁺({v}))=x(δ⁻({v}))=1 for every v, and x(δ⁺(S))≥1 for every nonempty proper S⊊V. The degree equalities imply x(δ⁺(S))=x(δ⁻(S)), so an additional incoming-cut inequality would be redundant. No integrality restriction is placed on x. The feasible set is nonempty and compact; both optima are attained. The inequality, rather than division by LP_ATSP(c), also covers zero-cost instances. For positive LP value, the integrality ratio is OPT_ATSP(c)/LP_ATSP(c), and the overall gap is its supremum over all n and directed metrics. The question is a universal comparison of optimum values, without a running-time restriction on finding the tour. It concerns closed tours, not a prescribed-start/end path.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed factor-2 inequality for every finite directed metric and every size, or exhibit a finite directed metric with a rigorously proved strict violation. An affirmative answer need not attain ratio 2 on a finite instance: known families approach 2. An approximation algorithm proved only relative to the true tour optimum, or a result restricted to a subset of LP extreme points, does not establish the universal LP inequality.

context_blocks.title: Buying fractions of directed arcs
context_blocks.text: A tour buys each used arc completely. The relaxation permits fractional amounts of several arcs, while requiring one unit to enter and leave every city and at least one unit to leave every proper group of cities. Every tour is feasible for the LP, so the LP gives a lower bound on the tour cost. The question asks whether converting the best fractional cost into an actual tour ever entails a factor larger than two. A fractional solution need not be a probability distribution over whole tours.

context_blocks.title: Why subtour constraints matter
context_blocks.text: Suppose six cities form two groups of three, with travel cost 1 within a group and 10 between groups. Two separate three-city directed cycles satisfy every degree condition and cost only 6, but do not form a tour visiting all cities. The cut inequality for either group rules out this disconnected solution. These inequalities therefore add a global requirement to the local degree constraints; whether that requirement is strong enough to keep the full gap at two is the unresolved issue.

context_blocks.title: The current general gap
context_blocks.text: Families of directed instances have ratios tending to 2, so no smaller universal factor can work. Traub and Vygen’s 2022 article establishes an upper bound of 22. Their 2024 book improves the proved bound to 17 and explicitly retains the factor-2 question. Its circulation LP has the same optimum as the degree-constrained LP on directed metrics, so the model matches this card. The book also notes room for a small further numerical improvement; 17 is a stated theorem, not a claim that no refinement exists.

context_blocks.title: Finite computations and half-integral vertices
context_blocks.text: Vercesi and coauthors construct improved lower-bound instances at particular sizes. The June 2026 revision by Sosso, Bernardelli and Gualandi computes the gaps for all half-integral extreme points through twelve vertices, where half-integral means coordinates in {0,1/2,1}. An extreme point is a feasible LP solution that cannot be written as a nontrivial convex combination of two distinct feasible solutions. Other denominators and arbitrarily large instances remain outside that enumeration. These computations add evidence without proving the universal conjecture.

context_blocks.title: What a resolution would establish
context_blocks.text: The comparison measures the strength of this specific relaxation. A polynomial-time method achieving cost at most twice the LP optimum would settle the inequality and give an approximation guarantee, but the existence inequality itself does not promise an efficient construction. The symmetric metric TSP has a different classical 4/3 conjecture; its constants and finite verifications do not transfer to the larger family in which travel costs can depend on direction.

cards.title: k-server conjecture
cards.formal: For every integer k≥1, every metric space (M,d) with at least k+1 points, and every initial placement C_0 of k servers, does there exist a deterministic online serving rule A and a finite constant β≥0 such that cost_A(σ;C_0)≤k·OPT(σ;C_0)+β for every finite request sequence σ∈M*? The rule and β may depend on M,d,k,C_0, but neither may depend on future requests or on the length of the request sequence.
cards.definitions: The metric is symmetric, has finite real distances, is zero exactly on equal points, and satisfies the triangle inequality; the space may be finite or infinite and is known to the online rule. There are exactly k interchangeable, unweighted servers, whose current positions form a multiset. A request r_t must be served before r_{t+1} is revealed. If a server is already at r_t, no movement is needed; otherwise the rule chooses one of the k servers and moves it to r_t, paying the metric distance. Restriction to these lazy moves loses no competitive power. A deterministic online rule is a function of the known metric, initial placement and revealed request prefix, with arbitrary memory and no access to future requests; this card imposes no running-time bound. OPT is the minimum total movement cost of an offline rule serving the same finite sequence from C_0 with the same k servers and advance knowledge of the sequence. The additive β must be fixed before requests arrive and cannot grow with the number or cost of requests. Randomization, advice about future requests, and extra servers are not supplied.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A central problem in competitive analysis that asks whether the number of available servers exactly captures the worst-case price of future uncertainty. Its techniques and limitations inform caching, online movement and broader metric optimization problems.

importance.reason: A foundational conjecture about online decision-making, with an optimal lower bound, one broadly applicable candidate algorithm, and a persistent gap on general metrics despite many resolved special cases.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The April 2026 primary source retains the deterministic conjecture and the general (2k−1) upper bound. The 2023 randomized disproof concerns O(log k), not the deterministic factor k. This card fixes all finite request sequences, identical initial placements, exactly k servers and an additive constant independent of requests; it asks for any deterministic online rule, not specifically WFA.

context_blocks.text: The problem isolates the price of making placement decisions without seeing future demand. Servers can represent cache slots, mobile resources or copies of data; a movement pays for changing which demand locations are covered. On a uniform metric, where every distinct pair has distance one, serving a request is precisely the paging problem. The online rule and the offline optimum have the same number of servers. Their difference is information about the future, not available capacity.

The proposed factor k is a sharp target, already forced by paging lower bounds. The classical work of Manasse, McGeoch and Sleator establishes the lower-bound framework and settles the two-server case on general metrics. An additive constant is included so that a fixed initial placement does not distort asymptotic performance. Allowing that constant to depend on the request sequence would make the definition vacuous, which is why its quantifiers are explicit.

Koutsoupias and Papadimitriou prove that the work-function algorithm is (2k−1)-competitive on every metric space. Its work function records the minimum offline cost of serving the already revealed prefix and ending in each possible server configuration. The algorithm uses these values to weigh movement against how well a configuration fits the past. This provides a single general strategy and leaves a factor approaching two between the known guarantee and the conjectured optimum.

It is widely conjectured that the same algorithm is actually k-competitive. Proving that stronger statement would settle this card, but the card permits a completely different algorithm. Similarly, failure of one proposed potential function only identifies a gap in that proof method. A potential proof typically compares changes in a quantity assigned to the current work function with the online and offline costs, so that the inequalities telescope over an arbitrarily long request sequence.

Several geometric settings attain the target. Chrobak and Larmore give k-competitive algorithms on tree metrics, covering line-like settings as well. Trees have unique connecting paths, which support movement rules unavailable in arbitrary metrics. This is substantial positive evidence, but arbitrary metric spaces can contain cycles and distance patterns that do not admit the same analysis.

Huang and Zhang prove that the work-function algorithm is 3-competitive on a circle, with distance measured along the shorter circular arc. Their result first appeared in a 2022 preprint and was published in Theoretical Computer Science in 2024. They also give computer-assisted evidence excluding their defined canonical family of potential functions for the general three-server case. The geometric theorem and the limitation of that proof family are different conclusions.

Bubeck, Coester and Rabani’s STOC 2023 theorem disproves the randomized O(log k) conjecture by constructing metrics with randomized competitive ratio Ω(log²k). It does not refute the deterministic target k: these are different claimed rates, and log²k is asymptotically smaller than k. The deterministic lower bound and the (2k−1) upper bound remain the relevant endpoints here.

Brilliantov, Bamas and Abbé’s April 2026 benchmark studies automated searches for potentials, particularly for four servers on a circle. A violated checked inequality refutes a candidate under the chosen formulation, while passing the finite checks is not a proof for every metric configuration and request sequence. Their experiments leave the open case unresolved. This offers concrete research tooling without changing the status of the conjecture.

cards.title: Beating factor two for unrelated-machine makespan
cards.formal: Does there exist a constant ε with 0<ε<1 and a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm which, for every unrelated-machine scheduling instance, assigns all jobs to machines with makespan at most (2−ε)OPT?
cards.definitions: An instance consists of m≥1 machines, n≥0 independent jobs, and an explicitly given m×n matrix of processing times pᵢⱼ in the nonnegative rationals or ∞. Rational numerators and denominators are binary encoded; ∞ forbids an assignment. Every job has at least one finite processing time. A schedule is a function σ:{1,…,n}→{1,…,m} with p_{σ(j),j}<∞. Its makespan is Cmax(σ)=maxᵢ Σ_{j:σ(j)=i} pᵢⱼ, and OPT is the minimum of this quantity over all feasible schedules. Jobs are available at time zero, indivisible and processed without interruption on one machine; there are no precedence constraints or communication costs. Jobs assigned to one machine can run consecutively in any order. The algorithm must output σ, not merely an estimate of OPT. Its bit running time is polynomial in the entire input length. ε and the polynomial are independent of m, n and all processing times; no predictions or promises on matrix structure are supplied. Empty or zero-optimum instances require makespan zero. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A defining unresolved approximation barrier in scheduling. Beating two by any fixed constant would also imply a constant approximation for general Santa Claus allocation, while known relaxation gaps rule out a large family of straightforward proofs.

importance.reason: A decades-old central scheduling problem with a large hardness gap, robust LP barriers and formal consequences for fair allocation.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The full worst-case constant-improvement question remains open in the checked primary literature. The known 2−1/m ratio and prediction-assisted results have different quantifiers from the fixed-ε target. The 3/2 hardness is conditional on P≠NP.

context_blocks.text: Each job can have a completely different processing time on each machine. There need not be a single ranking from fastest to slowest machines, as in the related-machine model. The challenge is to balance total load while respecting which assignments are expensive or forbidden. Even when every job has an individually attractive machine, sending all jobs to their favorite machines can create a severe bottleneck.

Lenstra, Shmoys and Tardos obtain a polynomial-time factor-2 approximation by rounding a fractional assignment. For a candidate makespan T, assignments with pᵢⱼ>T are forbidden; the relaxation divides each job fractionally among the remaining machines while bounding each machine’s fractional load by T. Their rounding can charge the overload to at most one additional job per machine. Since every eligible job fits individually within T, the resulting schedule has load at most 2T.

The same foundational work establishes NP-hardness of approximation below 3/2. This leaves a genuine gap: the known hardness is compatible with an algorithm of ratio 1.9, 1.75 or 1.5. Moreover, Shchepin and Vakhania improve the general guarantee to 2−1/m. That is strictly less than two for each finite number of machines, but it approaches two as m grows. The ε in this question must be one fixed positive constant, so this refinement is not a resolution.

A stronger relaxation uses configurations: a variable represents an entire subset of jobs that fits on one machine within T. This remembers much more local packing structure than individual fractional assignments. Nevertheless, Verschae and Wiese construct an integrality gap approaching two even when each job is eligible on at most two machines. Thus rounding this relaxation solely against its own optimum cannot prove a universal constant improvement. This is a limitation of the relaxation, not a hardness theorem for all algorithms.

Restricted assignment is a special case in which job j has one processing time pⱼ on all eligible machines. It is substantially more structured than arbitrary unrelated processing times. Bamas and coauthors obtain a polynomial-time (1.75+δ)-approximation for the further restriction to two finite job sizes. Their general two-value unrelated-machine result instead gives 2−1/nᵟ for fixed δ>0, whose improvement still depends on instance size. Neither guarantee extends to the full target here.

The same SODA 2024 paper gives a formal connection to the Santa Claus allocation problem, where indivisible resources must be distributed to maximize the least satisfied player’s additive value. A (2−1/α)-approximation for makespan, for constant α≥2, would yield an (α+δ)-approximation for general Santa Claus for any fixed δ>0. Thus even a small fixed improvement here would also resolve a major constant-factor approximation question in fair allocation.

Baba, Bampis and Mitropoulos’ June 2026 preprint studies predictions of assignments for heavy jobs. For accurate predictions their algorithm approaches factor one, while its worst-case guarantee with arbitrary prediction error remains two. This identifies valuable information that helps scheduling, but the classical question supplies no such information. A worst-case proof cannot assume that a learned assignment resembles an optimal schedule.

The fundamental issue is whether indivisibility forces an approximation barrier at two, or whether a stronger global argument can control the interactions that fractional rounding loses. Progress would clarify both the power of optimization relaxations and the complexity of balancing heterogeneous resources.

A better guarantee would improve a basic benchmark for scheduling heterogeneous work across heterogeneous resources.
The saved review distinguishes fixed improvements from factors such as 2−1/m, which approach two as the number of machines grows and therefore do not meet the target.

cards.context:
Each job can have a completely different processing time on each machine. There need not be a single ranking from fastest to slowest machines, as in the related-machine model. The challenge is to balance total load while respecting which assignments are expensive or forbidden. Even when every job has an individually attractive machine, sending all jobs to their favorite machines can create a severe bottleneck.

Lenstra, Shmoys and Tardos obtain a polynomial-time factor-2 approximation by rounding a fractional assignment. For a candidate makespan T, assignments with pᵢⱼ>T are forbidden; the relaxation divides each job fractionally among the remaining machines while bounding each machine’s fractional load by T. Their rounding can charge the overload to at most one additional job per machine. Since every eligible job fits individually within T, the resulting schedule has load at most 2T.

The same foundational work establishes NP-hardness of approximation below 3/2. This leaves a genuine gap: the known hardness is compatible with an algorithm of ratio 1.9, 1.75 or 1.5. Moreover, Shchepin and Vakhania improve the general guarantee to 2−1/m. That is strictly less than two for each finite number of machines, but it approaches two as m grows. The ε in this question must be one fixed positive constant, so this refinement is not a resolution.

A stronger relaxation uses configurations: a variable represents an entire subset of jobs that fits on one machine within T. This remembers much more local packing structure than individual fractional assignments. Nevertheless, Verschae and Wiese construct an integrality gap approaching two even when each job is eligible on at most two machines. Thus rounding this relaxation solely against its own optimum cannot prove a universal constant improvement. This is a limitation of the relaxation, not a hardness theorem for all algorithms.

Restricted assignment is a special case in which job j has one processing time pⱼ on all eligible machines. It is substantially more structured than arbitrary unrelated processing times. Bamas and coauthors obtain a polynomial-time (1.75+δ)-approximation for the further restriction to two finite job sizes. Their general two-value unrelated-machine result instead gives 2−1/nᵟ for fixed δ>0, whose improvement still depends on instance size. Neither guarantee extends to the full target here.

The same SODA 2024 paper gives a formal connection to the Santa Claus allocation problem, where indivisible resources must be distributed to maximize the least satisfied player’s additive value. A (2−1/α)-approximation for makespan, for constant α≥2, would yield an (α+δ)-approximation for general Santa Claus for any fixed δ>0. Thus even a small fixed improvement here would also resolve a major constant-factor approximation question in fair allocation.

Baba, Bampis and Mitropoulos’ June 2026 preprint studies predictions of assignments for heavy jobs. For accurate predictions their algorithm approaches factor one, while its worst-case guarantee with arbitrary prediction error remains two. This identifies valuable information that helps scheduling, but the classical question supplies no such information. A worst-case proof cannot assume that a learned assignment resembles an optimal schedule.

The fundamental issue is whether indivisibility forces an approximation barrier at two, or whether a stronger global argument can control the interactions that fractional rounding loses. Progress would clarify both the power of optimization relaxations and the complexity of balancing heterogeneous resources.
