cards.status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026, including the July 2026 splay result. The conjecture asks for linear total cost under insertions and deletions at either end.

context_blocks.text: A deque allows insertion and deletion at either end of a sequence. A linked representation can implement this abstract interface in constant time per operation. The conjecture concerns what happens when the same interface is implemented by a self-adjusting search tree: it asks whether the tree automatically achieves the linear total cost available for this restricted workload.

Deleting the minimum of a long left spine can require many rotations in a single operation. That does not disprove the conjecture, because the initial tree contributes an additive budget proportional to its size. The real difficulty is to understand whether alternating insertions and deletions at opposite ends can repeatedly rebuild expensive configurations.

For a concrete contrast, deleting keys in increasing order is a sequential-access pattern. A deque workload can switch ends after every operation and introduce new extreme keys between deletions. A bound for one monotone scan therefore does not immediately control this more flexible sequence.

The known total bound has an iterated inverse-Ackermann factor, which grows extraordinarily slowly but is asymptotically unbounded. Removing it would answer a structural question about how rotations reuse earlier work. This is a focused subproblem of the broader study of splaying, with updates included explicitly rather than only searches.

cards.title: Optimal decrease-key in pure pairing heaps
cards.formal: For the pure pairing heap defined below, is there a universal constant C such that every legal sequence of M operations starting with empty heaps costs at most $C[M+D(1+\log N)+K(1+\log\log(N+2))]$? Here D counts delete-min operations, K counts decrease-key operations, and $N\ge2$ is the maximum of 2 and the total number of live items across all heaps at any moment. The allowed operations are make-heap, insert, find-min, meld, decrease-key, and delete-min. Count comparisons and pointer-machine steps; keys are distinct opaque values in a totally ordered set, compared at unit cost. Handles to the affected items and heaps are supplied.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove this total-cost bound for the specified algorithm, or construct legal operation sequences for which its ratio to the displayed budget is unbounded. Changing the heap algorithm or obtaining the bound only for a different self-adjusting heap does not establish a positive answer.
cards.definitions: A heap is one rooted heap-ordered tree whose child lists are ordered from left to right. Linking two roots compares their keys and makes the larger root the leftmost child of the smaller; cut removes a node with its subtree from its parent in constant time. Store O(1) pointers per item, with doubly linked child lists. Make-heap creates an empty tree; find-min returns its root; insert links a singleton to the root; meld links the roots and destroys the old heap handles. Decrease-key changes the supplied key and, if its node is not the root, cuts that node and links its subtree with the remaining root. Delete-min removes the root and scans its children left to right, linking disjoint adjacent pairs; an unpaired last child remains. Winners keep their positions in the root list. Identify its minimum-key remaining root v, remove v from that list, and prepend all other remaining roots in their existing order to the child list of v. The resulting tree is the heap. Use the ordinary constant-time list splice, rather than doing an additional recursive linking pass. All loops, comparisons, pointer accesses, and writes are charged. Logarithms have base two.
cards.why: This is a precise opportunity to separate an analysis gap from a structural limitation of a simple data structure. Priority-queue costs propagate into graph algorithms, and the problem tests how little explicit balancing information is sufficient for optimal amortized behavior.

Tarjan and Xu introduce pure pairing heaps and bound decrease-key by O(log log n times log log log n), retaining O(log n) delete-min and O(1) insert/meld amortized bounds. Section 10 explicitly leaves the remaining factor open.

cards.status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026, including the July 2026 primary preprint. The displayed bound uses the maximum live population, while the source also develops finer bounds that omit items never deleted. This card fixes one algorithm and one total-cost target.

context_blocks.text: A decrease-key call changes an item that is already present. It may execute only a few pointer operations immediately, yet the structural disorder it creates can make later deletions more expensive. Its amortized cost measures this delayed effect. Counting only the instructions inside the decrease-key procedure would miss the question entirely.

The pure pairing heap simplifies deletion by pairing neighboring roots once and then attaching all survivors beneath the smallest survivor. It does not maintain a rank or balance invariant. The desired estimate asks whether this sparse restructuring still prevents expensive configurations from being recreated too often.

The operation budgets must be considered together. A sorting sequence already forces substantial comparison work when many minima are deleted, so the logarithmic delete-min allowance is intentional. The unresolved issue is how much additional work to attribute to key decreases while keeping insertions and melds cheap. Using the maximum live population N makes that accounting explicit for a whole finite sequence.

Other self-adjusting heaps already attain the desired decrease-key order. This makes the remaining gap an informative algorithm-analysis problem: is the simpler rule equally efficient, or does its exact restructuring lose something asymptotically? A bound for slim or smooth heaps does not answer this question about pure pairing heaps.

cards.title: Constant-factor approximation of the smallest grammar
cards.formal: Do there exist an absolute constant C and a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, for every explicit nonempty string s, outputs an acyclic context-free grammar generating exactly s whose size is at most $C g^*(s)$? There is one production per nonterminal, one designated start nonterminal, and every right-hand side is a nonempty string of terminals and nonterminals. The dependency graph on nonterminals must be acyclic. Grammar size is the sum of all right-hand-side lengths, and $g^*(s)$ is the minimum such size. The alphabet is part of the input, encoded by integer symbols in {1,...,|s|}.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove existence of one polynomial-time algorithm with some fixed approximation constant valid for all strings, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A hardness theorem conditional on P != NP should be reported with that assumption. Exact optimization and ratios tending to one are stronger targets than the constant-factor question.
cards.definitions: Expanding a nonterminal means repeatedly replacing it by its unique right-hand side. Acyclicity guarantees termination, and the start expansion must equal the input string with no extra strings generated. Each terminal or nonterminal occurrence on a right-hand side contributes one unit to size. Runtime is measured in the ordinary binary encoding of the explicit input, not the compressed output length. Constant C cannot depend on the alphabet size, string length, or optimal grammar size. Arbitrarily long right-hand sides are permitted; the size convention is not just the number of productions.
cards.why: This is a fundamental compression-versus-optimization question: can an efficient procedure recover a representation within a fixed factor of the best hierarchical description? It also supplies a benchmark for compressed-data algorithms, whose costs often depend on grammar size rather than on the original string length.

progress.text: Charikar and coauthors give an O(1+log(|s|/g*(s))) approximation and rule out approximation ratios below 8569/8568 unless P = NP.
Casel and coauthors establish hardness over fixed alphabets of size at least 17 and retain constant-factor approximation as Open Problem 2. The hardness result does not rule out every constant.

cards.status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026 using the primary approximation and fixed-alphabet papers, with a search for later results. No general constant-factor algorithm was located. Recent assembly-index work uses additional size conventions and is not treated as resolving this proposition.

context_blocks.text: A grammar can share repeated pieces of a string and then share larger pieces assembled from them. For example, a sequence of doubling rules represents an exponentially long run using only a linear number of rules. This makes grammar size a useful concrete measure of repetitive structure, with a finite optimum that can in principle be found by exhaustive search.

The problem is to choose the shared pieces. Two useful repeated substrings may overlap, and a locally attractive substitution can prevent a better organization at a larger scale. A method that compresses some families extremely well can therefore still have an unbounded ratio to the best grammar on other families. The proposed guarantee must cover every input, not only average compression performance.

Known approximation guarantees depend logarithmically on the ratio between the explicit string length and its optimal grammar size. Hardness rules out sufficiently accurate approximation under P != NP, but this does not exclude a coarser universal constant. The space between these two conclusions is the question on this card.

The size measure is essential. Counting productions, binary concatenations, or all right-hand-side symbols gives related but different optimization problems. Stating the measure explicitly also avoids confusing exact binary-alphabet hardness questions with the unrestricted constant-factor approximation target.

cards.title: Constant-factor approximation for Santa Claus
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: Is there a universal constant C≥1 and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm that allocates indivisible items with arbitrary nonnegative additive agent-specific values so that, with probability at least 2/3, every agent receives total value at least OPT/C, where OPT is the largest achievable minimum agent value?
cards.definitions: An input consists of n≥1 agents, m≥1 items and an explicit n×m matrix (v_ij) of nonnegative rational values, encoded by binary numerators and positive binary denominators. Agent i values a bundle S⊆[m] at v_i(S)=Σ_{j∈S}v_ij. An allocation is a tuple of pairwise disjoint bundles (S_1,…,S_n); unallocated items are permitted. Its value is F(S_1,…,S_n)=min_{i∈[n]}v_i(S_i), and OPT is the maximum of F over all allocations. Let L be the total input bit length. There must be one algorithm, one C independent of n,m and all numerical values, and one polynomial P such that the algorithm always outputs a feasible allocation within P(L) bit operations, for every random tape, and Pr[F≥OPT/C]≥2/3 on every input. The probability refers only to the algorithm’s independent internal random bits and requires the guarantee for all agents simultaneously. A deterministic algorithm is allowed as a special case. Zero values and OPT=0 are allowed, and no positive lower bound on OPT is supplied. The input values are used as given: one may not rescale each agent separately without changing the optimization problem. No identical-valuation, restricted-assignment, bounded-number-of-agents, bounded-number-of-values or bounded-item-degree assumption is imposed. All values are available to a centralized algorithm; incentives, payments and valuation oracles are not part of this problem.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct a polynomial-time algorithm achieving the stated guarantee for some fixed C, or prove that no such algorithm exists. Hardness results conditional on a complexity assumption must identify that assumption, including the distinction between deterministic and randomized algorithms. A factor depending on the number of items or agents, a quasi-polynomial-time constant approximation, an estimate without an allocation, or an expected-value guarantee separately for each agent does not meet the target.
cards.why: The central unresolved max-min allocation question: can all agents be protected to within a constant factor when indivisible resources have arbitrary heterogeneous additive values?

importance.reason: A major approximation barrier in fair allocation and scheduling, linked by reductions to beating two for unrelated makespan and by relaxation gaps to the limits of fractional methods.

cards.status_note: The SODA 2024 reduction paper and SODA 2025 submodular paper explicitly retain the general additive constant-approximation question. Later checked constant guarantees concern restricted assignment or identical valuations, not arbitrary additive matrices. No general resolution found through 11 September 2026. Randomization and simultaneous success for all agents are explicit in this formulation.

context_blocks.text: The objective protects the least satisfied participant. Suppose two agents value each of two items at one. Allocating one item to each gives minimum value one, whereas giving both items to either agent gives minimum value zero. A lottery that gives both items to a uniformly chosen agent gives each agent expected value one, but its minimum value is always zero. This illustrates why the guarantee must concern the quality of one simultaneous allocation.

Even additive values allow substantial heterogeneity: an item can be extremely valuable to one agent, moderately valuable to another, and worthless to a third. Maximizing total welfare would assign each item to an agent valuing it most, independently of the other items. Maximizing minimum welfare couples those decisions because every agent needs adequate value from resources that cannot be reused. The valuations are inputs to the optimization problem, without strategic reporting constraints.

The name Santa Claus is used differently across papers. Some reserve it for restricted assignment, where each item j has a single intrinsic value w_j and v_ij is either w_j or zero. This card uses the broader max-min allocation problem with arbitrary entries. The difference is decisive: constant-factor algorithms are known for restricted assignment, while the general constant-factor question remains open.

Chakrabarty, Chuzhoy and Khanna give an approximation within m^ε for every fixed ε>0, where m is the number of items in this card’s notation. Their approximation–time tradeoff also yields a polylogarithmic factor in quasi-polynomial time. Choosing a smaller fixed ε improves the approximation exponent but increases the polynomial running-time exponent. Letting ε depend on m to try to force a constant factor does not preserve the known polynomial-time guarantee.

Their work also highlights a limitation of a standard configuration relaxation. For a target T, a configuration for agent i is a bundle worth at least T; fractional variables select configurations while respecting item capacities in aggregate. Integral feasible configurations would give every agent enough value. In the general setting, however, the relaxation can overestimate the integral optimum by a factor of order √n. The algorithm uses the relaxation recursively on transformed instances, instead of relying on a constant-loss rounding of its original optimum.

Restricted assignment has stronger structure. Haxell and Szabó’s 2025 work improves its configuration-LP integrality-gap bound from 3.808 to 3.534 using topological criteria for independent transversals. This is a bound on the distance between fractional and integral optima in the restricted model. It does not assert a 3.534 algorithm for the arbitrary-value matrix, and an existence argument for a good integral solution must be distinguished from an efficient way to construct it.

There is a striking link with minimizing makespan on unrelated machines. Bamas, Lindermayr, Megow, Rohwedder and Schlöter show that a (2−1/α)-approximation for unrelated makespan, for fixed α≥2, would yield an (α+δ)-approximation for general Santa Claus for every fixed δ>0. Thus any fixed improvement below two in that scheduling problem would answer this question positively. Their general implication goes in this direction; equivalence is established for a specified two-value case.

Bamas, Morell and Rohwedder’s SODA 2025 result extends the m^ε and quasi-polynomial polylogarithmic guarantees to arbitrary monotone submodular valuations. It uses a recursively structured LP with exponentially many variables and constraints. This broadens the class of preferences that can be handled, while retaining a growing approximation factor even on the additive instances considered here.

More recent constant guarantees also require attention to their input promise. Boehmer’s April 2026 paper obtains value at least 0.4OPT for identical monotone submodular valuations. Identical preferences are a substantial restriction, even though submodularity is more general than additivity. The outstanding question concerns unrestricted disagreement about item values. Settling it would clarify whether balancing heterogeneous indivisible resources admits a constant loss at polynomial computational cost.

cards.title: Randomized truthful unrelated-machine scheduling
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors as m→∞, the function R(m): the infimum worst-case expected-makespan approximation ratio achievable by truthful-in-expectation mechanisms with monetary payments for m unrelated machines and an arbitrary number of indivisible jobs. The infimum ranges over all mechanisms, without a computational or communication restriction. In particular, is R(m)=Θ(1)?
cards.definitions: There are m≥2 machines and n≥1 jobs. Machine i privately knows a vector t_i∈R_{≥0}^n; processing a set S costs it Σ_{j∈S}t_{ij}. Every entry is finite. A direct-revelation mechanism maps reported vectors b=(b₁,…,b_m) to a distribution over assignments σ:{1,…,n}→{1,…,m} and payments to the machines. Jobs are indivisible and every job is assigned exactly once. Let x_{ij}(b)=Pr[σ(j)=i] and let p_i(b) be the finite expected payment to i. Risk-neutral utility is payment minus true processing cost. Truthfulness in expectation means that for every i, true t_i, alternative report b_i and fixed reports b_{−i}, p_i(t_i,b_{−i})−Σ_j t_{ij}x_{ij}(t_i,b_{−i})≥p_i(b_i,b_{−i})−Σ_j t_{ij}x_{ij}(b_i,b_{−i}). This is a dominant-strategy condition against arbitrary fixed reports, without a prior on types. The makespan is C(σ,t)=max_i Σ_{j:σ(j)=i}t_{ij}, and OPT(t)=min_σ C(σ,t). For each m, consider a family M=(M_{m,n})_{n≥1} satisfying this incentive condition for every n and report profile. Its ratio is sup_{n,t:OPT(t)>0} E[C(M_{m,n}(t),t)]/OPT(t), and it must also have expected makespan zero when OPT(t)=0. R(m) is the infimum of those ratios. Random assignments may be correlated across jobs. No budget balance, bound on transfers, individual-rationality constraint, anonymity, task independence or efficient representation is imposed. Since only expected utilities matter, payments can equivalently be deterministic amounts p_i(b).
cards.answer_criterion: Give an explicit asymptotic scale f(m) and universal constants a,b>0 such that a f(m)≤R(m)≤b f(m) for all sufficiently large m, with matching incentive-theoretic lower bounds and mechanisms achieving the upper scale. A constant-factor mechanism for all numbers of machines and jobs would settle the target as Θ(1). Showing only that R(m) is unbounded would rule out that possibility but would not determine the requested asymptotic order without matching bounds. Restrictions on the mechanism class or input distributions must not be silently added.
cards.why: Determine the asymptotic efficiency loss caused solely by truthful multidimensional incentives when randomization and payments are fully available.

importance.reason: The central randomized counterpart of the resolved Nisan–Ronen conjecture, with a constant-versus-linear gap independent of computational restrictions.

cards.status_note: The Nisan–Ronen proof, now published in JACM in February 2026, resolves only deterministic truthful mechanisms. Its randomized discussion records 2−1/m and (m+5)/2 bounds. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no matching unrestricted randomized bounds; results for task-independent mechanisms, fractional objectives, Bayesian types or no-payment models do not resolve this formulation.

context_blocks.text: A machine has a reason to exaggerate how long jobs take: receiving fewer jobs reduces its work. Payments are intended to counteract that incentive while keeping the overall schedule short. The private information is a whole vector, since a machine may be fast on one job and slow on another. A single speed parameter would describe a different and substantially more structured scheduling model.

The optimization objective creates the difficulty. Minimizing total processing cost can be implemented truthfully by a VCG mechanism, which assigns each job to a cheapest machine. But total cost and makespan differ. The largest load is at most the total cost, while the total cost of an optimal makespan schedule is at most m times its makespan. Thus this familiar truthful rule gives an m-approximation. Without incentive constraints and with unlimited computation, one could simply choose an optimal assignment.

Christodoulou, Koutsoupias and Kovács prove that the factor m is unavoidable for deterministic truthful mechanisms, resolving the Nisan–Ronen conjecture. Their result appeared as a 2023 preprint and in the Journal of the ACM in February 2026. It is an unconditional incentive restriction, independent of computational hardness. The paper’s related-work discussion expressly separates the unresolved randomized setting from this deterministic conclusion.

There are two different ways to randomize truthfully. A universally truthful mechanism draws a deterministic truthful mechanism before seeing the reports. Truthfulness in expectation only asks that honest reporting maximize expected utility; individual random outcomes need not implement truthful rules on their own. Universal truthfulness implies the latter condition, but the definition in this card permits the larger class. Mu’alem and Schapira nevertheless prove a lower bound of 2−1/m even for that larger class.

Randomization already helps when there are two machines. Lu and Yu’s STACS 2008 mechanism is universally truthful and beats the deterministic factor two. Their later WINE 2008 paper gives a truthful-in-expectation mechanism with ratio (m+5)/2 for general m, using a fractional allocation and a suitable rounding procedure. The improvement is substantial in its leading constant, but the guarantee still grows linearly with the number of machines.

The WINE paper also proves a lower bound (m+1)/2 for its task-independent class. A mechanism in the full question may use all reported jobs together and correlate their assignments. Consequently, a lower bound that treats each job separately does not close the gap between the general constant lower bound and linear upper bound. Whether such global dependence can change the asymptotic answer is part of what makes this question interesting.

Expected makespan must be distinguished from the largest expected machine load. Consider m identical machines and m unit jobs. Assigning all jobs to one uniformly random machine gives expected load one on every machine, yet the makespan is always m. Assigning one job per machine has makespan one. Thus the same marginal load target can conceal a factor-m difference in the objective. A truthful fractional solution, or an argument that controls only marginal probabilities, needs a valid rounding analysis before it yields a guarantee for this card.

Fine numerical results for small cases illuminate mechanisms without settling the asymptotic problem. Kuryatnikova and Vera obtain almost matching bounds near 1.505996 for two machines and two jobs within a class of randomized monotone scale-free algorithms. Their paper does not identify the optimal ratio over every truthful-in-expectation mechanism, every job count and a growing number of machines. Both the input restriction and mechanism restriction matter when interpreting the result.

The final question is whether allowing random outcomes fundamentally reduces the price of truthful multidimensional cost reporting. A constant answer would permit useful load balancing despite unrestricted private processing times. A growing lower bound would show that even risk-neutral incentives and unrestricted payments cannot recover the efficiency available to a scheduler who knows the true costs. Matching bounds would quantify that loss as a function of system size.

cards.definitions: An election E consists of disjoint finite labeled sets V of n≥1 voters and C of m≥1 candidates, and a strict total order ≻_v on C for each v∈V. A consistent distance d is a pseudometric on V∪C: d(x,x)=0, d(x,y)=d(y,x)≥0, and d(x,z)≤d(x,y)+d(y,z) for all points, with a≻_v b implying d(v,a)≤d(v,b). Distinct named points may be colocated. Equal distances may be broken in any order in the reported ranking; the guarantee must hold for every consistent pair (E,d). The social cost SC_d(a)=Σ_v∈V d(v,a), and OPT_d=min_a∈C SC_d(a). A randomized ordinal rule f assigns each election E a lottery p=f(E), where p_a≥0 and Σ_a p_a=1. Its expected cost is Σ_a p_a SC_d(a). The lottery depends only on n,m and the full rankings, not on d or additional distance queries. It may use arbitrary real probabilities and unbounded computation. No anonymity, neutrality, incentive-compatibility or tournament-only restriction is imposed. Define Dist(f)=inf{D≥1: for every E and every consistent d, Σ_a f(E)_a SC_d(a)≤D·OPT_d}, taking inf∅=+∞. This inequality requires zero expected cost if OPT_d=0 and avoids dividing by zero. Set D*=inf_f Dist(f), over single rule families defined on all finite elections. The expectation is over the selected candidate, while elections and consistent metrics are worst-case choices. Replacing total cost by average cost divides both sides by n and gives the same distortion.
cards.answer_criterion: Give an exact real value or unambiguous exact expression for D* and prove equality: for every η>0 there must be a rule with universal distortion at most D*+η, and every rule must have distortion at least D*. An attained optimum with the matching lower bound also suffices. A numerical interval, a better upper bound alone, or an exact optimum within a restricted family of rules does not determine the unrestricted infimum.

context_blocks.title: Rankings hide the size of a preference
context_blocks.text: Two voters rank candidates a and b in opposite orders. Put a at 0 and b at 2 on a line. If voter 1 is at 0 and voter 2 at 1, the total costs of a and b are 1 and 3; if voter 1 is at 1 and voter 2 at 2, they are 3 and 1. Both arrangements fit the same rankings when a distance tie is resolved in the reported direction. The rule therefore has to make one choice of lottery that works in both possible geometries.

context_blocks.title: What randomization changes
context_blocks.text: If the lottery selects a with probability p, its distortion in these two examples is respectively 3−2p and 1+2p. At least one is at least 2. Choosing each candidate with probability one half reaches 2 for this pair of examples, whereas a deterministic choice suffers factor 3 in one of them. This demonstrates why randomization can help, but it is only a small lower-bound example. It does not establish the optimum over all elections.

context_blocks.title: The old value-2 conjecture is false
context_blocks.text: Charikar and Ramakrishnan construct larger elections giving a universal randomized lower bound of approximately 2.11264. Consequently, the target is to identify the optimal value above two, not prove the former conjecture. The lower bound concerns all randomized rules that use rankings, with no restriction to a particular named procedure or to pairwise summaries.

context_blocks.title: Recent upper bounds leave a smaller gap
context_blocks.text: Frank’s August 2026 preprint gives an upper bound of 2.5. Shah’s revision of 6 September improves this to 2.1441; its first version had the weaker value 2.3282. The 8 September preprint of Cai and coauthors states an upper bound of 2.13713, leaving a gap of less than 0.025 above the reported general lower bound. These are recent theorem claims with checked model matches; this review has not independently verified their proofs or numerical certificates. They still leave an interval rather than an exact value.

context_blocks.title: Restricted rules answer different questions
context_blocks.text: A weighted tournament records how many voters prefer a to b for each pair. It need not preserve all the information in their complete rankings. The optimal factor 3 for randomized tournament rules therefore does not bound what full-ranking rules can achieve. Similarly, Shah’s lower bound of 2.136 concerns his random-size-stable-lottery family; it is not a new universal lower bound for every rule. The scope of both upper and lower bounds matters when comparing them with D*.

context_blocks.title: Why this constant matters
context_blocks.text: D* measures how much total distance can be lost solely because a decision rule knows the order of preferences but not their intensities. It makes no assumption that voters behave strategically, and it does not require a truthful mechanism. The mathematical guarantee is robust across every metric consistent with the ballots, rather than an average over a chosen model of elections.

cards.definitions: An instance has n≥1 agents, m≥0 goods and an explicit table of values v_i,g=p_i,g/q_i,g, with integers p_i,g≥0 and q_i,g>0 in binary. Its bit length N includes n, m and the table. For S⊆[m], v_i(S)=∑_{g∈S}v_i,g. An allocation (A₁,…,A_n) partitions [m] into labeled bundles, possibly empty; its output lists one owner for each good. It is α-EFX if v_i(A_i)≥α·v_i(A_j∖{g}) for every pair i,j and every g∈A_j, including goods worth zero to i. All comparisons use i’s values. Empty A_j imposes no inequality; a singleton leaves value zero. Each fixed α in the set must have one finite, always-correct deterministic Turing machine and constants C,k with runtime at most C(N+1)^k on every instance. The machine, C and k may depend on α, but not on n, m or the valuations. α is a fixed guarantee, not an input; no polynomial dependence on an accuracy parameter is required. The supremum is the least upper bound of these achievable factors; attainment at the endpoint is not assumed. The set is nonempty since α=0 is trivial, and is bounded by 1 by definition.
cards.answer_criterion: Identify a real a∈[0,1] and prove that a=α_alg: achievable polynomial-time factors approach a arbitrarily closely from below, and no such algorithm guarantees any factor greater than a within [0,1]. An algorithm attaining a suffices for the first part but is not required. A conditional hardness result establishes only the corresponding conditional bound; a guarantee for one fixed number of agents does not establish the universal value.

context_blocks.title: How to read the approximation factor
context_blocks.text: Higher α means a stronger guarantee, with α=1 giving exact EFX. Suppose an agent values her own bundle at 4 and the goods of another bundle at 5 and 1. For this pair, the restrictive removal leaves value 5, so the inequality holds exactly when α≤4/5. This illustrates one pair’s test, not a lower bound for every allocation of an instance.

context_blocks.title: The known general guarantee

cards.definitions: An instance has n≥1 agents, m≥0 indivisible chores, and finite real costs c_i,g≥0. Agent i assigns a bundle S⊆[m] the additive cost c_i(S)=∑_{g∈S}c_i,g; lower cost is better. Let Π_n([m]) be the finite set of ordered partitions of [m] into n disjoint bundles, allowing empty bundles. Define μ_i=min_{(P₁,…,P_n)∈Π_n([m])} max_{1≤j≤n} c_i(P_j). All bundles in this minimum are evaluated using the same agent i’s costs. A complete allocation belongs to Π_n([m]): each chore has exactly one owner, with no splitting, disposal or payments. The allocation must satisfy all agents’ inequalities simultaneously, although their benchmark partitions can differ. The inequalities also apply when μ_i=0, without dividing by zero; in that case every chore has zero cost to i. There is no computation-time requirement or fixed bound on n or m. The smallest universal factor exists: for each finite instance its feasible factors form a closed upper interval, and the known universal upper bound makes the intersection of these intervals nonempty.
cards.answer_criterion: Identify a real a≥1 and prove both that every instance admits an allocation with c_i(A_i)≤aμ_i for all i, and that for every β with 1≤β<a there is an instance with no such β-allocation. The lower-bound instances may depend on β; one instance need not attain the worst universal ratio. A guarantee restricted to a fixed number of agents or a special class of costs does not determine α*.

context_blocks.title: The burden an agent can guarantee herself
context_blocks.text: Imagine partitioning all chores into n bundles before receiving the most costly bundle. The minimax share is the smallest worst burden that the agent can arrange. With two bundles and chore costs 4, 3 and 3, this benchmark is 6, achieved by {4} and {3,3}; the proportional cost is only 5. Indivisibility is why the two benchmarks differ.

context_blocks.title: Exact fairness can fail
context_blocks.text: Different agents can disagree about which chores are difficult, so their individually optimal partitions need not fit together. Feige, Sapir and Tauber give a three-agent, nine-chore example in which every agent’s minimax share is 43 but every complete allocation gives someone cost at least 44. Thus α*≥44/43>1.

context_blocks.title: The universal gap
context_blocks.text: Huang and Segal-Halevi prove that factor 13/11 always suffices. Together with the negative example, the checked bounds are 44/43≤α*≤13/11, approximately 1.0233 to 1.1818. The upper bound is an existence statement at the exact factor; finding such an allocation within a specified running time is an additional question.

context_blocks.title: What newer guarantees cover
context_blocks.text: The 2025 bin-packing paper gives a 15/13 multiplicative guarantee for personalized bivalued costs and improves a different, ordinal MMS benchmark in general. These do not replace the general multiplicative bound here. The September 2026 comparison-query preprint still uses 13/11 as the general frontier and studies how little preference information an algorithm needs.

context_blocks.title: Why this optimum matters
context_blocks.text: The factor measures the unavoidable loss caused by allocating whole burdens while respecting everyone’s own costs. A factor closer to 1 means that every agent can be kept closer to her personal benchmark. The easy/difficult-chores source gives exact fairness in special cost models, illustrating why those models must be distinguished from unrestricted additive costs.

cards.definitions: An instance consists of a finite set G of m≥0 indivisible goods and n agents. Each number vᵢg is a nonnegative real, and vᵢ(S)=∑g∈S vᵢg for S⊆G. Let Πd(G) denote all labeled partitions (P₁,…,Pd) of G into d pairwise disjoint bundles, allowing empty bundles. The 1-out-of-d maximin share of agent i is μᵢ(d)=maxP∈Πd(G) min1≤j≤d vᵢ(Pⱼ). The maximum is attained because the set of partitions is finite. A complete allocation A belongs to Πₙ(G): every good goes to exactly one agent, with no copies, payments, disposal or fractional goods. Define Dₙ as the set of positive integers d such that for every m and every valuation table there exists such an A with all n inequalities. Then d*(n)=min Dₙ. Increasing d weakens each benchmark. Known universal upper bounds make Dₙ nonempty, so this minimum is attained. The quantifiers are ∀n, choose d*(n), then ∀instances, ∃allocation; d may not depend on the number or values of the goods. This is an existence extremum, with no computation-time or preference-query restriction.
cards.answer_criterion: Give the exact function d*(n) for all positive integers n, with a universal existence proof at the proposed value and a matching impossibility proof for every smaller positive denominator. By monotonicity, when d*(n)>1 a counterexample at d*(n)−1 suffices for the latter part. An improved upper bound, an asymptotic leading constant, or a result permitting additional copies does not determine the requested exact function.

context_blocks.title: Relax the number of benchmark bundles
context_blocks.text: An agent imagines dividing all goods and then receiving her least valuable bundle. Ordinary MMS uses n bundles, one per real agent. Using a larger imaginary number d lowers the required share, while the actual allocation still has n recipients. The question is how little this benchmark must be weakened to make it universally achievable.

context_blocks.title: A small example
context_blocks.text: If an agent values each of six goods at 1, her 1-out-of-2 share is 3 and her 1-out-of-3 share is 2. Those numbers describe her personal benchmarks, not how many agents must actually receive goods. Different agents can value the same goods differently, so their best benchmark partitions need not coincide.

context_blocks.title: What ordinal means here
context_blocks.text: The fairness comparison is determined by each agent’s ranking of complete bundles. It is preserved if that ranking stays the same. Knowing only an ordering of individual goods does not generally determine the ordering of their sums. Thus this question does not assume an algorithm receives only individual-item rankings.

context_blocks.title: The known denominator bounds
context_blocks.text: For n≥2 the checked results give d*(n)≤min{2n−2, ⌊3n/2⌋, 4⌈n/3⌉}; retaining the minimum handles rounding for small n. The last bound comes from the 2024 result. Trivially d*(1)=1 and d*(n)≥n: with only d<n goods valued at 1 by everyone, a 1-out-of-d guarantee would require a good for every agent. The exact universal denominator remains undetermined.

context_blocks.title: Why the exact threshold matters
context_blocks.text: An exact answer would identify how much competition an indivisible-resource fairness benchmark must tolerate before everyone can be protected. Recent work combines ordinal shares with envy guarantees in restricted preference classes. Those additional guarantees are useful, but they do not settle the unrestricted denominator function asked for here.

The allocation itself still distributes the goods among n actual agents.

Known bounds allow roughly four benchmark bundles for every three agents, with separate rounding improvements for smaller n.

cards.definitions: For agent i, each good g has a nonnegative real value vᵢg and every bundle B⊆G has value vᵢ(B)=∑g∈B vᵢg; the empty bundle has value zero. A complete allocation partitions all goods into n labeled, disjoint bundles, possibly empty. Each good goes to exactly one agent. The displayed condition is envy-freeness up to any k goods, abbreviated EFkX: each comparison uses the potentially envious agent i’s values on both sides. The removed set S is hypothetical and is chosen universally, not chosen by the allocation algorithm to make the inequality easier. Actual goods are not removed or discarded. If |Aⱼ|≤k, the comparison is automatically satisfied because its right side is zero; this agrees with treating the source’s k-item condition as vacuous for shorter bundles. Zero-valued goods count as goods and may belong to S. The constant k is chosen before the instance and is independent of n, the number of goods and all values. This is exact existence; it imposes no efficiency requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that at least one universal constant k satisfies the stated existence claim, or prove its negation: for every integer k≥1 there is a finite additive goods instance such that every complete allocation violates at least one of its required inequalities. A counterexample for one k, or an allocation with a multiplicative factor below 1, does not resolve this quantifier structure.

context_blocks.title: How much envy can indivisibility explain?
context_blocks.text: One indivisible valuable item can prevent exact envy-freeness. EFkX allows a bounded number of items in the envied bundle to account for that discrepancy. It requires envy to disappear even after deleting the least helpful k items from the envious agent’s perspective. The question is whether some fixed allowance works for arbitrarily many agents.

context_blocks.title: Any removal versus a favorable removal
context_blocks.text: Suppose an agent values her own bundle at 5 and another bundle’s three goods at 6, 1 and 1. Removing its 6-valued good eliminates her envy, but removing either 1-valued good leaves value 7, so the pair fails EF1X. It also fails EF2X: removing the two 1-valued goods leaves value 6. This illustrates why an existential choice of removed goods is a different, weaker condition.

context_blocks.title: The connection to EFX
context_blocks.text: For k=1 this is the usual any-item EFX condition, including zero-valued items. A universal EFX existence theorem would answer this question positively. This card permits any fixed k, so it asks for a weaker universal guarantee. Choosing k separately for each instance, for example as its total number of goods, would make the property vacuous and is excluded.

context_blocks.title: Exact results for a fixed number of agents
context_blocks.text: The AAAI 2025 result establishes EF2X for four agents, in a valuation class that includes additive goods. That is a concrete exact existence theorem. It fixes the number of agents and therefore does not supply the universal constant-k guarantee for unrestricted n.

context_blocks.title: The 2026 approximation result
context_blocks.text: The May 2026 preprint gives (k+1)/(k+2)-EFkX allocations for every fixed k≥2 and any number of agents. This relaxes the inequality to vᵢ(Aᵢ)≥αvᵢ(Aⱼ∖S), where α<1. Although α approaches 1 as k grows, no finite k in that theorem attains exact fairness. Its negative graph-orientation results additionally restrict who may receive a good.

cards.title: Permanent versus determinant
cards.formal: Over the complex numbers, is the sequence dc_C(permₙ) unbounded by every polynomial in n? Explicitly, for every C>0 and integer k≥1, must there be n≥1 such that dc_C(permₙ)>C(n+1)^k?
cards.definitions: The polynomial permₙ(X)=Σ_{σ∈Sₙ}∏_{i=1}ⁿx_{i,σ(i)} has n² algebraically independent commuting variables and degree n; Sₙ is the set of permutations of {1,…,n}. Its determinantal complexity dc_C(permₙ) is the smallest positive integer m for which there exist constant complex m×m matrices A₀ and Aᵢⱼ satisfying the exact polynomial identity permₙ(X)=det(A₀+Σ_{i,j=1}ⁿxᵢⱼAᵢⱼ). Thus every matrix entry is an arbitrary affine-linear form in all input variables. The representation may depend on n and use arbitrary complex constants without a bit-length or constructibility restriction. The resource is matrix dimension m. No symmetry, sparsity, multilinearity of intermediate expressions, regularity, or read-once restriction is imposed. Equality is in C[X], for every complex substitution, not only on 0/1 inputs. Border complexity, which permits a limit of representations, is a separate measure. Characteristic two is excluded by fixing C: in that characteristic the permanent equals the determinant. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A central concrete target in algebraic complexity: determine whether one canonical efficiently computable polynomial can simulate a canonical algebraic counting polynomial at polynomial cost. Its formulation invites tools from algebraic geometry and representation theory while retaining a precise computational meaning.

importance.reason: The principal permanent-versus-determinant lower-bound problem, connecting algebraic computation, branching programs, geometry, and symmetry.

progress.text: Valiant establishes the foundational algebraic simulation framework: formulas and branching programs have small determinantal representations, and the permanent is complete for VNP.
Mignon and Ressayre prove dc_C(permₙ)≥n²/2 using Hessian ranks at zeros. This remains a polynomial lower bound.

Grenet gives a 2ⁿ−1-dimensional representation; Landsberg and Ressayre prove exponential optimality when specified symmetries must be respected. Their unrestricted-versus-equivariant comparison is left open.
Kumar and Volk survey the permanent bounds and develop a new singular-locus method for a different explicit polynomial, a diagonal power sum. That theorem does not raise the permanent lower bound.
The algebraic cost of Boolean summation distinguishes permanent and determinant under a local fixed-additive-size simulation requirement, leaving general polynomial-size representations open.
Bogart and Valero’s journal paper studies generalized permanents and continues to state the superpolynomial ordinary-permanent problem as open.

cards.status_note: Open in the cited foundational and recent papers; checked through 10 September 2026. This card fixes exact unrestricted representations over C. Symmetric, equivariant, real-field, border, and other-polynomial bounds are not substituted for this model.

context_blocks.text: The permanent and determinant sum the same products indexed by permutations; the determinant attaches a permutation sign. Those signs enable cancellations behind efficient determinant computation. A determinantal representation asks whether a larger matrix with carefully chosen affine entries can reproduce the unsigned sum exactly. Merely showing that changing signs in the original n×n matrix fails leaves almost all permitted representations untouched.

The model is nonuniform and algebraic. It asks about the existence of a family of polynomial-size representations even if finding their complex coefficients is computationally difficult. Determinants characterize polynomial-size algebraic branching programs up to polynomial overhead, whereas unrestricted arithmetic circuits define the potentially larger class VP. The requested lower bound separates the permanent from the branching-program model; it should not be identified without qualification with a separation from all of VP.

The unrestricted complex-field lower bound is still quadratic in the original matrix dimension: Mignon and Ressayre prove dc_C(permₙ)≥n²/2. Their argument compares the rank of the matrix of second partial derivatives, the Hessian, at carefully chosen zeros of the two polynomials. Because the permanent has n² input variables, this is only linear in its number of variables, despite being quadratic in n.

There is also an explicit exponential upper bound, dc_C(permₙ)≤2ⁿ−1, due to Grenet. Landsberg and Ressayre prove that this construction is optimal under particular equivariance requirements involving permutations and diagonal rescaling. Removing those requirements is essential: the question allows a representation to break every visible symmetry of the polynomial. Whether symmetry can be imposed with only polynomial overhead is itself another open problem.

Progress can reveal structural differences without giving an unrestricted lower bound. Orzel, Srinivasan, Tavenas, and Yehudayoff show that a local Boolean-summation operation can be absorbed into a permanent by a fixed additive increase in dimension, whereas the analogous uniform fixed-additive-cost property fails for determinants. Their FSTTCS 2025 result explains a step in the VNP-completeness construction; it does not exclude a different, global polynomial-size determinant representation.

Bogart and Valero extend upper- and lower-bound techniques to two generalized permanent families. Their 2026 journal version still identifies the Mignon–Ressayre estimate as the best known characteristic-zero bound for the ordinary permanent for n≥5. This provides a recent status check while illustrating how sensitive the geometric lower-bound method is to the polynomial being studied.

cards.title: Shub–Smale τ-conjecture
cards.formal: Does there exist an absolute constant C≥1 such that, for every nonzero polynomial f∈Z[x], the number z_Z(f) of distinct integer roots satisfies z_Z(f)≤(1+τ(f))^C, where τ(f) is its minimum number of addition, subtraction, and multiplication operations starting only from 1 and x?
cards.definitions: A straight-line program begins with registers containing 1 and the indeterminate x. Each subsequent register contains u+v, u−v, or u·v for two previously available registers; the two operands may be equal. Previously computed registers may be reused without restriction. A designated register must equal f as a formal polynomial over the integers. The cost is the number of arithmetic operations, and τ(f) is the minimum over all such programs. A zero-operation program may output 1 or x. No arbitrary integer constants are supplied: for example 2 must be built as 1+1, and all operations constructing other constants count. Division, comparisons, branching, and exponentiation as a primitive are forbidden. Multiplication counts even when both operands are constants; no bound is placed on intermediate degree or coefficient bit length. This is arithmetic operation count, not bit running time or formula size. Define z_Z(f)=|{a∈Z:f(a)=0}|; repeated roots are counted once. The zero polynomial is excluded. The same universal C must work for all f, regardless of degree, coefficients, or root magnitudes.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove a polynomial bound with one absolute exponent C, or prove that no such exponent exists. A negative answer must yield polynomials violating every candidate polynomial exponent—for example, a family whose integer-root counts grow faster than every fixed power of their exhibited program lengths. One polynomial violating a proposed small exponent, or exponentially many real or complex roots, is insufficient. No uniform efficient procedure for finding the roots is requested.
cards.why: A precise number-theoretic route to major arithmetic circuit and algebraic machine lower bounds. It probes whether sharing intermediate computations can create many independent integer zeros cheaply, linking computational compression with arithmetic geometry and proof complexity.

importance.reason: A central arithmetic complexity conjecture with a very elementary statement and strong consequences for algebraic P versus NP and constant-free circuit lower bounds.

progress.text: Shub and Smale relate integer-root complexity to the intractability of complex polynomial feasibility and the separation P_C≠NP_C.
Rojas gives the fixed-prime digit reduction and exp(O(s log(s+1))) rational-root bounds in the different additive-complexity parameter. Neither proves a polynomial root bound in τ.
Alekseev, Grigoriev, Hirsch, and Tzameret publish conditional Ideal Proof System lower bounds from the τ-conjecture for a binary-value variant over rational functions.

Santibañez-Leal’s version 0.03 reports an exact census through eight operations in a convention with free −1,0,1. This finite computational claim is not independently reproduced here and gives no asymptotic resolution.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The universal integer-root bound remains unresolved in the sources reviewed. The August 2026 census is explicitly a finite computational claim, not a resolution. Full operation count, distinct integer roots, and the exclusion of the zero polynomial are fixed.

context_blocks.text: A short arithmetic program can represent an enormous polynomial. After s squarings, x^(2^s) has exponential degree although its computation has only s operations. Degree therefore gives only the elementary bound z_Z(f)≤2^τ(f). The conjecture says that distinct integer roots are much harder to pack into such a compressed representation than degree alone suggests. Multiplicity cannot replace distinctness: the same repeated-squaring example already has a root of exponential multiplicity.

The restriction to integer roots is substantive. Iterating q_0(x)=x and q_(j+1)(x)=q_j(x)^2−2 uses only a constant number of new operations per stage and gives 2^j distinct real roots for j≥1. Indeed q_j(2 cos θ)=2 cos(2^j θ), so the roots can be written down through distinct cosine values. Thus the unrestricted statement with real roots in place of integer roots is false. Conjectures about real roots of particular sparse sums of products impose additional circuit restrictions.

Shub and Smale connect a polynomial integer-root bound to P_C≠NP_C in the Blum–Shub–Smale model, where exact complex arithmetic has unit cost and branching tests equality. This explains why an apparently elementary univariate question belongs among fundamental complexity problems. The conclusion concerns computation over complex numbers; it must not be silently identified with a proof of Boolean P≠NP.

Rojas develops a p-adic approach, including a reduction showing that a polynomial bound only for integer roots congruent to 1 modulo one fixed prime would already imply the full conjecture. He also bounds rational roots by exp(O(s log(s+1))) in terms of additive complexity s, which charges additions and subtractions while allowing powers and multiplicative structure more freely. This is useful when additive complexity is small; it is not a polynomial bound in the full operation count τ.

The conjecture has consequences beyond the original machine model. Alekseev, Grigoriev, Hirsch, and Tzameret recall its implication for separating the constant-free algebraic classes VP^0 and VNP^0, and use it to obtain conditional lower bounds for a variant of the binary value principle in the Ideal Proof System over rational functions. These implications do not establish the conjecture, and their non-Boolean instances do not directly yield Frege lower bounds.

An August 2026 preprint reports exhaustive enumeration through eight operations, using the convention that −1, 0, and 1 are all free. Such a fixed change of constants can be simulated with constant extra cost in the model here, but exact small-length records depend on the convention. The computation is finite experimental evidence and has not been reproduced for this card; it cannot settle the existence of a universal exponent.

cards.title: Word problem for one-relation monoids
cards.formal: Is there a single algorithm that, given a finite alphabet A and four finite words u,v,s,t∈A*, always halts and decides whether s and t represent the same element of the monoid presented by ⟨A | u=v⟩?
cards.definitions: A* consists of all finite strings over A, including the empty word ε, with concatenation as multiplication and ε as identity. The presentation ⟨A | u=v⟩ denotes A*/≡, where ≡ is the least equivalence relation containing u≡v that is compatible with concatenation on both sides. Equivalently, s≡t exactly when some finite sequence s=w_0,w_1,…,w_k=t exists in which each adjacent pair is xu y,xv y in either order for some x,y∈A*. The fixed words u and v are literal strings, not variables that can be substituted by arbitrary words. Empty sides are permitted: replacing ε means inserting the other side at a gap in the current string. The alphabet and all four words form a finite explicit input; one may encode A as {1,…,a} and its letters as integers. The requested algorithm is one deterministic Turing machine for all presentations and all word pairs, with no oracle and no unbounded advice. There is no polynomial-time or other prescribed resource bound, but termination is required on both equal and unequal pairs. This is an ordinary monoid presentation. No inverse operation, cancellation law, group axiom or commutativity assumption is present. The presentation itself varies with the input: the card asks for uniform decidability, not merely a separate non-effectively selected procedure for each fixed presentation.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct an always-terminating uniform decision procedure with a correctness proof, or prove that the language of positive presentation-and-word-pair instances is undecidable. One explicit fixed one-relation monoid with undecidable word problem would suffice for a negative answer, but is stronger than is logically required to refute uniform decidability. Enumeration that halts only on equal words, or a procedure whose termination on unequal words is unproved, is insufficient. An exponential derivation-length lower bound is compatible with decidability.
cards.why: A foundational decidability boundary for rewriting: can reachability under one literal reversible string rule already escape every terminating uniform algorithm?

importance.reason: One of the central minimal-presentation decision problems, connecting string rewriting, algebraic normal forms, computability and reductions between monoids, inverse monoids and groups.

progress.text: Magnus solves the one-relator group word problem; later work solves major ordinary-monoid special cases, without providing a general procedure.
Nyberg-Brodda surveys the unresolved problem, reduction methods, special cases and gaps in earlier claimed arguments.
The survey’s corrigendum fixes historical attributions and technical wording, including nontermination versus literal looping of Adian’s procedure.
Nyberg-Brodda gives monadic one-relation monoids with exponential Dehn functions but decidable word problems, separating short derivations from decidability.
Gray–Reilly prove undecidability for certain two-generator one-relator inverse monoids; their introduction explicitly leaves the ordinary-monoid question open.

cards.status_note: The August 2026 primary paper explicitly retains the ordinary one-relation-monoid word problem as open. Its inverse-monoid undecidability theorem does not resolve this ordinary presentation problem. Checked through 11 September 2026. The inherited input includes the presentation, so the card explicitly targets uniform decidability and distinguishes it from the per-presentation quantifier.

context_blocks.text: This is a minimal string-transformation problem. There is only one reversible replacement rule, and it can be applied inside any surrounding context. Starting with a word, repeated replacements can generate many others. Equality asks whether the target lies in this reachability set. The alphabet symbols themselves have no hidden arithmetic meaning; any complicated computation would have to emerge from overlaps and repeated applications of this one rule.

Positive answers are always semidecidable. Enumerate all finite replacement sequences from s and stop if t appears. Every individual stage has finitely many choices, even when one side of the relation is empty. The missing ingredient is an effective stopping argument for negative instances. Seeing no derivation within a long search does not establish inequality when intermediate words may continue to grow.

Length-preserving relations illustrate an easy case. If |u|=|v|, every reachable word has length |s|, so exhaustive search takes place in a finite graph. Unequal input lengths immediately imply inequality. When the relation changes length, that finite-state argument disappears. The question permits enormous running times, so even an impractical computable bound on the needed search would be a meaningful resolution.

Simply orienting a rule toward shorter words need not produce unique normal forms. For the relation baba=aba, the word bababa can shorten through ababa to aaba, or directly to baaba. Neither aaba nor baaba contains baba, so both are irreducible under the shortening rule, although they are equal in the presented monoid. This example shows why termination of one chosen reduction strategy is different from a complete equality test.

The surrounding algebra offers major positive results. Magnus proved decidability for one-relator groups in 1932. For ordinary monoids, classical work handles important cases such as a single relation equating a word to the identity, and presentations satisfying appropriate cycle-free conditions. Group algorithms cannot simply be applied to every monoid presentation: adjoining inverses may identify additional words, so equality in a related group can lose information.

The historical source needs its correction. Nyberg-Brodda’s survey traces the string-rewriting background to Thue, while its 2022 corrigendum identifies Novikov’s 1957 question as the earliest explicit formulation known to the author. The correction also replaces an informal claim that Adian’s procedure may loop with the more precise statement that it may fail to terminate. An infinite computation need not repeat a previously seen state.

There is concrete evidence that short relations can require very long equality proofs. Nyberg-Brodda constructs the family ⟨a,b | baa(ba)^N=a⟩ for N≥2 with at least exponential Dehn function. Here the Dehn function measures the maximum, over equal word pairs of bounded total input length, of the minimum number of relation applications needed to connect them. Nevertheless, the same paper proves that every monoid in this family has decidable word problem.

Gray and Reilly’s August 2026 paper proves the existence of a two-generator one-relator inverse monoid with undecidable word problem. Inverse monoid presentations are interpreted in a different algebraic theory that includes a generalized inverse operation and its identities. One displayed relation in that theory is not one ordinary string relation in the present sense. The paper’s introduction explicitly retains the ordinary-monoid problem and the relevant reduced-relator inverse-monoid case as open.

The inverse-monoid connection is still useful: positive decidability results for the appropriate intermediate class would imply positive results for ordinary one-relation monoids. A negative result in a broader intermediate class need not transfer backwards through that implication. The fundamental goal remains an exact boundary for algorithmic equality under extremely small presentations, with consequences for rewriting systems, normal forms and the ways finite algebraic syntax can encode unbounded computation.

cards.title: Conjugacy problem for one-relator groups
cards.formal: Is there a total algorithm which, on input a finite one-relator group presentation G=⟨x₁,…,x_k | r=1⟩ and two words u,v, decides whether some word w satisfies w⁻¹uw=v in G?
cards.definitions: The input consists of an integer k≥1 and three explicitly written finite words r,u,v over the letters x₁,…,x_k and their formal inverses. The group is the quotient of the free group F(x₁,…,x_k) by the normal subgroup generated by r. The relator may be empty, in which case G is free. Equality in the displayed equation is equality in this quotient, rather than literal equality of strings. A conjugating word w may have any finite length. The algorithm is a single deterministic Turing machine that must halt with the correct yes/no answer for every valid input; the presentation is part of the input. No polynomial-time or other specified resource bound is imposed. This is the uniform decision formulation; a separate algorithm for each fixed group, without an effective way to obtain it from a presentation, is not by itself sufficient.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct a uniform terminating decision procedure for all such presentations and pairs of words, or prove that this input language is undecidable. A one-relator group with an undecidable fixed-group conjugacy problem would suffice for a negative answer. A result only for torsion groups, a decision procedure for word equality, or undecidability of a different equation or membership problem does not settle this question.
cards.why: A central decision problem at the boundary between decidable symbolic equality and existential reasoning in finitely presented algebraic structures.

importance.reason: One of Dehn’s classical algorithmic problems, still unresolved in a basic class defined by a single relation; it tests how far decidability survives beyond word equality.

progress.text: Magnus establishes decidability of the word problem for one-relator groups. This does not decide conjugacy.
Newman proves decidability of the conjugacy problem for all one-relator groups with torsion.
Minasyan–Zalesskii prove hereditary conjugacy separability for one-relator groups with torsion.
Linton–Nyberg-Brodda’s comprehensive survey records the general conjugacy problem as open and describes why the word-problem induction does not automatically extend.
Gray–Levine obtain undecidability results for related Diophantine problems, including subgroup-constrained equations; these do not settle unrestricted conjugacy.
Nyberg-Brodda proves undecidability of unrestricted Diophantine problems in one-relator groups while explicitly retaining conjugacy as an open question.
Gray–Reilly obtain two-generator inverse-monoid word and group prefix-membership undecidability, which are distinct from this group conjugacy question.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The general conjugacy problem remains open in the checked primary literature. This card fixes the uniform presentation-input formulation. The 2026 undecidability results cited concern different equation, membership or inverse-monoid problems.

context_blocks.text: A finite presentation describes a group through generators and identities. Here there is just one defining identity, but it can be reused inside arbitrarily long products. The conjugacy question asks whether two elements become equal after a change of reference element: u and v are equivalent when v=w⁻¹uw. It is one of Dehn’s classical decision problems. The 2025 survey explicitly identifies the general one-relator conjugacy problem as unresolved.

Conjugacy is already different from equality in a free group. The words ab and ba are conjugate, since a⁻¹(ab)a=ba, although they represent different free-group elements. At the opposite extreme, the identity element is conjugate only to itself. Consequently, a conjugacy algorithm also decides whether an input word represents the identity, by setting v to the empty word. The reverse implication is the difficult part.

Magnus’s 1932 theorem supplies a uniform algorithm for word equality in one-relator groups. Its inductive approach, clarified through the Magnus–Moldavanskii hierarchy, decomposes presentations into simpler group constructions. The corresponding transfer of conjugacy algorithms is much more delicate: the survey gives examples of HNN extensions and amalgams with undecidable conjugacy even though the relevant word problems are decidable. These examples explain a barrier to extending the proof; they are not one-relator counterexamples.

The known word algorithm does at least give a positive semidecision procedure for the present question. Enumerate all finite words w and test whether w⁻¹uwv⁻¹ represents the identity. If u and v are conjugate, a witness eventually appears. If they are not, this search continues forever. A complete decision procedure must also provide a way to terminate on every negative input.

Equivalently, one could give a computable uniform bound on the length of a shortest necessary conjugator as a function of the input length. Such a bound permits a finite search. Conversely, a decision procedure permits computing a bound: enumerate the finitely many inputs of bounded encoding length, identify the positive ones, and search for one witness for each. This observation concerns computability, without claiming that a useful or small bound follows.

The torsion case has been solved for decades. Newman’s 1968 thesis proves decidability of conjugacy for one-relator groups with torsion, including an extended conjugacy problem relative to specified subgroups. Standard presentations for this class have relator R^m with m≥2 and R not a proper power. The spelling theorem controls the possible cancellations strongly enough to support effective arguments. A solution for this class leaves the general torsion-free case to address.

A later structural theorem gives another source of negative certificates in the torsion case. Minasyan–Zalesskii prove that one-relator groups with torsion are hereditarily conjugacy separable: nonconjugate elements in every finite-index subgroup remain nonconjugate in some finite quotient of that subgroup. In particular, for the original group, a finite quotient can witness a negative conjugacy answer.

To see the algorithmic significance, enumerate finite multiplication tables and assignments of the presentation’s generators that satisfy its relator. Each assignment defines a homomorphism to a finite group, where conjugacy can be checked exhaustively. In a conjugacy-separable group, this search eventually finds a separating image for every nonconjugate pair. Run it alongside the search for a conjugator. The argument requires the separation property; finite images alone are not a general-purpose certificate system.

Recent developments illustrate why the exact decision problem matters. Gray–Levine prove undecidability of Diophantine problems in several classes close to one-relator groups, and also obtain undecidability with a fixed subgroup constraint in a one-relator group. General systems of equations, or restrictions on where variables may range, are more expressive than the single unrestricted conjugacy equation on this card. Undecidability for those tasks does not imply undecidability here.

Nyberg-Brodda’s August 3, 2026 preprint goes further: it proves that the unrestricted Diophantine problem is undecidable in certain one-relator Baumslag–Gersten groups. Its introduction still explicitly identifies general one-relator conjugacy as open. Undecidability for arbitrary systems of equations therefore cannot be substituted for undecidability of the special single conjugacy equation.

Gray–Reilly’s August 2026 preprint constructs two-generator one-relator inverse monoids with undecidable word problem. It also constructs a two-generator one-relator group with an undecidable prefix membership problem. Inverse monoids are a different algebraic structure, while prefix membership asks about a particular submonoid of the group. Neither result contradicts Magnus’s word algorithm or supplies a conjugacy counterexample.

The significance is a sharp computability boundary inside an extremely economical symbolic formalism. One defining group relation is sufficient to create complicated infinite behavior, yet ordinary equality remains decidable. Settling conjugacy would determine whether this additional existential search can always be controlled. A very slow total algorithm would answer the card; an efficient algorithm for a broad but restricted subclass would be progress without completing it.

cards.title: Isomorphism problem for one-relator groups
cards.formal: Is there a total algorithm which, given any two finite one-relator group presentations G=⟨x₁,…,x_k | r=1⟩ and H=⟨y₁,…,y_ℓ | s=1⟩, decides whether G and H are isomorphic as abstract groups?
cards.definitions: The input consists of integers k,ℓ≥1 and explicitly written finite words r and s in the respective generators and formal inverses. The groups are the free groups on these generators modulo the normal closures of r and s. An empty relator is permitted and presents a free group. An isomorphism is a bijective homomorphism of the resulting abstract groups; it need not carry a listed generator to a listed generator, preserve the spelling of a relator, or come from an automorphism of a free group on the given generators. The numbers of displayed generators may differ. The sought procedure is one deterministic Turing machine which halts and answers correctly on every valid pair of presentations. No polynomial-time, elementary-time or other quantitative runtime bound is imposed. There is no promise of torsion, hyperbolicity, nontrivial center, genericity or a supplied geometric decomposition.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a uniform terminating decision procedure for all such pairs, or prove that the isomorphism language on these one-relator presentations is undecidable. A procedure that halts only for isomorphic pairs, or one correct only on a specified subclass or almost all random presentations, is insufficient. Undecidability for arbitrary finite presentations, systems of equations or other algebraic structures must be connected to this exact input class by a valid reduction to count as a negative solution.
cards.why: One of the central decision problems for finitely presented groups, testing whether a single defining relation permits effective recognition of abstract algebraic structure.

importance.reason: A classical unresolved computability boundary with deep connections to geometric group theory, effective classification and the limitations of presentation-based invariants.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No uniform algorithm or undecidability theorem for isomorphism of arbitrary one-relator group presentations was found in the checked sources. The 2026 generic algorithms and Diophantine undecidability result do not settle this all-input isomorphism question.

context_blocks.text: A group presentation is a finite description of an often infinite algebraic object. The same group can have quite different descriptions: for example, ⟨a,b | b=a²⟩ and ⟨x | empty relator⟩ both describe an infinite cyclic group. The question is whether one defining relation leaves enough structure to recognize abstract equality of group types algorithmically, even when the supplied generators and words look unrelated.

This is the third of Dehn’s classical decision problems. Word equality compares elements within one fixed presentation; conjugacy asks for a particular kind of equivalence between elements; isomorphism compares the entire groups. Linton and Nyberg-Brodda’s survey records the general one-relator isomorphism problem as open, despite broad positive results for subclasses.

The known uniform word algorithm gives a useful positive semidecision procedure. Enumerate possible word images u₁,…,u_k for the generators of G in H and v₁,…,v_ℓ for the generators of H in G. Check that the images satisfy each defining relation and that the two compositions fix every generator. Every check is a finite collection of word-equality tests. If mutual inverse homomorphisms exist, their finite descriptions eventually appear.

The missing part is termination on nonisomorphic inputs. Searching longer for generator images cannot certify that none exist. Equivalently, an effective bound on the lengths of some pair of mutually inverse generator-image tuples, depending only on the input length, would permit a finite search. Conversely, a total isomorphism algorithm would allow such a computable bound to be assembled by checking the finitely many inputs of bounded length and finding witnesses for the positive cases.

Easily computable invariants can reject some pairs. Abelianization, for example, takes the exponent sums of the relator and gives a finitely generated abelian quotient whose isomorphism type can be computed by integer linear algebra. But it is incomplete: the free group on two generators and ℤ² have the same abelianization, whereas one is nonabelian and the other is abelian. The free group is represented here using the allowed empty relator, and ℤ² by the commutator relation.

Another tempting simplification is to ask whether an automorphism of the free group carries one relator to the other, allowing inversion. Whitehead’s algorithm handles the corresponding orbit question. The survey explains that this sufficient condition is not necessary for isomorphism of the quotient groups: the Magnus conjecture asserting such a converse was disproved, and some groups have infinitely many inequivalent one-relator descriptions.

Hyperbolic groups form a large positive case. Dahmani and Guirardel solve isomorphism uniformly for all hyperbolic groups, including those with torsion. Their result also handles peripheral structures and automorphism computations, reflecting how geometric decompositions can organize otherwise unbounded searches. It is a decision theorem, not merely a heuristic for finding likely isomorphisms.

All one-relator groups with torsion are hyperbolic, so this theorem covers that entire subclass. The survey also records decidability for one-relator groups with nontrivial center and other structured families. General torsion-free one-relator groups remain beyond these combined results. Even elementary examples such as ℤ² show that the one-relator condition does not imply hyperbolicity.

Generic-case results explain why many randomly generated instances may nevertheless be tractable. Kapovich, Schupp and Shpilrain establish rigidity for large classes of random one-relator presentations: isomorphism can be forced by simple transformations of the displayed generators and relator. The exceptional inputs are small in a specified distributional sense, but an undecidable set of inputs could still lie among such exceptions.

Kapovich’s August 18, 2026 preprint extends a generic rigidity program to fixed numbers of generators and relators. It gives an algorithmically recognizable generic family and a quadratic-time generic isomorphism algorithm, using small-cancellation stability and rigidity under free-group automorphisms. Its one-relator specialization is relevant progress, while its guarantee remains a generic one rather than a terminating decision procedure for every input.

A different August 2026 result by Nyberg-Brodda proves undecidability of the Diophantine problem for certain one-relator Baumslag–Gersten groups. That task asks whether arbitrary systems of equations with coefficients have solutions. It demonstrates that one relation does not ensure decidability of every natural algebraic question. However, it supplies no automatic reduction to isomorphism between two one-relator presentations, so the present problem remains distinct.

A resolution would clarify whether this very economical presentation format has an effective classification in principle. The positive answer could be extremely slow and still be decisive. The negative answer would require encoding undecidable information into abstract group type while retaining a single defining relator—a much more specific construction than demonstrating difficult equations inside one fixed group.
